p.h: A Kalmyk prince with a wooden castle and a piano
p.g: Not every Kalmyk lord lived in a tent. Prince Sered-Dscheh, a colonel in the Russian army, had a large wooden castle on the left bank of the Volga, fortified with Russian-style outworks after the Napoleonic wars and furnished with mahogany, mirrors, clocks, a billiard table and a piano. Even so, he held court out on the steppe for part of the summer.
p.q: He resides on the left bank of the Volga, in a large wooden castle, thirty paces in front, which he fortified with Russian outworks when he returned from the French war … His castle is well fitted up in the interior, and contains a number of saloons, with mahogany furniture, lustres, mirrors, a billiard table, piano-forte, a number of clocks, &c.
p.s: Heinrich August Zwick (English edition, 1831)
p.tg: castle timber prince russian influence

p.h: The 'city of idols' and its tower of bells
p.g: Four days later the embassy passed another ruined city, Burgankoron ('idol city'), said to have been home only to the highest pagan priests. In the middle stood a tall octagonal stone tower hung with countless little bells that rang in the wind; inside were thousands of small Chinese idols, and holes in its sides were stuffed with writings in Mongol or 'East Tartar' left by passing lamas.
p.q: Mitten in der Stadt stund ein hoher steinerner achteckigter Thurm, daran unzehlich viel Glöcklein hingen, welche, wann sie vom Winde gerührt, ein überaus laut Gethön verursachten. in diesem Thurm war ein Eingang, worin wir viele 1000 kleine Chinesische Götzen, von vielerley Gestalt fanden. An der Seite des Thurms waren viel Löcher, diese lagen voll Schrifften, welche auf Mongalisch oder Ost-Tartarische Sprache geschrieben waren
p.s: Adam Brand (Neu-vermehrte Beschreibung, Lübeck 1734)
p.pl: Inner Mongolia (between the Nen River and the Great Wall)
p.t: In the middle of the city stood a tall octagonal stone tower on which hung countless little bells which, when stirred by the wind, made a very loud ringing. In this tower was an entrance, in which we found many thousands of small Chinese idols of many shapes. On the side of the tower were many holes, full of writings in the Mongol or East Tartar language
p.tg: pagoda bells idols mongol script ruins

p.h: Tash Rabat: a Moghul khan's stone caravanserai
p.g: Mirza Haidar credits Muhammad Khan, the khan who pushed the Moghuls into Islam, with building a rabat (travellers' lodge) of huge stones north of the Chadir Kul pass, with a tall entrance hall, a dome, cells and a mosque. He had seen it himself. The editor's note matches it with the ruin now called Tash Rabat and rejects a later claim that it was a converted Hindu temple, since no manuscript says so.
p.q: In the construction of this building he employed stones of great size, the like of which are only to be seen in the temples … of Kashmir. The Rabat contains an entrance hall 20 gaz in height. … The whole building is of stone, and over the doors there are huge solid blocks of stone, which I thought very wonderful, before I had seen the temples in Kashmir.
p.s: Mirza Haidar Dughlat (translated by E. Denison Ross, 1895)
p.c: The editor's note weighs the identification with the surviving ruin and rejects a later story that it was a converted Hindu temple.
p.tg: tash rabat stone caravanserai builder ruins

p.h: Brick houses on the plain, flat turf roofs in the mountains
p.g: Reuilly contrasts two kinds of settled Tatar house. Plains Tatars live in small Turkish-style houses of stone or, lacking stone, brick, and burn dried cakes of turf and dung. Mountain Tatars build on steep slopes with flat turf roofs, packed so closely that each row of roofs forms a street for the row above.
p.q: they inhabit small houses built after the Turkish fashion, and make use of bricks, when they cannot procure stone… their houses, which are built on the steep sides of the mountains, are roofed with turf in a flat manner… and they are built so close together, that these flat roofs seem like a street for the row of houses which stands next above them
p.s: Jean Reuilly (English translation, 1807)
p.tg: houses brick stone flat roofs mountain villages

p.h: A vanished Tatar village turned into an orchard
p.g: Holderness's own estate was a huge wild orchard made from the lands of a Tatar village of 1,700 people that had emptied after the Russian conquest. Only foundations, wells, the ruins of a Tatar bath and a mosque with its minaret remained. She is explicit that these ruins were a recent Tatar village, not something ancient or mysterious.
p.q: The village of Karagoss, at the time of the subjugation, contained 1700 inhabitants … Not a single house now remains within its circuit, though the foundations of them are to be found in every part … also the ruins of a Tatar bath, and a Tatar metchet, or mosque, the minaret of which, seen from all parts of the estate, embowered in wood, has a remarkably picturesque appearance
p.s: Mary Holderness
p.c: The population figure at the conquest is presumably what she was told.
p.tg: ruins mosque minaret bath depopulation

p.h: Chinese renegades build a walled town and palaces: 'bansheng' means 'house'
p.g: The history says that Chinese outlaws led by Qiu Fu and Zhao Quan, who had gone over to the Mongols, gathered fugitives at Fengzhou, built a walled town to protect themselves, put up palaces and broke irrigated fields. Their settlements were called bansheng, which the history explains as the Mongol word for 'house'. Zhao Quan also taught the Mongols siege warfare.
p.q: 時富等在敵招集亡命居豐州築城自衛搆宮殿墾水田號曰拜甡拜甡華言屋也趙全教敵益習功戰事
p.s: Zhang Tingyu and the Qing history office, History of the Ming (Siku quanshu Wenyuange copy, Kanseki Repository transcription)
p.pe: Tumed Mongols under Altan Khan; Chinese deserters
p.t: At that time Qiu Fu and the others, living among the enemy, gathered fugitives and settled at Fengzhou. They built a walled town to defend themselves, put up palaces and opened irrigated rice fields, calling them baisheng; baisheng in Chinese means 'house'. Zhao Quan taught the enemy to become more practised in attack and warfare.
p.c: The Siku copy writes 拜甡 for the usual 板升 (bansheng, from Mongolian baishing 'building'). 功 is a copyist's slip for 攻 ('attack').
p.tg: bansheng walled town palaces chinese builders altan khan

p.h: Birch-bark tents and reindeer in the Siberian forests
p.g: The note on the Kyrgyz lands of the upper Yenisei describes a forest people whose poor lived in tents of birch bark, loaded their goods on white deer (reindeer), drank deer milk, gathered pine nuts and roots, and hunted in winter on 'wooden horses' (skis). Nearby Qianzhou had a few thousand households of Mongols and Uighurs, and workshops of Chinese craftsmen moved there early in the dynasty.
p.q: 貧民無恒産者皆以樺皮作廬帳以白鹿負其行裝取鹿乳採松實及斸山丹芍藥等根為食冬月亦乗木馬出獵…居民數千家悉蒙古囘紇人有工匠數局葢國初所徙漢人也
p.s: Song Lian and the Ming history office, History of the Yuan (Siku quanshu Wenyuange copy, Kanseki Repository transcription)
p.pe: Kyrgyz and forest peoples of Qianzhou (Kem River)
p.t: The poor, who have no fixed property, all make their tents of birch bark and load their baggage on white deer. They take deer's milk, gather pine nuts and dig up the roots of mountain lilies and peonies for food. In winter they also ride 'wooden horses' (skis) to hunt... [In Qianzhou] the inhabitants, several thousand households, are all Mongols and Huihe (Uighurs); there are several workshops of craftsmen, who are Han Chinese moved there at the start of the dynasty.
p.c: Based on reports of the Yuan official Liu Haoli, sent there in 1270; the Siku copy re-spells the place names.
p.tg: birch bark tents reindeer skis siberia chinese craftsmen

p.h: A half-millionaire who still lives in a yurt
p.g: In an oval valley once held by a Tungus chief and later taken by Yakuts from the south, Wrangel found a thriving settlement: many yurts, some as big as Russian houses, two good churches with towers, and big herds of cattle and horses. The Yakut headman had paid for both churches and was said to be worth half a million roubles, yet he still lived in a yurt by an open hearth, drank kumis and ate horse-flesh.
p.q: Numerous Jurti, some approaching to the dimensions of Russian houses, two good churches with towers … owes much of its prosperity to the Jakutian Golowa or superintendent, who has built and endowed the two churches at his own expense. His fortune is said to amount to half a million of roubles, nevertheless he has in no respect altered his original national customs. He lives in a Jurte
p.s: Ferdinand von Wrangel (English translation by Mrs Sabine, 1840)
p.pl: Yakutsk region, between the Lena and the Aldan
p.c: The size of the headman's fortune is hearsay ('is said to').
p.tg: yurts churches wealth settlement

p.h: Cave homes at Inkerman, later reused by Tatars
p.g: Webster examined the rock-cut chambers and chapel at Inkerman, near Sevastopol. From the altar, carved cross and style he judged them medieval Christian dwellings, and he noticed rafter marks showing some were part built, with a few 'reinhabited, or reconstructed by the Tartars'. He credits the builders to Christians, not Tatars, and says the Tatars reused them.
p.q: Some seem to have been partly excavated and partly built, which is proved by the marks of the rafters in the rocks, as also by these being, in a few instances, reinhabited, or reconstructed by the Tartars … the inference is natural that these excavations were the dwellings of the Christians.
p.s: James Webster
p.pe: Medieval Christian cave-dwellers; later Crimean Tatars
p.c: His dating ('middle ages') is his own reasonable guess; the previous page blames damage on 'Mohammedan conquerors' without evidence.
p.tg: cave dwellings inkerman rock-cut reuse

p.h: Hundreds of fallen stone castles in Dauria
p.g: Travelling from Nerchinsk toward the Argun, Ides saw hundreds of old, half-fallen castles of rough stone scattered through the valleys. His Tungus guides said warriors built them long ago, when Mongols and 'Western Tartars' raided the old kingdom of Nieucheu (the Jurchen or Manchu country). Iron-bound wagon wheels and millstones had also been dug up, which Ides took as a sign that a settled people once farmed and worked there.
p.q: In several scattered places in the Valleys, I observed hundreds of old, and partly fallen Castles, built with Rock-stones, which, as the Tunguzians told me, were built by several Warriours long since, when the Mongalian and Western Tartars made joint incursions into this Kingdom of Nieucheu. … And it is not long since that Waggon Wheels bound with Iron, and large Milstones were found in this Country
p.s: Evert Ysbrants Ides (English translation, 1706)
p.pe: Tungus informants; Mongol and 'Western Tartar' raiders
p.c: Ides saw the ruins himself, but the story of who built them comes from his Tungus guides, and the idea that the Nieucheu people once lived there is his own guess.
p.tg: ruins stone castles builders dauria

p.h: Mud houses, felt tents, bricks from old ruins
p.g: Many Khivans, even the rich, lived in felt tents all year because they were used to nomad life. Houses were of cheap mud with a hole in the roof for smoke. The fine buildings were a few mosques, above all the turquoise-domed great mosque, and bridges were built of fired bricks taken from old ruins.
p.q: The houses are very bad and wretched, and a great portion of the people live in felt tents all the year round. Even the wealthy do this, although they possess houses, because they are so accustomed to a nomadic life. The houses are of mud … Bridges are numerous, and are constructed of the burnt bricks which they get from old ruins.
p.s: Nikolai Muraviev (translated by W. S. A. Lockhart, 1871)
p.pe: Uzbeks and other people of the Khiva khanate
p.tg: mud houses felt tents reused brick ruins khiva

p.h: Ablai-kit: a walled Buddhist monastery whose books reached Peter the Great
p.g: The chief ruins of the steppe, Levshin says, are those of Ablai-kit on the left bank of the Irtysh, a stone-walled enclosure about a verst long. Inside stood two buildings, one a Buddhist temple where statues, paintings of burkhans (Buddhas) and many manuscripts were still to be seen early in the 18th century. Leaves of those manuscripts were sent to Peter the Great in 1720 and on to the Paris Academy. This is the same town the envoy Baikov saw being built for Ablai taisha by craftsmen from China in 1655 (W171).
p.q: Внутри ограды были два зданія; одно служило Ламайскимъ капищемъ, и въ началѣ прошедшаго столѣтія еще видны въ немъ были статуи, живописныя изображенія бурхановъ, и многія письмена, изъ коихъ нѣкоторые листы въ 1720 году были доставлены Императору Петру Великому, а имъ посланы въ Парижскую Академію надписей и изящныхъ искусствъ.
p.s: Aleksei Levshin (1832)
p.w: built 1650s; leaves sent to Peter I in 1720; described 1832
p.t: Inside the enclosure there were two buildings; one served as a Lamaist temple, and at the beginning of the last century statues, painted images of burkhans and many writings could still be seen in it, some leaves of which were delivered in 1720 to the Emperor Peter the Great and sent by him to the Paris Academy of Inscriptions and Fine Arts.
p.c: Levshin compiles this from Müller, Pallas and others; he does not claim to have visited the site. The name 'Ablai-kit' (Ablai's monastery) itself records who built it.
p.tg: ablai-kit buddhist monastery stone wall manuscripts peter the great

p.h: Glazed tiles and mosaic on a khan's tomb
p.g: Pallas describes the finest building at the Selitrennoye ruins as a khan's family mausoleum with a prayer house above, its foundation walls two fathoms high. The brickwork was the most elegant he had seen among any Tartar ruins, set with glazed tiles in green, yellow, white and blue, with stucco flowers, shell-work and mosaic panels. He adds that whole cargoes of its bricks had been carried off to build Astrakhan.
p.q: In the whole brickwork, which consists of beautiful broad squares, disposed in the most regular manner, there is a degree of taste and elegance of which I have no where seen an instance among the ruins of the Tartars. The outside of the walls is not only embellished in all the interstices between the bricks with glazed earthen ornaments, of a green, yellow, white, and blue colour,
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas, quoting his own earlier Travels (vol. 3), in the English translation (1812 edition)
p.tg: mausoleum glazed tiles brick mosaic sarai

p.h: Winter houses shaped like cut-off pyramids
p.g: In winter the Yakuts moved into their jurti: cottages of thin boards shaped like a truncated pyramid and covered thickly with branches, grass and mud. The small windows were closed with plates of ice in winter and fish-skin or oiled paper in summer. The floor was beaten mud sunk a few feet into the ground, or boarded in richer homes, with an open hearth burning all winter. Wrangel thought these suited the climate better than Russian-style houses.
p.q: These are cottages formed of thin boards in the shape of a truncated pyramid, and covered thickly on the outside with branches, grass, and mud. A couple of small openings which admit a scanty light are closed in winter by plates of ice, and in summer by fish-membrane, or oiled paper. The floor is generally of beaten mud, and is sunk two or three feet below the ground
p.s: Ferdinand von Wrangel (English translation by Mrs Sabine, 1840)
p.tg: winter house timber mud ice windows

p.h: A marble mosque for Samarkand, and a builder dragged to death
p.g: Timur had seen a mosque of white marble in India and wanted one like it in Samarkand. Ibn Arabshah says he ordered solid marble to be quarried and put a man named Muhammad Jald in charge, who raised four minarets and outdid the master builders. When Timur came back from campaign and looked at the mosque, he had Muhammad Jald thrown on his face, his feet tied, and dragged until he was torn to pieces.
p.q: وان يقطع له احجار من المرمر الصلد وفوض امره الى رجل يقال له محمد جلد … فلما آب من سفرته وتفقد ما حدث في غيبته توجه الى الجامع لينظر اليه فبمجرد ما وقع نظره عليه امر بمحمد جلد فالقوه على وجهه وربطوا رجليه ولا زالوا يجرونه وعلى وجهه يسحبونه حتى بضعوه

p.c: A hostile anecdote about the building of Timur's great mosque in Samarkand; the cruelty may be exaggerated.

p.h: How a Kalmyk kibitka is put up
p.g: Camped in bitter cold above Astrakhan, Bruce's detachment was lent sixty kibitkas by the Kalmyk prince Dasan. He describes them closely: 24 feet across, folding lattice walls six feet high, a round wooden crown raised on lances with holes for the rafters, and a felt covering laid from the bottom up. He found them warmer and more weatherproof than a house.
p.q: they are all round, the sides being made of a kind of checkered wicker-work, and the cross sticks neatly jointed for folding together or extending … they raise with their lances a round board, three feet diameter, with a hole in the middle of it … the large hole serves for their chimney, the small holes receive the ends of so many strait rafters

p.h: Russian forts of timber beams filled with clay
p.g: Massa describes how Moscow secured Siberia: strongholds were built in the plain along the Ob from big beams cut in the nearby forests, then filled with clay, and garrisoned. p.q: First some castles were built, for which large beams were supplied from the neighbouring forests and then filled up with clay; then these strongholds were filled with soldiers, while many people were sent thither daily, and in time, formed large communities composed of Poles, Tartars, Russians and other nations.
p.s: Isaac Massa's description of Siberia, as printed by Hessel Gerritsz in 1612 (English translation by F. J. Millard in the 1878 facsimile edition)

p.h: The Khan holds court in a felt tent
p.g: At his first audience Abbott found the ruler of Khiva not in a hall but in a plain black felt tent pitched inside his court, with a wood fire burning in the middle. Even a settled king with a brick citadel kept the nomad's tent as his reception room.

Before him a wood fire blazed up, sending its smoke and sparks through the sky-light of the tent. … The black tent of felt which he occupied, was of the usual dimensions, i. e. about 24 feet in diameter, and quite unadorned, its sole furniture being the carpet and cushions, on which he reclined.

p.h: Haloed figures: 'built by Christians'?
p.g: Looking at the carvings on the ruined tower, Ides saw kings seated cross-legged, crowned queens with folded hands, and attendants with rays around their heads 'as Saints are commonly painted'. From the haloes he concluded that Christians must have built the tower. Other panels showed warriors with pikes 'after the Chinese manner' and figures with 'hideous Diabolical Visages'. Seated, haloed, crowned figures with guardians are typical of Buddhist pagoda reliefs, so this is Ides's own guess, not a local tradition.
p.q: Others shew us several Figures seeming to represent Queens folding their Hands together, with their Servants on each side: The Queens having Crowns on their Heads, and the other being adorned with Rays or Lustres, as Saints are commonly painted, and also folding their Hands: all which hints that this Tower must needs be built by Christians.
p.s: Evert Ysbrants Ides (English translation, 1706)
p.c: The carvings are eyewitness; the Christian builders are Ides's inference from haloes.

p.h: The Porcelain Tower: said to be built by Chinese on a Tartar's orders
p.g: Nieuhof admired the nine-storey glazed Porcelain Tower of Nanjing and repeats what he was told: the Chinese built it at their own cost on the orders of a Tartar conqueror seven hundred years before, and the new Tartar conquerors chose to spare it. In fact the tower was built by the Ming Yongle emperor in the early 1400s, so the story he was told is wrong, but it shows buildings being linked to Tartar conquerors in popular memory.
p.q: This wonderful Pile (as they inform us) the Chineses built at their own charges, commanded by the insulting Conquerour the Tartar, to them a Pillar of Honour, to the Subdued of Obloquie, seven hundred years since, when in like manner, as lately, they over-ran all China
p.s: Johan Nieuhof (English translation by John Ogilby, 1669)
p.pe: Tartars (an earlier conquest, and the Manchus)
p.c: The dating and the Tartar command are hearsay and do not match the tower's known Ming date.

p.h: A Chinese monk lays out the Mongols' new capital (Shangdu)
p.g: Finding Holin (Karakorum) inconvenient, Möngke had a new capital chosen in Tartary. The task went to a learned Chinese Buddhist monk, Lieoupingtchong (Liu Bingzhong), who picked a site east of Huanzhou; a city, imperial palace, temples, lords' palaces and courts were built inside high thick walls, and it soon filled with Chinese and Tartars. Gaubil notes it was later called Changtou (Shangdu, the Xanadu of legend).
p.q: Il ordonna de choisir un lieu en Tartarie qui seroit désormais la capitale de ses Etats. Ce soin fut donné à un Bonze Chinois appellé Lieoupingtchong. … On y bâtit une grande ville, un palais pour l'Empereur, des temples, des palais pour les Seigneurs, & des tribunaux. On l'investit de hautes & épaisses murailles.
p.s: Antoine Gaubil, translating the Chinese annals
p.pe: Mongols (Möngke Khan); the Chinese monk Liu Bingzhong
p.t: He ordered a place in Tartary to be chosen that would henceforth be the capital of his states. This task was given to a Chinese monk named Lieoupingtchong. … A great city was built there, a palace for the Emperor, temples, palaces for the lords, and courts of justice. It was enclosed with high, thick walls.

p.h: A Russian husband who built houses for the Tartars
p.g: At the Mongol court Rubruck met Paquette, a woman from Metz captured in Hungary, who had married a young Russian. She told him her husband was expert in building, 'an art much valued and needed among the Tartars', and that a Parisian goldsmith was working at Karakorum. The Mongols' building work, in other words, was often done by captives from conquered lands.
p.q: ayant vn ieune mary de Russie, dont elle auoit trois beaux enfans, & son mary s'entendoit fort aux bastimens, qui est vn art bien estimé & requis entre les Tartares. Elle nous donna encor aduis qu'à Caracarum il y auoit vn Orfeure Parisien, nommé Guillaume Boucher

p.pe: Tartars (Mongols); Paquette of Metz and her Russian husband
p.t: having a young husband from Russia, by whom she had three fine children; and her husband was very skilled at building, which is an art much esteemed and in demand among the Tartars. She also told us that at Karakorum there was a Parisian goldsmith named Guillaume Boucher

p.h: Brick halls in Kalmyk country, built by craftsmen from China
p.g: Following the upper Irtysh through Kalmyk country, Spafarii notes its few buildings. The Kalmyk prince Ablai had built two halls of fired brick in a strong place among stone mountains, and the craftsmen had been sent to him from China, because Mongol and Kalmyk princes exchanged envoys and gifts with the Chinese emperor, 'since now a Kalmyk and Tatar race rules in China'. On the same page he mentions the Kontaisha's clay town with two brick halls where Kalmyk lamas lived.
p.q: А на той рѣчкѣ Аблай тайша сдѣлалъ 2 палаты изъ зженаго кирпичю въ крѣпкомъ мѣстѣ межъ горъ каменныхъ, а мастеры къ нему присланы были изъ Китайского государства, потому что Мугалскіе и Калмыцкіе тайши ссылаются часто съ Китайскимъ ханомъ и поминки емлютъ и даютъ для того, что нынѣ въ Китаехъ владѣетъ родъ Калмыцкой и Татарской.
p.s: Nikolai Spafarii (ed. Yu. V. Arsenyev, 1882)
p.pe: Kalmyks (the Oirat prince Ablai taisha); 'Tatars' here means the Manchu rulers of China
p.t: And on that stream Ablai taisha built 2 halls of fired brick in a strong place among stone mountains, and the craftsmen were sent to him from the Chinese state, because the Mongol and Kalmyk taishas often exchange envoys with the Chinese khan and take and give presents, since now a Kalmyk and Tatar race rules in China.
p.c: Not eyewitness: the editor says Spafarii took the upper Irtysh from the reports of the envoys Baikov (1654) and Seitkul Ablin. Historians link Ablai's buildings to the Ablai-kit monastery of the 1650s; the text does not use that name.

p.h: A Tartar house like a giant poultry basket
p.g: On his first night among the Nogais, de Tott is given a brand-new felt tent (oba) and inspects how it is made: a circular lattice wall, a dome open at the top, and a covering of camel-hair felt. It was like a large poultry basket, built in lattice work, and formed in a circular inclosure, over which was a dome, open at the top; a felt of camel's hair covered the whole on the outside, and the hole at the top, intended occasionally as a vent-hole for the smoke.

p.h: Ruined walls, 'the old home of the Khitans'
p.g: Crossing a level, well-watered and crowded land between two mountain ranges, Chang De saw many old ramparts and ruined walls. Asking about them, he was told they were the former home of the Khitans, meaning the Qara Khitai empire that ruled here before the Mongols. He reckoned the place nearly 15,000 li from Karakorum.
p.q: 二月二十四日過亦堵两山間土平民夥溝洫映帶多故壘壊垣問之盖契丹故居也計其地去和林萬五千里而近

p.h: Round houses of wands and felt, doors to the south
p.g: Polo describes the classic Mongol dwelling: a round frame of light, tightly bound wands covered with felt, carried from camp to camp, always pitched with the door facing south. Families also had felt-covered wagons, rainproof and drawn by oxen and camels, in which women and children travelled. Yule's note compares the Kirghiz yurts of his own day.
p.q: Their houses are circular, and are made of wands covered with felts. These are carried along with them whithersoever they go ; for the wands are so strongly bound together, as well as so well combined, that the frame can be made very light. Whenever they erect these huts the door is always to the south.
p.s: Marco Polo (translated by Henry Yule, 1871)
p.c: Yule notes the manuscripts differ on 'felts' (one reads 'ropes'); he chose felt as the right reading.

p.h: Houses of wood or unburnt brick, leaving no trace
p.g: Inside the ramparts of Isker Müller found no remains of houses, only uneven ground and some pits that might have been cellars. He concludes that any buildings must have been of wood in the Siberian Tatar manner, or of unburnt brick in the Bukharan way, since nothing of them survives, and notes that some pits were dug later by treasure seekers, not always in vain.
p.q: Wenn solches ist, so müssen sie nach Sibirisch-Tatarischer Art nur von Holze, oder nach Bucharischer Gewohnheit von ungebrannten Ziegeln, gebauet gewesen seyn, weil nichts davon mehr bemerket wird. An einigen Orten sind Gruben, welche zu Kellern gedienet haben können. Man sagt aber auch, daß einige Gruben in neuern Zeiten gemacht seyn, weil man daselbst Schätze gesuchet
p.s: Gerhard Friedrich Müller (Sammlung Russischer Geschichte, vol. 6, 1761-1762)
p.t: If so, they must have been built only of wood in the Siberian Tatar manner, or of unburnt bricks after the Bukharan custom, since nothing more is to be seen of them. In some places there are pits which may have served as cellars. But it is also said that some pits were made in recent times, because people searched for treasure there

p.h: Houses built on wheels and covered in white felt
p.g: Rubruck opens his description of the Tartars with their homes. The sleeping-houses sit on wheels, are made of interlaced wooden laths that rise to a smoke-hole like a chimney, and are covered with white felt smeared with lime, white earth or powdered bone so that they gleam. He stresses that the Tartars have no fixed dwelling and divide the steppe from the Danube eastward into seasonal pastures.
p.q: Les maisons où ils habitent pour dormir sont fondées sur des rouës … des pieces de bois entrelassées, & abboutissent en haut en vne ouuerture comme vne cheminée, & couurent cela de feutre blanc, qu'ils enduisent de chaulx ou terre
p.s: William of Rubruck (French translation by Pierre Bergeron, 1634)
p.t: The houses in which they sleep are set on wheels … [made of] interlaced pieces of wood, and they come together at the top in an opening like a chimney, and they cover this with white felt, which they coat with lime or earth

p.h: A tent palace on thirty-six poles and five hundred cords
p.g: Outside Samarkand Timur held his feasts in a vast camp. Clavijo measured the great pavilion by eye: square, three lances high, a hundred paces across, raised on twelve painted poles each as thick as a man's chest, with cart-wheel winches to lift them, porticoes on twenty-four more poles, and silk hangings inside. It shows that the tent tradition of the steppe survived as palace architecture beside Timur's brick buildings.
p.q: there was a great and lofty pavilion, which was like a tent, only square, and three lances high. It was a hundred paces broad, and had four corners, and the ceiling was round, like a vault. It was pitched against twelve poles, each as large round as a man, measured round the chest.
p.s: Ruy González de Clavijo (translated by Clements R. Markham, 1859)

p.h: Nothing left at Alba but bones and broken walls
p.g: After escaping as the Tartars withdrew, Roger and a companion walked for eight days through empty country, guided by the bell towers of churches, and reached the cathedral town of Alba (Alba Iulia in Transylvania). There they found only the bones and heads of the dead and the broken, undermined walls of churches and palaces, the stones still stained red. It is a rare eyewitness description of a town just ruined by the Mongols.
p.q: Tamdem vix octauo die a siluae recessu ad Albam venimus ciuitatem, in qua nihil potuit reperiri praeterquam ossa et capita occisorum, basilicarum et palatiorum muros diruptos et suffossos, quos nimia Christiani cruoris effusio macularat. Et licet terra innoxium sanguinem quem inebriata suxerat non monstraret, ostendebant se lapides adhuc cruore roseo purpurati
p.s: Master Roger (Rogerius), Carmen miserabile, in the 1885 Budapest edition (Chronica minora)
p.pe: Ruins left by the Mongol army
p.t: At last, hardly on the eighth day after leaving the forest, we came to the city of Alba, in which nothing could be found but the bones and heads of the slain, and the walls of churches and palaces broken and undermined, which the great outpouring of Christian blood had stained. And although the earth, drunk with the innocent blood it had soaked up, did not show it, the stones still showed themselves dyed rose red with gore

p.h: Brick houses and a painters' street under the 'Emperor of the Tartars'
p.g: Ramusio adds to his Marco Polo commentary what a Persian merchant, Hajji Muhammad ('Chaggi Memet'), told him in Venice about Campion (Ganzhou), a city of idol-worshippers subject to 'Daimir Can, great Emperor of the Tartars'. Its houses were built 'in our manner' of fired brick and stone, two or three storeys high, with painted ceilings, and one whole street was lived in only by painters. He also mentions temples like churches, colossal gilded statues and printing.
p.q: La città di Campion è habitata da popoli che sono idolatri: soggetta alla signoria de Daimir Can, grande Imperatore de Tartari … Le fabriche delle lor case son fatte al modo nostro di pietre cotte, & di pietre viue, con due & tre solari, quali sono soffittati & dipinti di pittura di varij & diuersi colori, & di figure: vi sono anco infiniti pittori: & vi è vna contrada doue non habita altri, che pittori.
p.s: Giovanni Battista Ramusio, Dichiaratione on Marco Polo, reporting the Persian merchant Hajji Muhammad
p.pe: 'Idolaters' of Campion, subjects of 'Daimir Can, great Emperor of the Tartars'
p.t: The city of Campion is inhabited by peoples who are idolaters, subject to the lordship of Daimir Can, great Emperor of the Tartars ... The buildings of their houses are made in our manner, of fired brick and of living stone, with two and three storeys, which are ceiled and painted with pictures of various and different colours and with figures; there are also countless painters, and there is a quarter where no one lives but painters.
p.c: Second-hand merchant's report. 'Daimir Can' is probably the Ming emperor ('Dai Ming Khan'), so here 'Tartars' is a loose label for the ruler of China.

p.h: A ruined brick city 'built by Tamerlane', quarried for Astrakhan
p.g: Sailing down the Volga, Bruce passed the ruins of a great city called Czarefgorod. He reports the local belief that Tamerlane built it, says its palace and walls were brick, and notes that the Russians had been carting the bricks away for years to build Astrakhan's walls, churches and monasteries. It was most likely one of the Golden Horde's Volga towns.
p.q: About forty miles from this, and at a small distance from the river-side, are to be seen the ruins of a great city, formerly called Czaresgorod, built, as is related, by Tamerlane : its palace and walls were all of brick, and have served the city of Astrachan with materials, these many years, for building their walls, churches, and monasteries.
p.s: Peter Henry Bruce (published 1782)
p.pl: Lower Volga between Kamyshin and Volgograd
p.pe: Golden Horde (credited by local tradition to Tamerlane)

p.h: Russian stoves, Tatar benches: a village house
p.g: Lodging in a large Tatar peasant house, Haxthausen found it split into a men's half and a women's half. He noticed it looked much like a Russian house and honestly admits he cannot tell who borrowed from whom. The rooms mixed Russian stoves, Tatar sleeping benches, a samovar, European chairs and a Black Forest clock, with 'God is great' written over the door.
p.q: This was divided into two parts ; the right half is the dwelling of the men (our host lived with four of his brothers), the left that of the women and children. It bore much resemblance to Russian arrangements : whether the Russians borrowed of the Tatars, or the latter of the former, cannot be determined. In the rooms the stoves were Russian, the sleeping-benches Tatar
p.s: August von Haxthausen (translated by Robert Farie, 1856)

p.h: A town of leather tents, with streets and markets

p.h: A hundred thousand huts, and no wood or stone
p.g: Describing the Horde under the kingmaker Edigü, Schiltberger says the people roam winter and summer with families and herds, and a hundred thousand huts go up whenever the khan camps. Elsewhere (p.50) he says Tartary stretches three months' journey with no wood or stones, only grass and shrubs.
p.q: The vassals in Tartary wander about in winter and summer, with their wives and children, and their cattle, and when the king encamps, there must be erected one hundred thousand huts.
p.s: Johann Schiltberger (translated by J. Buchan Telfer, 1879)
p.c: 'One hundred thousand' is a round, probably exaggerated figure.

p.h: A Tibetan king of Tartar descent in a four-storey castle
p.g: The Jesuit Johann Grueber crossed the 'sands of desert Tartary', the Kokonor lake and Tangut to Lhasa. As told to a Florentine visitor in 1665, the king descends from an ancient race of Tartars of Tangut and lives at Butala (the Potala), a castle on a high mountain built like a European house, four storeys of fine architecture. The same page reports the Grand Lama worshipped as a god and said to have risen from death seven times.
p.q: La ville capitale de ce royaume s'appelle Lassa; le Roy se nomme Teva, qui descend d'une race tres-ancienne des Tartares de Tangut. Il fait sa residence à Butala, chasteau basty sur une haute montagne à la façon des maisons d'Europe; il a quatre étages de fort bonne architecture.
p.s: Johann Grueber, as reported by an unnamed Florentine interviewer (generally identified as Lorenzo Magalotti), French translation in Thévenot, 1696
p.pe: Tibetans; the king, of the 'Tartars of Tangut'
p.t: The capital city of this kingdom is called Lassa; the King is named Teva, and descends from a very ancient race of the Tartars of Tangut. He lives at Butala, a castle built on a high mountain in the fashion of European houses; it has four storeys of very fine architecture.
p.c: Interview notes, translated; Grueber saw Lhasa, but the reporter wrote from conversation. 'Teva' is probably the Tibetan title Depa (the regent), not a personal name.

p.h: Ulugh Beg's three-storey observatory
p.g: Among the works of Timur's grandson Ulugh Beg, Babur singles out the observatory on the hill of Kohik: three storeys high, fitted with instruments, where the astronomical tables still in use in his day were made. He places it among the seven or eight observatories ever built, alongside Hulagu's at Maragha.
p.q: Another remarkable edifice is the observatory, erected on the skirts of the hill of Kohik, which is provided with an astronomical apparatus, and is three stories in height. By means of this observatory, Ulugh Beg Mirza composed the Zich-Korkani (or Korkani Astronomical Tables), which are followed at the present time, scarcely any other being used.
p.s: Babur (translated by John Leyden and William Erskine, 1826)

p.h: 'They have tents, you have castles and cities': a Mongol threat
p.g: Kuun quotes a letter from a Mongol commander to King Bela IV of Hungary, brought back by the Dominican Friar Julian. The Mongol calls the Cumans who fled into Hungary 'our slaves' and warns the king: the Cumans live without houses and move about with tents, so they might escape, but a king who lives in houses and has castles and cities cannot. It is a clear contemporary statement of the difference between steppe tents and settled towns, seen from the Mongol side.
p.q: Facilius enim est Cumanis evadere quam tibi, quia illi sine domibus cum tentoriis ambulantes possunt forsitan evadere. Tu autem in domibus habitans habes castra et civitates, quomodo effugies manus meas?
p.s: A Mongol commander's letter to King Bela IV (c.1237), as brought back by Friar Julian; quoted by Geza Kuun (1880)
p.t: For it is easier for the Cumans to escape than for you, because they, going about without houses, with tents, may perhaps escape. But you, living in houses, have castles and cities: how will you escape my hands?
p.c: The letter survives in Friar Julian's Latin report, so its wording is a translation; the original, Julian says, was in 'pagan letters and the Tartar tongue'.
p.n: Checked against the page image.

p.h: Ulu-Mehmed's new timber fortress, stronger than the old
p.g: After his 'ice town' at Belev melted in the sun, the exiled Golden Horde khan Ulu-Mehmed crossed the Volga and occupied empty Kazan, 'Sain's yurt'. The surviving Bulgars asked him to protect them, and he built a strong wooden town on a new site near the old Kazan that Russian armies had ruined. Settlers came from the Golden Horde, Astrakhan, Azov and Crimea. The builder, material and reason are all named.
p.q: Царь же вселися въ жилище ихъ и постави себѣ древяны градъ крѣпокъ, на новомъ мѣсте, крѣпчайше старого, недалече отъ старыя Казани разоренныя отъ Руския рати. И начаша збиратися ко царю мнози варвари отъ различныхъ странъ, ото Златыя Орды и отъ Асторохани, отъ Азуева и отъ Крыма
p.s: Anonymous author of the History of the Kazan Tsardom, PSRL vol. 19 (1903)
p.pe: Ulu-Mehmed, exiled khan of the Golden Horde, founder of the Kazan khanate
p.t: And the tsar settled in their dwelling place and built himself a strong wooden town, on a new site, stronger than the old one, not far from old Kazan, which had been ruined by the Russian army. p.h: Grave-robbers melt the gold of the old steppe graves
p.g: All along the Irtysh Gmelin saw very many graves, which he took for remains of former Kalmyk or Bukharan settlement, and nearly every one had been dug open. Local people treated them as a mine for 'grave silver': horse ornaments, big seals, bracelets, sometimes idols. The unopened ones near Ust-Kamenogorsk were ringed with upright field stones or slates and filled with stones and earth.
p.q: Allein diejenigen, die hier zu Lande die Gräber eröffnen, haben die Gewohnheit, daß sie zu ungemeinem Verlust der Historie das Gold und Silber gemeiniglich schmelzen, das Kupfer und Eisen aber wegwerfen.
p.s: Johann Georg Gmelin (German original, Göttingen, 1751)
p.pl: Upper Irtysh between Yamyshevo and Ust-Kamenogorsk, Kazakhstan
p.pe: Ancient graves, thought to be Kalmyk or Bukharan
p.t: But those who open the graves in this country have the habit, to the uncommon loss of history, of generally melting down the gold and silver and throwing away the copper and iron.
p.c: The attribution of the graves to Kalmyks or Bukharans is a guess; many such steppe graves are far older.

p.h: Stone ruins that an old Tatar called tombs of a people who left for China
p.g: Along the Uy frontier line Rychkov notes ruins of stone buildings, some still whole. An old Tatar of Iset province told Lieutenant-Colonel Rennenkampf, from his ancestors' tradition, that the peoples who once lived here had moved away to China, and that the standing buildings were nothing but cemeteries of their notable men. An early record of local explanations for steppe ruins.

p.h: 'Not so much as a single house' in all Mongolia
p.g: Staunton footnotes the embassy's entry into Mongol lands with John Bell's description of the Mongols. Bell says that in all Mongolia there was not a single house: everyone, even the prince and the high priest at Urga, lived in tents and moved with their herds. It is a clear eyewitness statement, from a Scot who crossed the region, that the Mongol heartland had no built settlements in his day.
p.q: It is very remarkable that in all the vast dominions of Mongalia, there is not so much as a single house to be seen. All the people, even the prince and high priest, live constantly in tents, and remove all their cattle from place to place as conveniency requires.
p.s: John Bell of Antermony, quoted in a footnote by the translator G. T. Staunton
p.c: These are Bell's words from his own journey, not Tulishen's.

p.h: Russian forts and towns built across 'Great Tartary'
p.g: Fontaney explains how the Muscovites had pushed from Moscow through Siberia along the Irtysh, Ob, Yenisei and Angara to the Selenga and the Amur ('Sangalien-oula' to the Tartars, the Black Dragon river to the Chinese), building forts and towns as they went. The nearest to China were Selenginsk, Nerchinsk and Albazin. In this corner of 'Tartary' the builders were Russians.
p.q: Les Moscovites ne se contenterent pas de faire ces découvertes; ils bâtirent de distance en distance des forts & des villes sur toutes ces rivieres, pour s'en assurer la possession. Les plus proches de la Chine étoient Selinga, Nipchou & Yacsa.
p.s: Jean de Fontaney, letter to Père de La Chaise (1703)
p.pe: Russians (Muscovites); Eastern Tartars, subjects of the Qing
p.t: The Muscovites were not content with making these discoveries; they built forts and towns at intervals on all these rivers to secure possession of them. The nearest to China were Selinga, Nipchou and Yacsa.

p.h: The Fountain of Tears inscription: 'never such a fountain'
p.g: Jesse copies the translated inscription on the Selsabil fountain in the palace vestibule (the famous 'Fountain of Tears'). It credits Khan Krym Giray with finding the spring and giving water to his people, and boasts that Damascus and Baghdad never saw its equal. He notes that the palace's rooms were small and the furniture mean and modern.
p.q: The town of Bagtché-Serai rejoices in the beneficent solicitude of the luminous Crim-Gheri-Khan: it was he, who with generous hand quenched the thirst of his countrymen … If there exists such another fountain, let it present itself. The towns of Scham and Bagdad have seen many things, but never such a fountain.
p.s: Inscription on the Selsabil fountain, in an English translation printed by Captain Jesse
p.c: Jesse does not say who translated the Ottoman Turkish inscription. 'Scham' is Damascus.

p.h: A Tatar village of ten houses and many felt tents
p.g: While his ship loaded salt, Chardin walked to a nearby Tatar settlement to buy food. He saw only ten or twelve houses and a little mosque, but round them many tents, round and square, and closed covered wagons that served as houses. The best tents were made of poles laid crosswise and covered with light felts, with an opening at the top for light and smoke, a felt door, and carpets on walls and floor.

p.s: Jean Chardin (English translation, London, 1691)

p.h: Gold in the old graves: 'from whom but the former Tatars?'
p.g: Arguing that the history of Chinggis Khan belongs to Siberian history, Müller points to the antiquities of southern Siberia: old entrenchments across the steppes, many memorial stones and statues, and graves from which gold and silver had been dug. He asks from whom such treasure could come but the former Tatars, to whom the riches of China, Persia, Russia, Poland, Bohemia and Hungary had fallen as plunder. On the next page he adds that the poorer old graves near Baikal show the earliest owners lived simply.
p.q: was für Kostbarkeiten an Gold und Silber hat man nicht aus den Gräbern hervorgeholet? von wem können dieselbe anders, als von den ehmahligen Tataren, herstammen, indem bekannt ist, daß alle Schätze von China, Persien, Rußland, Polen, Böhmen, Ungarn, ihnen zum Opfer werden müssen?
p.s: Gerhard Friedrich Müller (Sammlung Russischer Geschichte, vol. 6, 1761-1762)
p.pe: The 'former Tatars' (the Mongol empire of Chinggis Khan)
p.t: what treasures of gold and silver have not been brought out of the graves? From whom can they come but from the former Tatars, since it is known that all the treasures of China, Persia, Russia, Poland, Bohemia and Hungary had to fall to them as prey?
p.c: Müller's inference; modern archaeology dates many Siberian gold-bearing kurgans far earlier (Scythian and Hunnic periods).

p.h: The Xiongnu town that was never built
p.g: The Chinese annals tell how a Chinese defector at the Xiongnu court, Wei Lü, advised the young shanyu to dig wells, build a town and two-storey granaries, and give the grain to Chinese captives to keep. Hundreds of wells were dug and thousands of logs felled, but others argued that the Xiongnu could not defend towns and the grain would only fall to the Chinese, so the plan was dropped. A vivid example of steppe rulers weighing fixed buildings against mobility.
p.q: Вэй Люй подалъ Шаньюю совѣтъ выкопать колодцы, построить городъ и двухъ-этажные магазины для содержанія хлѣба, а храненіе хлѣба поручить Китайцамъ династіи Цинь. Тогда хотя и придутъ китайскія войска, ничего сдѣлать не могутъ. Уже выкопано было нѣсколько сотъ колодцевъ, срублено нѣсколько тысячъ бревенъ, какъ нѣкоторые представили, что Хунны не могутъ защищать городовъ
p.s: Chinese dynastic history (Han shu), translated by Iakinf Bichurin, 1851
p.pe: Xiongnu, with Chinese defector Wei Lü
p.t: Wei Lü advised the shanyu to dig wells, build a town and two-storey storehouses to keep grain, and to entrust the keeping of the grain to 'Qin Chinese'. Then, even if Chinese troops came, they could do nothing. Several hundred wells had already been dug and several thousand logs cut, when some pointed out that the Xiongnu cannot defend towns
p.c: Bichurin's footnote explains 'Qin Chinese' as descendants of Chinese who had fled to the Xiongnu.

p.h: Low roofs, minaret chimneys and a wooden harem
p.g: Seen from the garden, the Khans' palace was a low building, in parts only one storey, with white roofs and chimneys shaped like little minarets. The harem was a square building of three lofty rooms with verandas and small wooden-grated windows, behind a high wall. The palace of the Crimean Khans, in other words, was modest in scale.
p.q: This harem is a square building, with verandas, having only three rooms: these are large and lofty … Each room has a double range of small windows, with wooden gratings … The appearance of the exterior of the palace, as seen from the garden, is that of a low building, in some parts only one story. Its roof is white, and the chimnies appear like so many minarets
p.s: James Webster

p.h: Houses with fold-down wooden fronts
p.g: In Bakhchysarai's single long, narrow street the houses had no windows: the whole front was a set of wooden flaps that could be raised or lowered and used as counters. So every trade was on show, from a baker at his oven to a brewer of 'boussa' (boza, a fermented millet drink) and a tailor with his journeymen.

In one house you may see a baker at work … In the next you may overlook all the manipulations required in the preparation of the Turkish beverage entitled “boussa,”

p.h: Karakorum's mud wall and its Chinese artisans
p.g: Rubruck describes who lived in and built up Karakorum: a Muslim ('Saracen') quarter with the markets, and a quarter of Cathayans (northern Chinese), all artisans. The city is surrounded by a mud wall and has iiii gates.

p.h: A Tibetan temple in Tartary that looked European
p.g: Near the summer palace the party visited the 'Poo-ta-la', the great lama temple the emperor had built (today's Putuo Zongcheng temple, modelled on the Potala of Lhasa). Staunton found it unlike any Chinese building and oddly like a European front, eleven stories of windows high, with a golden chapel inside whose roof plates were said to be solid gold. He credits the building to the emperor himself.
p.q: the outside very much resembling the front of an European edifice. It was of great height, containing eleven rows of windows, implying as many stories, or ranges of apartments, one above another. … The square, or principal building of Poo-ta-la, includes a quadrangle, in the centre of which is the golden chapel, so termed from the materials in which it, apparently at least, abounds.
p.s: George Leonard Staunton
p.pe: Manchus and Mongols (Qing court); Tibetan Buddhist lamas
p.c: The 'European' look is Staunton's comparison; the page before says the temples round Zhe-hol 'had been erected by the Emperor'. The gold was 'said to be' solid.

p.h: The 'palaces' of Semipalatinsk were lama cells
p.g: The town of Semipalatinsk ('seven palaces') took its name from old ruins. Humboldt, who saw them, thought they were a Buddhist establishment like Ablai-kit, whose painted cells had housed lamas. He compares the little roadside shrines of the Volga Kalmyks near Sarepta: cages on tall poles holding an idol and a few religious books.
p.q: Il est probable que les Palates dont j'ai vu les ruines à Semipolatinsk, étaient un établissement tout semblable dont les cellules, jadis couvertes de peintures, servaient d'habitation à des lamas. Dans la steppe des Kalmuks du Wolga, voisine de Sarepta, colonie des frères Moraves, on trouve en plein champ des cages surmontées de poteaux élevés et renfermant, près d'une idole du culte bouddhistique, une petite collection de livres religieux.
p.s: Alexander von Humboldt (footnote)
p.t: It is probable that the Palaty whose ruins I saw at Semipalatinsk were a very similar establishment, whose cells, once covered with paintings, served as dwellings for lamas. In the steppe of the Volga Kalmyks, near Sarepta, the Moravian Brethren's colony, one finds out in the open fields cages topped by tall posts and containing, beside a Buddhist idol, a small collection of religious books.
p.c: Humboldt saw the Semipalatinsk ruins; his identification of them as a lama monastery is his inference.

p.g: In the same description Chardin is precise about materials: every house, bazaar, public building, mosque and bath in Caffa was built of earth. p.h: The Devil's Fort: an empty town of the old Bulgars on the Kama
p.g: The author describes an empty little town on the high bank of the Kama, which the Russians called the 'Devil's gorodishche'. A demon lived there, answering questions through soothsayers, and people of the Kazan land came to sacrifice; travellers on the river threw it some of their goods or risked drowning. He credits the ruin to the 'old Bulgars', whose sacrificial prayer-place it had been. Several manuscripts call it a 'small stone town'.

p.s: Anonymous author of the History of the Kazan Tsardom, PSRL vol. 19 (1903)
p.pe: Kazan Tatars, Cheremis and their soothsayers; the 'old Bulgars'
p.w: 1540s to 1551 (while the author lived in Kazan)
p.t: there is an empty little town standing on the high bank of the river Kama, which the Rus call the Devil's Fort, in which a demon lived, working illusions for many years; and it was a sacrificial prayer-place of the old Bulgars.

p.h: Log houses with windows of ice
p.g: The Vogul 'Tartars' lived in square log rooms like Russian peasant huts, with an open hearth instead of an oven. Once the fire burned down to coals, they sealed the smoke-hole with a sheet of ice, which kept the heat in and let daylight through. Wide benches around the walls served as seats by day and beds by night.
p.q: Their Dwellings are quadrangular wooden Rooms, like those of the Russian Peasants; only instead of Ovens they use Hearths, on which they burn Wood, and dress their Victuals. The Smoak-hole which is in the Roof, is covered with Ice, as soon as the Wood is burnt to a Coal, which keeps the warmth in the Room, and the light strikes through the bright and clear Ice.
p.s: Evert Ysbrants Ides (English translation, 1706)

p.h: A New Year banquet in a felt tent 14 metres wide
p.g: At the Mongol New Year (Tsagan Sar, 'White Month') about 300 nobles feasted in one enormous round felt kibitka, some 20 arshins (about 14 metres) across. The lattice walls were hung with blue cloth and a fire burned on an iron hearth in the middle. Tea, meat and vodka were served and musicians played fiddles, long flutes and a three-stringed instrument.

p.h: The 'pyramids' of Tartar kings on old maps
p.g: Strahlenberg describes the burial mounds of southern Siberia: some are earth heaps as high as houses, lying so thick that they look like a ridge of hills; others are ringed with rough or squared stones, and some are built entirely of stone. He explains that the 'pyramids' drawn on old European maps of Great Tartary, labelled 'Pyramidal Sepulchres of the Tartarian Kings', must mean these tombs, which are not really pyramids.
p.q: Some are only raised up of Earth, as high as Houses, … that, at a Distance, they appear like a Ridge of Hills. … In some Places these Tombs are entirely built of Stone. Hence we find in the ancient Maps of Tartary the Greater, a Number of Pyramids, with these Words, in Latin; viz. The Pyramidal Sepulchres of the Tartarian Kings,
p.s: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (English translation, 1738)
p.pl: Southern Siberia (Yenisei, Irtysh and Tobol steppes)
p.pe: ancient peoples of the Siberian steppe (Strahlenberg's 'Scythians')

p.h: The ruined Musalla of Herat, built by a Timurid king
p.g: North of Herat Conolly explored a 'pile of magnificent ruins', the Musalla, which he was told was built by a king of the house of Timur to receive the body of Imam Reza, then abandoned when the saint was buried at Mashhad. He describes a towering iwan, a court a hundred paces square decorated with mosaic of white quartz and coloured enamel tile, and domed halls. On the next page he counts the remains of twenty minarets.
p.q: A mile to the north of the city are the remains of what anciently was the wall of Heri, … is a pile of magnificent ruins, … the "Moosullah," or place of worship, built by a pious king of the house of Timour, to receive the remains of the Imaum Reza
p.s: Arthur Conolly (1834)
p.c: The reason given for its building is local tradition; historically the Musalla complex was built by Timurid rulers in the fifteenth century.

p.g: Travelling on with the Tartars, Pinto describes Lechune, 'head of the false religion of this heathendom, as Rome is among us', with a sumptuous temple holding the tombs of twenty-seven kings or emperors 'of this Tartar monarchy' in chapels lined with silver, and nearby a walled enclosure of 280 monasteries with 42,000 priests. It is a vivid and entirely unverifiable picture of Tartar monumental building.

p.h: 'Nogai' graves of heaped stone, with gold horse-trappings inside
p.g: Besides their own cemeteries, Levshin says, the Kazakh steppes hold many ancient graves that the Kazakhs attribute to the Nogais who once lived there. These stand out for their height and size, often being huge heaps of stones brought from far away, and sometimes contain gold and silver horse-harness ornaments and coins. The attribution is Kazakh tradition; archaeologists now date many such kurgans to far older peoples.
p.q: Кромѣ кладбищъ, принадлежащихъ Киргизъ-Казакамъ, въ степяхъ ихъ находятся многія древнія могилы, которыя приписываютъ они Ногайцамъ, нѣкогда въ сей странѣ обитавшимъ. Ногайскія могилы отличаются высотою, обширностію и часто состоятъ изъ огромныхъ насыпей такихъ камней, кои перевезены издалека; иногда находятъ въ нихъ золотыя и серебряныя украшенія для конской сбруи, монеты и проч.
p.s: Aleksei Levshin (1832)
p.t: Besides the cemeteries belonging to the Kirghiz-Kazakhs, in their steppes there are many ancient graves which they attribute to the Nogais, who once lived in this country. The Nogai graves are distinguished by their height and extent, and often consist of huge heaps of stones brought from far away; sometimes gold and silver ornaments for horse harness, coins and so on are found in them.
p.c: The Nogai attribution is Kazakh tradition as reported by Levshin.

p.h: Burial mounds with stone crosses, credited to the Alans
p.g: Describing the land around Tana, Barbaro says the countless mounds on the steppe are graves, each topped with a pierced stone holding a stone cross. He credits them to the Alans, a Christian people destroyed by the Tartars, not to the Tartars themselves.
p.q: These have been Christen men, and were chased awaie and destroied by the Tartares. In that region are hills, ryvers, and plaines : wheare are to be seene an infinite nombre of little hills forced in signe or steede of sepultures, and on the toppe of everie of them a great stone with an hole : wherein standeth a crosse of one peece made of an other stone.
p.s: Giosafat Barbaro (Tudor translation by William Thomas, c. 1550)
p.pe: Alans (As), 'chased awaie and destroied by the Tartares'
p.c: The crosses may be later Christian additions or Barbaro's reading of stone markers; most steppe kurgans are far older than the Alans.

p.h: The church vaults that collapsed under the refugees
p.g: When the Tatars broke through, the townspeople threw up a last ring of defences around the Church of the Mother of God (the Tithe Church, Kiev's first stone church, built by Prince Vladimir about 990). Next day, as people crowded onto the church and its vaults with their goods, the walls gave way under the weight, and the city fell. The chronicler credits the building to Rus princes and its ruin to the siege.
p.q: Наутрѣя же придоша на нѣ, и бысть брань межи ими велика; людемъ же узбѣгшимъ на церковь и на комары церковныя, и съ товары своими, отъ тягости повалишася съ ними стѣны церковныя, и пріятъ бысть градъ сице воими.
p.s: Hypatian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 2 (1843)
p.t: Next morning they came against them, and there was a great battle between them; and as the people ran up onto the church and onto the church vaults, with their goods, from the weight the church walls fell down with them, and so the city was taken by the warriors.
p.c: The church is not named in this sentence; the identification with the Tithe Church comes from the preceding line and from archaeology.

p.h: Lead domes, gilded cupolas and three classical orders
p.g: The book dresses its Tartar city in the European classical style of its own day: porticos on pillars and pilasters of the Doric, Ionic and Corinthian orders in the three wards, house roofs of lead shaped like domes with gilded copper cupolas, and at the centre a temple 'like the Pantheon at Rome'. It is a European architect's dream set in Tartary, not a description of anything built there.
p.q: The Roof of these Portico's is supported by Pillars without, and Pilasters within … The Doors and Windows observe the same Symmetry. The tops of their Houses are cover'd with Lead, in a Figure of a Duomo

p.h: How a Kalmyk felt tent is put together
p.g: Pallas gives a step-by-step account of the Kalmyk tent, keyed to an engraved plate: folding lattice walls of willow rods tied into a circle, a wooden crown ring lifted on long roof rods, the frame painted red, and a large cut felt thrown over the roof like a raincoat. In summer the sides stay open; in cold weather they are wrapped in felt or reed mats.
p.q: Alsdenn ist das Gerüste, dessen Theile roth angefärbt zu seyn pflegen fertig. Ueber das Dach desselben wird ein grosser, darnach zugeschnittener Filz, wie ein Regen-Mantel herum gelegt, und mit darüber geschlungenen Seilen befestigt. Die Seiten bleiben im Sommer offen, wenn es aber kalt ist, so werden Stücken Filz, oder Schilfmatten, oder auch beyde darum gelegt
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (Reise, first edition, St Petersburg 1771-1776)
p.t: Then the frame, whose parts are usually painted red, is finished. Over its roof a large felt, cut to fit, is laid round like a raincoat and fastened with ropes slung over it. The sides stay open in summer, but when it is cold pieces of felt or reed mats, or both, are laid around them.

p.h: Tatar tents that ride on two-wheeled carts
p.g: Along the Akhtuba Pallas saw the camps of the Kundurov Tatars, Nogais from the Kuban who had stayed behind when many Kalmyks fled east in 1771. Unlike Kalmyk tents, their round felt-and-reed huts could not be taken apart and were small enough to set whole onto a tall two-wheeled cart (arba), which they covered like a parasol. He compares them to the wagon-dwelling 'Hamaxobii' of the ancient geographers and quotes Horace on the Scythians whose carts drag their wandering homes.
p.q: Ihre Jurten sind in der Gestalt und Bauart, von denen bey Kalmücken und andern asiatischen Nomaden gebräuchlichen sehr verschieden. Sie können nicht stückweise aus einander genommen werden, sind aber desto leichter gebaut und nur so groß, daß sie über einen grossen Karren gesetzt werden können
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (Reise, first edition, St Petersburg 1771-1776)
p.t: Their yurts are very different in shape and construction from those used by the Kalmyks and other Asian nomads. They cannot be taken apart piece by piece, but are all the more lightly built and only so large that they can be set over a big cart.

p.h: Karakorum's quarters, temples and mud wall
p.g: Rubruck describes Karakorum as two quarters: one of Muslims (Saracens) with the markets, where merchants gathered because of the court, and one of 'Cathayans' (northern Chinese), who were all craftsmen. Outside them stood the large palaces of the court secretaries. There were twelve temples of various idolaters, two mosques and one church; a mud wall with four gates enclosed the town, each gate with its own market for grain, sheep and goats, oxen and carts, or horses.
p.q: Sarracenorum in quo sunt nundine, et multi mercatores confluunt ibi propter curiam … alius est vicus Catharanorum, qui omnes sunt artifices. Extra istos vicos sunt magna palatia, que sunt scriptorum curie. Sunt ibi duodecim ydolatrie diversarum nationum, due mahummerie in quibus clamatur lex Machometi, una ecclesia cristianorum in extremitate ville. Villa clausa est muro luteo, et habet .iiijor. portas.
p.s: William of Rubruck
p.pe: Muslim merchants, Chinese craftsmen and Mongol court scribes
p.t: [one quarter] of the Saracens, where the markets are, and many merchants gather there because of the court … the other is the quarter of the Cathayans, who are all craftsmen. Outside these quarters are large palaces belonging to the court secretaries. There are twelve idol temples of different nations, two mosques in which the law of Mahomet is proclaimed, and one Christian church at the far end of the town. The town is enclosed by a mud wall and has four gates.

p.h: Atil: a capital of tents with one brick palace
p.g: The Khazar capital on the Volga is described as mostly tents. Only a few market halls and bathhouses were of clay, and the king's residence was the only burnt-brick building in the country, because nobody else was allowed to build in brick. It is a precise picture of a steppe capital before the Mongols, on the same river where Sarai and Astrakhan later stood.
p.q: Here are many tents ; and in this country there are but a few edifices of clay, such as bazars (market-places) and bathing houses. … it is constructed of burnt bricks ; and this is the only building of such materials in all the country : they will not allow any body but the king to erect such a dwelling.
p.s: The 10th-century author attributed to Ibn Hawqal (translated by William Ouseley, 1800)
p.c: The Khazars are not called Tartars in the original; this is the pre-Mongol Volga.

p.h: Mongol farmers in earthen houses near Hohhot
p.g: Following the Kangxi emperor's march of 1696, the note describes hamlets of a few earthen houses lived in by Mongols who farmed the nearby fields, lining the road to greet the emperor with sheep, butter and cream. Near Kouei-hoa-tching (Hohhot) the garrison knelt on the road and some two hundred lamas in ceremonial dress, with rough musical instruments and banners, waited at the main temple. Not every 'Tartar' lived in a tent.
p.q: On passa devant plusieurs hameaux, composés de quelques maisons de terre, habitées par des Mongous qui cultivent les champs voisins. Ces pauvres habitans se rangeoient sur le chemin pour saluer l'empereur, auquel ils offroient des moutons, du beurre, de la crème & divers bois odoriférans.
p.s: Editor's note in Mailla's Histoire générale de la Chine (Qing volume), narrating Kangxi's 1696 journey
p.t: We passed several hamlets made up of a few earthen houses, inhabited by Mongols who farm the neighbouring fields. These poor inhabitants lined up along the road to greet the emperor, offering him sheep, butter, cream and various fragrant woods.
p.c: The note does not name its source on this page; it reads like a Jesuit companion's journal retold by the Paris editor.

p.h: White plastered chimneys and a raised sleeping floor
p.g: Near Tara Cochrane passed neat Tatar villages whose white plastered chimneys and ovens reminded him of home. Inside, half the room was raised about fourteen inches and used for sitting, sleeping and storage; there were no chairs, only clean bedding and many pillows, which were always offered to a guest. A few pages earlier he stayed in a Tatar district of seventy miles without a single Russian, praising the clean houses and well-kept land.
p.q: At Kamenski I quitted the great Siberian road not far from Tara, passing several neat Tartar villages, whose white plastered chimneys and ovens reminded me a little of those in my own country. The furniture consists of a few earthenware utensils, and a set of tea things: one half of the room is elevated above the other about fourteen inches
p.s: John Dundas Cochrane (1824)
p.c: On the same page Cochrane calls the Tatars near the Vagai river 'of the Bashkire race'; they were Siberian Tatars.

p.h: Grey felt for the poor, red cloth for sultans, reeds for the poorest
p.g: After describing the Kazakh yurt (a round tent of wooden lattice covered with felt, with a smoke hole at the top, 'exactly like the Kalmyk ones', 4 to 8 arshins high), Levshin shows how its covering marked rank. Ordinary Kazakhs used grey felt, the rich and noble white felt, some great sultans red broadcloth lined with silk, and the very poorest covered their homes with matting, turf and reeds.
p.q: Кибитки простыхъ Киргизовъ обыкновенно дѣлаются изъ войлоковъ сѣрыхъ; знатные и богатые употребляютъ для сего бѣлые войлоки; а у нѣкоторыхъ сильныхъ Султановъ Средней и Большой Орды, юрты бываютъ обтянуты краснымъ сукномъ и подбиты шелковыми тканями. Въ противоположность послѣднимъ самые бѣдные, вмѣсто войлоковъ, покрываютъ жилища свои рогожами, дерномъ и камышемъ.
p.s: Aleksei Levshin (1832)
p.t: The kibitkas of ordinary Kirghiz are usually made of grey felts; the noble and rich use white felts for this; and some powerful sultans of the Middle and Great Horde have yurts covered with red broadcloth and lined with silk fabrics. p.h: Mangup: a ruined mountain city of many peoples
p.g: With a Tatar guide Alexander climbed to Mangup Kale, a deserted fortress-city on a table mountain. He credits its battlemented walls to the Genoese and reads the ruins as layers of occupation: a Tatar mosque, a synagogue, a small church, and Muslim, Jewish and Christian graves. The only living things were a few grazing Tatar horses.
p.q: passed through some noble remains of battlemented walls of Genoese architecture, flanked with square and round towers. Before us were the remains of a Tartar mosque, a Jewish synagogue, a small church, and the tombs of Moslems, Israelites, and Christians, pointing out the successive occupiers of this strange city, the ruins of whose habitations were very numerous
p.s: James Edward Alexander (1830)
p.pe: Crimean Tatars and earlier occupants of the site
p.c: 'Genoese' is his guess: Mangup was the capital of the Orthodox principality of Theodoro until the Ottomans took it in 1475.

p.h: Ablai-kit: a Kalmyk monastery with a printing press
p.g: Near the upper Irtysh stand the ruins of Ablai-kit, a Buddhist monastery that the Kalmyk prince Ablai founded in the mid-17th century, with a Mongol-Tibetan library and a woodblock press. p.s: Alexander von Humboldt
p.w: mid-17th century; ruins seen by Russians in the 18th century
p.t: which a Kalmyk prince, Ablai, had founded in the middle of the 17th century and endowed with a Mongol-Tibetan library and a woodblock printing press. … Even today one finds half-torn leaves of Tibetan books scattered in the steppe grass around the ruins of Ablai-kit.

p.h: Yakut winter house of poles, planks and dung
p.g: Sarychev, who slept in these houses on the road, explains how a Yakut winter jurt is built: three rows of posts, beams laid across and sloping, rough planks, then a covering of grass, earth and dung. A hearth with a pitch-lined chimney of sticks burns all winter, and the cattle live in an attached shed. Summer houses are different: conical frames of poles covered with bark.
p.q: On these poles they lay five beams crossways and sloping, which are covered with rough planks, and afterwards with herbs, mould, and dung. … The summer jurts are altogether different from the winter ones, and have another name, being called masses; they are round and conical, made of long poles, and covered on the outside with the bark of trees.
p.s: Gavriil Sarychev (English translation, 1806)
p.c: The OCR (and perhaps the 1806 print) reads the name of the summer house as 'masses'; the Yakut word is urasa.

p.h: They always live in tents, not villages or cities
p.g: In a chapter on the Tartars' outward appearance and way of life, the text says plainly that they always live in tents and never in villages or cities, because they are country herdsmen with vast flocks of sheep and goats, herds of cattle, camels and horses. p.h: Khiva's manor houses of rammed clay
p.g: Riding into the Khiva oasis, Abbott describes the country houses of the nobles: tall clay-walled compounds with towers at the corners, locally called 'castles'. He explains how the walls were built by ramming wet clay between hurdles of branches, which left a fluted pattern on the surface.

This name (Gullah) they bear at Khiva. … The walls, built with great regularity of rammed clay, are generally fluted, an effect given them perhaps by the hurdles of straight branches, between which the clay is supported whilst soft

p.g: Describing the Qianlong Emperor, Barrow cites as proof of his piety the many splendid Buddhist temples he built and endowed in 'oriental Tartary', the grandest being the Potala-style monastery at Jehol (Chengde), where Macartney was received.

p.h: Foreign masons build Timur's great mosque at Samarkand
p.g: Back from India, Timur ordered a congregational mosque for Samarkand. Yazdi says the foundations were laid at an astrologically chosen moment and that the work was done by masons brought from foreign countries, 200 from Azerbaijan, Persia and India inside alone. On the next page he adds 500 men cutting stone in the mountains, 95 elephants hauling blocks, and a finished hall of 480 hewn-stone pillars, a carved marble roof, four minarets and brass doors. Earlier (p. 67) he records that Timur kept the captured masons of Delhi for this very building.
p.q: The masons, brought from foreign countrys, as mention'd before, gave the greatest proofs of their art and skill, as well in the solidity and beauty of the angles, as in the strength of the foundations of this noble edifice. In the inside of the mosque were employ'd two hundred masons from Azerbijana, Persia and India:
p.s: Sharaf al-Din Ali Yazdi (English of 1723, via Pétis de la Croix)
p.pe: Timur and craftsmen from Azerbaijan, Persia and India
p.c: Written by Timur's dynasty's historian about twenty years later; the figures are the court's.

p.h: Ruins of a stone castle and horseman tombs at Uvek
p.g: Sailing down the Volga, Burrough's party stopped at Uvek on the 'Crims side' (west bank) and saw the ruins of a fine stone castle and tombs of important people. One tombstone showed a mounted archer, and inscriptions the English took for Armenian letters. The narrative does not say who built it; the editors' index labels Uvek an old Tartar town, and it was in fact a Golden Horde city.
p.q: At this place had beene a very fayre stone castle, called by the name Oueake … There remaineth, at this day, to be seene a part of the ruines of the castle and certain tombs, wherein, as it seemeth, haue beene laid noble personages ; for vpon a tombe stone might be perceiued the forme of a horse, and a man sitting on it with a bowe in his hand
p.s: Christopher Burrough's reports, in Hakluyt (ed. Morgan and Coote, 1886)
p.pe: Unnamed former inhabitants (the editors' index calls Uvek an 'old Tartar town')
p.c: The 'Armenian' reading of the inscriptions is the travellers' guess.

p.h: Felt huts that ride on carts
p.g: The Nogais, Pallas says, live in small felt huts four to five and a half arshines across that cannot be taken apart; two men lift the whole hut onto a two-wheeled cart to move it. The next page adds that the huts have a smoke-hole cover worked by a cord and are lined with reed mats, and that the Nogais must buy hazel poles from the Crimean mountain Tatars because the steppe has no timber. A footnote compares them to the ancient 'wagon-dwellers' of the Sea of Azov.
p.q: The Nagays, as well as their kinsmen near the Lines of Caucasus, and the Akhtouba, live in small huts constructed of felt, the largest of which are from about four to five and a half arshines in diameter, and, like those of the Kundure Tartars, cannot be taken to pieces, but are placed by two men upon a carriage, and thus removed from one place to another.
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (English translation, 1812 edition)
p.pl: Molochnaya River steppe, north of the Crimea

p.h: Mud ruins the Kazakhs credited to the Nogais
p.g: Along a dried-up river channel Meyendorff saw long earth mounds with canals and broken pottery, the remains of buildings of sun-dried brick. The Kazakhs could not say when or why they were built but guessed they were the work of the Nogais, who had held the steppe before them. The best-known ruin, Djankend, was of fired brick and said to be the seat of an Oghuz chief.
p.q: It is clear these buildings, whatever they may have been, were built with sun-burnt bricks; near these ruins are small canals about 1 toise or 6 feet broad and two deep; a great quantity of broken pottery is also to be met with. … The Kirghiz could give us no account of their use or date, but supposing they must have been erected by the Nogais
p.s: Georg von Meyendorff (translated by William Monteith, 1840)
p.c: The attribution to the Nogais is the Kazakhs' guess, as Meyendorff says.

p.h: The golden chamber of the Khans' palace
p.g: Webster describes the palace of the Khans set in a great courtyard with the palace, mosque and tombs together. Past a marble fountain, a staircase led to the 'golden chamber' with a ceiling of gilded stars. On the next page he adds the crimson walls, stained glass and divans, faded but still showing 'the magnificence of the Tartar rulers', and notes Russian repairs under way.
p.q: The most interesting object is the palace of the Khans, which stands in a large area … We entered the court-yard, which brought into our view the palace, the mosque, and the tombs … In the entrance we passed a marble fountain, and ascended a spacious staircase, which brought us to a large room, called the golden chamber, the ceiling of which, divided into compartments, and studded with gilded stars

p.h: Inside a Kazakh sultan's tent
p.g: At the Ilek River the embassy met its first Kazakh camp: about 50 tents of white or brown felt. Meyendorff then visited the sultan's large round tent, which mixed luxury and plain nomad gear: carpets, tiger skins, a woman's tall gold headdress set with turquoise and rubies, raw meat on hooks and leather bags of mare's milk.
p.q: the floor was covered with a carpet, wearing apparel hung on a cord, and skins of tigers were stretched against the sides; a rich diadem of gold, very high, and ornamented with turquoise and rubies, the head dress of Kirghiz women ; by their side might also be seen raw meat hanging on hooks, large leather bags of mare's milk, and some wooden vessels of different kinds
p.s: Georg von Meyendorff (translated by William Monteith, 1840)

p.h: Stone markers, idols and gold from the graves: whose were they?
p.g: Müller points to the traces of old towns on the steppes, the many stone markers and 'idols' (stone statues), old grave mounds, and the gold and silver objects dug out of them. He attributes them to the earlier Tatars, reasoning that the treasures of China, Persia, Russia, Poland, Bohemia and Hungary had fallen to them as conquerors. It is a scholar's inference, not a report from the graves themselves.
p.q: Сколько не видно слѣдовъ на разныхъ мѣстахъ по степямъ городковъ? Коликое множество въ память поставленныхъ каменныхъ маяковъ, болвановъ, старинныхъ могилъ и другихъ принадлежащихъ къ тому вещей на всѣхъ мѣстахъ не находится? Какихъ дорогихъ вещей, золотыхъ и серебреныхъ, изъ могилъ не выкопано? Откуда можно было имъ произойти, какъ только отъ прежнихъ Татаръ
p.s: Gerhard Friedrich Müller (Russian edition, 1787 issue)
p.pe: Tatars and Mongols of Chinggis Khan's era (as Müller supposes)
p.t: How many traces of small towns are seen in various places on the steppes? What a multitude of stone markers set up as memorials, idols, old graves and other such things are found everywhere? What precious objects, of gold and silver, have not been dug out of the graves? Where could they have come from, if not from the former Tatars
p.c: Müller's attribution to the Chinggisid Tatars is his own guess; modern archaeology dates many of these kurgans and stone figures far earlier.

p.h: 'No Cities nor fix'd Habitations'
p.g: Summing up the Kalmyks, who ranged from Mongolia to the Volga, Avril says plainly that they had no cities or fixed homes, only neat, comfortable felt tents, and that no people could strike camp faster. On the same page he calls them idolaters who, like the Mongols, look to the Dalai Lama.
p.q: The Calmoucs have no Cities nor fix'd Habitations, but only live in Tents made of Felts, which are very neat, and very commodious; nor is there any Nation so nimble at Camping and Decamping in an instant as they, there being no Nation so much accustom'd to it, in regard they never stay long in a place, and are always making Incursions.
p.s: Philippe Avril (English translation, 1693)
p.c: Avril met Kalmyks near Astrakhan, but this general statement comes from Moscow informants.
