p.h: New houses of mud and rubble among old walls
p.g: In place of the old cities, Verbiest saw only broken walls of brick and stone, with a few new houses thrown up on the outskirts. Some were of earth, some built from the rubble of the old buildings, and most were thatched rather than tiled. The capital, which he calls Kin-Yam (Shenyang), was the exception: fairly whole, with the remains of an old palace.
p.q: One can see nothing through the whole Country but old ruined Walls with Rubbell, Bricks and Stones. In the out skirts of these Citys there have been of late some few houses built, but without any order. Some of them made of Earth, others of the Rubbish of the old Buildings, the most part of them covered with straw or thatch, and but few with tyles.
p.s: Ferdinand Verbiest (English translation, 1686)

p.h: Nogai huts outside Astrakhan: round, of bark or reeds, covered with felt
p.g: The Nogais, though natives of the land, may not live inside the walls of Astrakhan and build poor huts outside, later protected by palisades. The huts are round, about ten feet across, made of bark or woven reeds covered with roughly joined felt, with an opening in the roof that serves as chimney and is closed with felt to keep in the heat.
p.q: Les Tartares du Nagai quoique naturels du pays, n'ont pas la liberté de demeurer dans l'enceinte de la Ville … Leurs hutes sont bâties en rond & ont d'ordinaire dix piés de diamètre: elles ne sont faites que d'écorce d'arbre ou de roseaux entrelacés, ni couvertes que de feutre grossiérement joint. Le toit est ouvert en forme de trape, & leur tient lieu de cheminée
p.s: Jan Struys (French translation by Glanius, Amsterdam 1681)
p.t: The Tartars of the Nogai, though natives of the country, are not free to live within the walls of the town … Their huts are built round and are usually ten feet across; they are made only of tree bark or woven reeds, and covered only with roughly joined felt. The roof is open like a trapdoor and serves them as a chimney
p.c: Some of this closely follows Olearius's description of the Nogai huts at Astrakhan.

p.h: Mortar harder than the bricks
p.g: At Tsarevy Pody ('the royal residence') on the Akhtuba, Pallas examined a flat vaulted tomb mound inside a sandstone wall. The vaults were of six layers of square bricks joined with a grey cement so hard that the bricks broke before the mortar did. He analysed it as lime, powdered charcoal and ground sandstone, and wondered whether sour milk, plentiful among a pastoral people, had been mixed in.
p.q: It has, however, acquired such a solid consistence, that it is easier to break the well-burnt bricks, than to separate the mortar. This grey cement appears to be a mixture of unslacked lime, pulverized charcoal, and pounded sandstone, instead of the sand used for building.
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (English translation, 1812 edition)
p.pe: Mongol Tartar princes of the Golden Horde
p.c: The sour-milk idea on the next page is his own guess.

p.h: Glazed tiles and bricks carted off to Astrakhan
p.g: Pallas says he had never seen such splendour in any Tatar ruin: brick walls laid with great regularity, the joints inlaid with green, yellow, white and blue glazed ornaments, and a facade with mosaic tiles. He blames time and plunder for the damage, adding that whole boatloads of bricks had been shipped to Astrakhan, and that to get a thousand whole bricks the workers smashed two thousand because the mortar was so hard.
p.q: Die äussere Seite der Mauern ist von aussen nicht nur Felderweise in allen Steinfugen mit glasurten Thonzierrathen von grüner, gelber, weisser und blauer Farbe in dreyeckigten und andern Figuren eingelegt… Aber die Zeit und noch mehr der Geitz des Pöbels hat diese denkwürdigen Ueberbleibsel des Alterthums vorlängst in Steinhaufen verwandelt.
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (Reise, first edition, St Petersburg 1771-1776)
p.t: The outer face of the walls is not only inlaid, panel by panel in all the joints, with glazed clay ornaments of green, yellow, white and blue colour in triangular and other figures… But time, and still more the greed of the rabble, long ago turned these memorable remains of antiquity into heaps of stones.

p.g: Spafarii copies the report of the party of Ivan Porshennikov, who rode from Selenginsk across Mongolia to China and back in 1675. A little further down the Tola stood an empty stone city, very strong, whose walls needed only a little repair.

p.h: Bakhchisaray: a stone palace, and mosques built from Christian ruins
p.g: The khan lives in a stone house in Bakhchisaray, a town between two mountains with a small river through it. Broniewski says the stone mosque and the khans' tombs were built from the ruins of Christian buildings. Next to it lies the town of Salachik, and a palace of the khans that, he says, the early Tatar princes adorned with buildings, mosques, tombs and baths. So he credits Tatars as builders, reusing older stone.
p.q: Oppidum non ignobile, & domum lapideam primariam, in qua ille semper residet, Baccasaraium nuncupatam ille habet. … Mahometicum templum lapideũ, & sepulturę Chanorum ex ruinis Christianorum penes oppidum exstructæ sunt. … Chanorum Regia vel domus à priscis Tartarorum Principibus sumptuosè ædificijs, templis, sepulturis, & balneis magnificè exornata est.

A stone Muslim temple and the tombs of the khans have been built near the town out of the ruins of the Christians. ... The palace or house of the khans was sumptuously and magnificently adorned by the early princes of the Tartars with buildings, temples, tombs and baths.

p.h: Clay tombs that looked like cities
p.g: The nomadic Kazakhs built lasting tombs of clay mixed with chopped straw, sometimes of unburnt brick, with a small prayer chamber inside. Rich families brought craftsmen from Bukhara to make them. Near the Syr Darya they were so many that from a distance they looked like cities.
p.q: All the tombs are of clay, mixed with chopped straw, except that of Khodja, which is of unburnt bricks. In the interior of these sepulchres there is another, smaller, where the Kirghiz pray. These monuments become more numerous as you approach the Sir, and appear like cities. The rich Kirghiz frequently bring artificers from Bokhara to make their clay tombs
p.s: Georg von Meyendorff (translated by William Monteith, 1840)

p.h: No towns, only felt tents: Cumans like the Nogais
p.g: Writing of the Cumans who held the land between the Danube, the Black Sea and the Dniester in the 13th century, Peyssonnel says they had no towns, villages or fixed homes and lived always in movable felt tents. p.s: Charles de Peyssonnel
p.t: These barbarians still had neither towns, nor villages, nor fixed dwellings; they were constantly camped under felt tents, which they carried from place to place; they were exactly like the Nogais of today, who are almost the same nation.

p.h: From tents to palaces: the Uighur khans' capital
p.g: In notes to the same volume the French sinologist Deveria writes that the Uighur khanate set up its main seat on the Orkhon in 745, but that the khans only later replaced the tents of their royal camp with palaces: the Tang history mentions a palace built for the Uighur ruler in 780 as something new, and in 784 a khan had an inscription carved on a stone stele 'before the gate of his capital'. The capital was burned by the Kirghiz in 841. It is a clear dated sequence from tent camp to built city.
p.q: La fondation du Khanat ouïgour et l'établissement du siège principal de ses Khakans sur les bords de l'Orkhoun remonte à l'année 745, mais ce ne serait que plus tard que les Khakans auraient substitué des palais aux tentes de leur camp royal. Ce n'est en effet qu'en 780 que l'histoire des T'ang parle, comme d'une chose nouvelle chez les Ouïgours, de la construction d'un palais
p.s: Gabriel Deveria, notes on the Chinese inscriptions, in Inscriptions de l'Orkhon (Helsingfors 1892)
p.t: The founding of the Uighur khanate and the setting of its khagans' main seat on the banks of the Orkhon go back to 745, but only later did the khagans replace the tents of their royal camp with palaces. Indeed it is only in 780 that the Tang history speaks, as something new among the Uighurs, of the building of a palace.
p.c: Deveria is summarising Tang annals.

p.h: The Dzungars live in tents, visiting their villages two months a year

p.h: A city built for a Mongol prince by imperial slaves
p.g: The Qianlong emperor married a daughter to a Khalkha prince, who hated court life and longed for his tents. As a compromise the emperor carved out land in the Chakhar, 'built for him' a small handsome city, and gave him a hundred families of slaves skilled in Chinese arts and crafts. The princess got her court; the prince could go back to the tent. Huc credits the city to the emperor and Chinese craftsmen, not to the Mongols.
p.q: He dismembered a portion of the Tchakar, and assigned it to the Mongol prince; he built for him, amid these solitudes, a small but handsome city, and presented to him a hundred families of slaves skilled in the arts and manufactures of China.

p.h: How a Kalmyk felt tent is put together
p.g: Zwick opens a whole chapter on the Kalmyk tent, called gerr by its owners and kibitka by Russians. He describes a round lattice wall of willow laths, painted in red stripes, that folds flat in seven or eight sections, with poles rising to a wooden crown and the whole covered in large felts tied down with woollen girths. It is one of the most exact eyewitness descriptions of a steppe yurt in English before 1850.
p.q: The Calmuc huts or tents, in their own language gerr, and in the Russian kibitka, consist of a number of parts, which are easily put together, and taken to pieces. The tents are round, with a funnel-shaped roof, and a blunt point at the top of it. The frame-work, which is of willow laths about an inch thick, carved and painted in red stripes, forms a circular wall of lattice-work
p.s: Heinrich August Zwick (English edition, 1831)

p.h: Timur's palace at Kesh: glazed tiles, and a doubt about who began it
p.g: At Kesh (Shahrisabz), Timur's birthplace, the envoys toured palaces said to have been under construction for twenty years: brick arches covered in glazed tiles, a court paved with white stone around a great pool, and a gateway in gold and blue tiles. Clavijo noticed the lion-and-sun device over the door and argued that an earlier lord of Samarkand must have begun it, since Timur's own device was three circles. A rare case of a medieval visitor questioning a building's attribution.
p.q: On the top of this doorway there was the figure of a lion and a sun, which are the arms of the lord of Samarcand ; and, though they say that Timour Beg ordered these palaces to be built, I believe that the former lord of Samarcand gave the order
p.s: Ruy González de Clavijo (translated by Clements R. Markham, 1859)
p.pe: Timur (Timour Beg) and an earlier lord of Samarkand
p.c: Clavijo's reasoning about the arms is his own inference.

p.h: Cuman mounds, stone statues and brick towers
p.g: Among the burial customs he saw on the steppe, Rubruck notes that the Cumans raised a great mound over the dead and set up a statue facing east holding a cup at the navel. For the rich they built small pointed 'pyramids', and in places he saw tall towers of baked brick and even stone houses, though no stone was found there. He also saw a newly dead man with the hides of sixteen horses hung on tall poles around him.
p.q: Comani faciunt magnum tumulum super defunctum, et erigunt ei statuam versa facie ad orientem, tenentem ciphum in manu sua ante umbilicum. Fabricant etiam divitibus piramides, id est domunculas acutas, et alicubi vidi magnas turres de tegulis coctis, alicubi lapideas domos, quamvis lapides non inveniuntur ibi. Vidi quemdam noviter defunctum, cui suspenderant pelles .xvj. equorum, ad quodlibet latus mundi quatuor, inter perticas altas
p.s: William of Rubruck
p.t: The Cumans raise a great mound over the dead man and set up a statue to him, its face turned to the east, holding a cup in its hand in front of the navel. For the rich they also build pyramids, that is, small pointed houses, and in some places I saw great towers of baked tiles, in others stone houses, although stones are not found there. I saw one man newly dead for whom they had hung the hides of sixteen horses, four towards each quarter of the world, between tall poles
p.c: On the same page Rubruck says the burial places of Mongol nobles were kept secret and guarded.

p.h: Bukhara's brick mosques and ruined bazaars
p.g: George Thompson went on alone to Bukhara. He describes low mud houses inside a slender earth wall, but caravanserais and many mosques of brick, and a college for priests of brick and stone. The bazaars had been 'stately buildings' but were now mostly in ruins. He adds a lurid note about guinea worms ('rishtas') from the bad water.
p.q: …the houses are low, and mostly built of mud: but the caravanserais and the mosques, which are numerous, are all of brick: the bazars, or market-places, have been stately buildings, but are now the greatest part of them in ruins; these are generally built of brick and stone.
p.s: British factors Reynold Hogg and George Thompson, their 1740 journal as printed by Jonas Hanway (1753)

p.h: A house thirty feet wide, pulled by twenty-two oxen
p.g: Some Mongol houses were never taken down but rode on huge carts. Rubruck measured one cart himself and counted the oxen. The axle was as thick as a ship's mast and a driver stood in the doorway of the house. On the next pages he describes felt-covered chests on carts and a rich man's camp of one or two hundred carts.
p.q: I myself once measured the width between the wheel-tracks of a cart xx feet, and when the house was on the cart it projected beyond the wheels on either side v feet at least. I have myself counted to one cart xxii oxen drawing one house, eleven abreast across the width of the cart, and the other eleven before them.
p.s: William of Rubruck (translated by W. W. Rockhill, 1900)
p.c: Rockhill thinks these carts were exceptionally large ones.

p.h: Clean Tatar rooms with two fireplaces and calf-skin windows
p.g: Riding east from Kazan through a string of Tatar villages, Gmelin lodged in Tatar houses. They had no 'black rooms' (smoky rooms without a chimney): every room had two fireplaces side by side, one for heat and one for cooking, and broad low benches laid with a carpet and a cushion for guests. The sentence that follows says that instead of window glass they stretched the outer skin of a calf's stomach over the frames.
p.q: Die Tatarn haben keine Schwarz-Stuben, sondern in einer jeden Stube sind 2. Camine neben einander, in deren einem eingeheizt, und in dem andern Essen gekocht wird. Ihre Stuben sehen sehr reinlich aus. Es sind sehr breite niedrige Bänke darin
p.s: Johann Georg Gmelin (German original, Göttingen, 1751)
p.pl: Tatar villages east of Kazan (Kursa to Seredni Shun)
p.t: The Tatars have no 'black rooms' [rooms without a chimney]; instead, in every room there are two fireplaces side by side, one used for heating and the other for cooking. Their rooms look very clean. There are very broad, low benches in them

p.h: A Nogai suburb of bulrush houses behind a wooden rampart
p.g: Avril describes Astrakhan as a mixed trading city. The Armenians had one suburb and the Nogai Tartars another, which looked like a town of its own: a wooden rampart, its own governor under the Russian governor, a mosque, and about two thousand houses made mostly of bulrushes. He adds that the Russians treated the Nogais more as allies than subjects because they fought for them.
p.q: Armenians possess one of the Suburbs entirely to themselves, and the Nogais Tartars another, which altogether resembles a City, being fortifi'd with a Wooden-Rampart, and having a Governour who commands there, under the Orders of the Chief Governor of Astrakan. Within that Enclosure stands a Mosquee ; but the Houses are for the greatest part made of Bulrushes, of which there may be about two thousand.
p.s: Philippe Avril (English translation, 1693)

p.h: Why a felt tent beats a house
p.g: Lodged in a Turkmen camp of about 300 black tents, Abbott was won over by the felt tent. He explains that the felt can be lifted in summer, a central fire warms it in winter with the smoke escaping through a roof opening, and the whole home can be moved to a better spot.
p.q: These Toorcumun tents are the most comfortable of dwellings … by removing a portion of the felt covering, this tent is open to the air in summer ; and in winter a fire lighted in the centre makes it the warmest of retreats, all the smoke rising through the skylight in the roof.
p.s: James Abbott
p.pl: Turkmen country between Herat and Merv

p.h: Tatar tents like parrot cages, carried on carts
p.g: De Bruyn often walked out to the Tatar camp three or four versts from Astrakhan and drew it. Each family camped apart. The tents were built like parrot cages from laths three or four inches wide, covered with felt, camel hair or horsehair, with a smoke hole and a pole carrying a turnable sail against wind and sun. When they moved, they set the tents on two-wheeled carts.
p.q: Ils campent par troupes, chaque famille separée, & à quelque distance des autres. Leurs tentes sont faites comme des cages de perroquets, hormis qu'elles ne sont pas si élevées à proportion; formées de lattes de trois à quatre pouces de large, couvertes de feutre, de poil de chameau ou de crin de cheval … Quand ils changent de lieu, ils mettent leurs tentes sur des chariots
p.s: Cornelis de Bruyn (French translation, Voyages de Corneille Le Brun, 1718)
p.t: They camp in groups, each family apart and at some distance from the others. Their tents are made like parrot cages, except that they are not so tall in proportion; formed of laths three to four inches wide, covered with felt, camel hair or horsehair … When they change place, they put their tents on carts

p.h: Yarkand: a clay fort, a stone fort and clay houses
p.g: Wathen's informants described Yarkand, the biggest town of Chinese Tartary, as having two forts: a large, empty one with clay walls, and a smaller, inhabited one with four gates, built of stone and chunam (lime plaster) with a ditch. Ordinary houses were one storey and built of clay, which served well because it hardly ever rained. The same page says the city had many mosques and colleges and two big bazaars.
p.q: It has two forts: the principal one is of large extent, but its walls are of clay; and it is uninhabited; the other, which is rather smaller, has four gates, is inhabited, and is considered by the natives as very strong, being built of stone and chunam, and surrounded with a ditch … The houses are generally one story high, and built of clay
p.s: W. H. Wathen, reporting his informants
p.c: Second-hand description from pilgrims interviewed in Bombay.

p.h: The caves and giant statues of Bamiyan
p.g: At Bamiyan Burnes found a valley honeycombed for eight miles with caves, still home to most of the people, and the two great statues. He reports local traditions: the caves were the work of a king named Julal, the statues were made by 'Kaffirs' (infidels) about the time of Christ, or by the Pandavas of Hindu epic. He notes a theory that they were Buddhist, which the long ears made likely. He does not credit them to Tartars.
p.q: A detached hill in the middle of the valley is quite honeycombed by them … It is called the city of Ghoolghoola, and consists of a continued succession of caves in every direction, which are said to have been the work of a king named Julal.
p.s: Alexander Burnes (1834)
p.c: The builders are given only as local tradition and conjecture.

p.h: Madzhary: streets of tombs, not a town
p.g: On the Kuma River Pallas visited the famous ruins of Upper Madzhary. In 1780 there were still thirty-two buildings, but settlers had since carted away the fine bricks. The ruins stood in rows, which made 'the ignorant' think they were the streets of a large town; Pallas concludes it was a great cemetery of domed sepulchral mosques. (Madzhar is now known to have been a Golden Horde trading town of the 1300s.)
p.q: …they have formerly stood in rows; a circumstance that has induced the ignorant to suppose they were the streets of a large town. But, upon close investigation, it appears that this place was a famous cemetry appropriated to persons of distinction;
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (English translation, 1812 edition)
p.pe: a Muslim people 'perhaps of Tartar origin'
p.c: His 'cemetery, not a town' verdict reflects his view that nomads did not build towns.

p.h: A brick 'Tatar prayer-house' whose builders were forgotten
p.g: Pallas rode out into the steppe beyond the Orenburg line to see a building the Russians called the Tatar Koshena. It was a square brick shrine with a pointed Gothic portal and a twelve-sided funnel dome, standing in a Kazakh cemetery. He thought it was not very old, yet neither the Kazakhs nor the Bashkirs remembered who had built it. On a following page he notes it is all of red brick, much like ordinary European brick.
p.q: Es ist noch in vollkommen gutem Zustand und scheint, wenigstens dem darinn befindlichen Holzwerk nach, von keinem ausserordentlichen Alterthum zu seyn. Gleichwohl ist unter den Kirgisen sowohl, als Baschkiren das Angedenken ihrer Auferbauung verloschen.
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (Reise, first edition, St Petersburg 1771-1776)
p.pl: Kazakh steppe between the Ui and Tobol
p.t: It is still in perfectly good condition and, at least to judge by the woodwork inside, seems to be of no extraordinary antiquity. Nevertheless the memory of its building has been lost among the Kirgis as well as the Bashkirs.

p.h: Walls and fortress towns built against the Tartars
p.g: Where the Great Wall ends in the far north-west, the account explains, there was a gap of some two hundred miles through which the Tartars, shut out by the Wall, kept trying to raid China. To stop them the Chinese built two heavily fortified cities, Kanchou (Zhangye) and Suchou (Jiuquan), with picked troops and their own viceroy. Here the walls and forts are Chinese works built to keep the Tartars out.
p.q: Ad occiduam Sinensis regni partem, qua in Boream flectitur, celebres illi muri finiuntur, & spatium erat ducentorum fere milliariorum, quo spatio Tartari muris exclusi, saepe in Sinarum regnum excurrentes tentabant ingressum, & etiamnunc, sed minore periculo tentant: extructae sunt enim ad retundendos eorum impetus urbes duae munitissimae
p.s: Nicolas Trigault, from Matteo Ricci's commentaries (1615)
p.t: At the western part of the kingdom of China, where it bends to the north, those famous walls come to an end, and there was a stretch of about two hundred miles through which the Tartars, shut out by the walls, often tried to break into China, and still try even now, though with less danger: for two very strongly fortified cities have been built to beat back their attacks

p.h: A wall of iron bricks bound with copper
p.g: Sallam describes how the wall was built: foundations dug thirty cubits deep and laid in iron and copper, then two great jambs, all of iron bricks sheathed in copper, carrying a 120-cubit iron lintel. He credits the work to Dhu'l-Qarnayn, the Quran's 'two-horned' king, usually identified with Alexander. Nothing here is credited to the Turks.
p.q: La muraille fut construite de la manière suivante. D'abord on creusa le sol jusqu'à une profondeur de 30 coudées et on y jeta les fondements qu'on construisit en fer et en cuivre jusqu'à ras de terre … Toute la construction se compose de briques de fer, revêtues de cuivre, dont chacune a une coudée et demie en long et en large sur 4 pouces d'épaisseur.
p.s: Sallam the Interpreter, as reported by Ibn Khurradadhbih (French translation by M. J. de Goeje, 1889)
p.pl: 'Wall of Gog and Magog' (perhaps the Gansu or Hami frontier, China)
p.t: The wall was built in the following way. First the ground was dug to a depth of 30 cubits and the foundations laid there, built of iron and copper up to ground level … The whole structure is made of iron bricks faced with copper, each a cubit and a half long and wide and 4 inches thick.
p.c: Sallam's account as dictated to Ibn Khurradadhbih; the 'history' of the building is legend.

p.h: A Tatar village you could ride across by the rooftops
p.g: Guided by a young villager named Ismael, Kohl climbed to the Tatar village of Derekoi near Yalta. Its houses leaned into the hillside so their big flat roofs, made of packed earth and pebbles rolled smooth and resting on thin tree trunks, served as courtyards; there was no window glass, only wooden flaps. On the next page he watches village life going on across the rooftops.
p.q: The dwellings lie thickly scattered about among the trees, and leaning on one side against the mountain, so that one may ride over their flat roofs. These are large, as they supply the place of a courtyard covered with earth and small stones, laid smooth with a sort of roller, and supported on thin trunks of trees. Glass windows there are not, but in their place wooden flaps

p.h: Golden roofs? No, glazed clay tiles
p.g: Describing the palace where the 'Great Cham' now lived, Nieuhof explains that the roofs are covered with yellow glazed tiles that shine brighter than gold in the sun. This, he says, is why some people reported that the palace was roofed with pure gold, when in fact the tiles are made of clay.
p.q: All the Roofs of the Buildings are covered with Yellow glazed Pantiles, which shine, when the Sun reflects, brighter then Gold; which has made some believe and report, that the Roof of this Royal Palace was covered with pure Gold; whereas in truth the Tiles are only made of Clay, and Glaz'd and Neil'd over with Artificial Yellow

p.h: A Mongol: 'We Mongols are formed for living in tents'
p.g: In Gechekten, where Chinese settlers had turned grassland into poor sandy fields, the priests asked a Mongol rider why his people did not farm. He answered that Mongols were made for tents and herds; since they had started farming and building houses they had grown poor, and the Chinese (Kitat) had taken their land, herds and houses. It is a Mongol's own verdict on houses versus tents.
p.q: "We Mongols are formed for living in tents, and pasturing cattle. So long as we kept to that in the kingdom of Gechekten, we were rich and happy. Now, ever since the Mongols have set themselves to cultivating the land, and building houses, they have become poor. The Kitats (Chinese) have taken possession of the country; flocks, herds, lands, houses, all have passed into their hands.
p.s: A Mongol horseman, as reported by Évariste Huc (translated by William Hazlitt, 1852)

p.h: Hangzhou's temples and ten thousand stone bridges
p.g: The Khan sent the legates home through Manzi, southern China, with its 'thirty thousand great cities'. Campsay (Hangzhou), the old Song capital, is to Marignolli the finest city in the world, full of buildings and temples, with thousands of monks living together. The ten thousand carved stone bridges he takes from earlier writers and cannot quite believe. These were Chinese buildings in a Chinese city under Mongol rule; he does not credit any of them to the Tartars.
p.q: Et inter illas est civitas famosissima nomine Campsay mirabilior, pulchrior, dicior, & maior cum maiori populo, & pluribus diviciis, & deliciis, edificiis, & maxime ydolorum templis … quam aliqua civitas, que sit in mundo, vel forte fuerit unquam. Ubi scribunt scribentes esse decem millia poncium nobilium de lapide cum sculpturis & ymaginibus principum armatorum, incredibile est non videnti, & tamen forte non menciuntur.
p.s: Giovanni de' Marignolli (Latin text ed. Gelasius Dobner, 1768)
p.pe: Chinese of Manzi (southern China) under the Great Khan
p.t: And among them is the most famous city called Campsay, more marvellous, more beautiful, richer and larger, with a greater population, more riches and delights, more buildings and above all temples of idols … than any city that exists in the world, or perhaps ever existed. There, writers write, are ten thousand fine bridges of stone with sculptures and images of armed princes; it is incredible to one who has not seen it, and yet perhaps they do not lie.
p.c: The bridge count is taken from earlier writers, as he says. Dobner's footnote wrongly identifies Campsay with Cambay in Gujarat.

p.h: Astrakhan: a low wall and a few brick houses
p.g: Contarini spent May to August 1476 at Astrakhan ('Citracan'). He says it belonged to three nephews of the Tatar emperor who wintered there and roamed the steppe in summer. The town was small, with a low wall and a few brick houses, but showed signs of larger buildings not long before, and was said to have once been a great trading place.
p.q: These three brothers remain in Citracan a few months in the winter, but in the summer do like the rest. Citracan is a small town situated on the Volga, and surrounded by a low wall. The few houses it contains are built of bricks ; but it is evident that it possessed several edifices at no very distant period.
p.s: Ambrogio Contarini (translated by S. A. Roy, 1873)

p.h: Mud castles of the Khivan landowners
p.g: Constant feuds had led landowners to build square fortified farmsteads with granaries, tanks, mills and stables for 100 to 150 people. Muraviev gives their size and materials: mud walls 18 to 20 feet high, sometimes of masonry, with domed corner towers and battlements that were only for show. He was himself held in one of these forts.
p.q: The buildings are in the form of a square, and are surrounded by walls generally of mud, but sometimes of masonry. The walls are 8 feet thick at the base, diminishing to 3 at the summit, and are from 18 to 20 feet high. They are supported on the exterior faces by round buttresses, also of mud, and are crenelated, but the battlements are merely for show
p.s: Nikolai Muraviev (translated by W. S. A. Lockhart, 1871)

p.h: A Mongol capital and a tomb of cut stone
p.g: Mustawfi credits the founding of Sultaniyyah to the Mongol Ilkhan Arghun and its completion to his son Uljaytu, who named it after himself. He gives the circuit of the walls built and planned, and describes a castle of cut stone at the centre that is Uljaytu's tomb. Elsewhere on the page he says the new capital drew settlers of all nations and that only Tabriz had as many great buildings.
p.q: The city was founded by Arghun Khan, grandson of Hulagu the Mongol, and his son Uljaytu Sultan completed it, naming it Sultaniyyah after himself … The walls which Arghun built were 12,000 paces in circuit … In the centre stands a Castle built of cut stone, which is the tomb of Uljaytu Sultan
p.s: Hamdallah Mustawfi (translated by G. Le Strange, 1919)

p.h: Kalmyk fishing camps of felt tents
p.g: Sailing down the Volga to the Caspian, Hanway slept within pistol-shot of a Kalmyk settlement and describes their round tents (kibitkas) of canes covered with thick camel-hair felt, with the fire in the middle and the smoke going out at the top. These were poor Kalmyks living by fishing, seven or eight tents together under a chosen chief; others migrated south for the winter.
p.q: At night we slept within pistol-shot of a Khalmuck settlement. The habitations of these people are round tents, which they call khabitka's, raised with canes in the form of a cone, and covered with wilocks. These tents are of 10, and some of 15 yards in circumference, and about 12 feet high; they make their fires in the center of the tent,
p.s: Jonas Hanway (Historical Account, 1753)

p.h: Kazan Tatars farm and live in houses, unlike the steppe hordes
p.g: Guagnini opens his survey of the hordes with the Kazan Tatars, conquered by Moscow in 1552. He sets them apart from the 'Campestrian' Tatars because they till fields, live in houses rather than in the open steppe, and trade with Muscovites, Turks and other Tatars. At the end of the section he adds that the steppe Tatars proper 'have no houses' and live in bands across the plains.
p.q: Hij Tartari Cazanenses reliquis ingeniosiores, & aliquantulum humaniores sunt, circa agriculturam, remque domesticam (qua a caeteris maxime differunt) versantur. In domibus non in campestribus degunt, mercimonia rerumque permutationes varias, cum vicinis Moschovitis, Turcis & caeteris Tartaris exercent
p.s: Alessandro Guagnini, Sarmatiae Europeae descriptio (Speyer, 1581)
p.t: These Kazan Tatars are cleverer and somewhat more civilised than the rest; they occupy themselves with farming and household affairs (in which they differ most from the others). They live in houses, not in the open steppe, and carry on trade and various exchanges with their neighbours the Muscovites, Turks and other Tatars
p.c: Largely drawn from Herberstein's description of Kazan.

p.h: The khan sent to China for sculptors
p.g: Bilge Qaghan says he brought sculptors from the Chinese emperor, who sent his own palace craftsmen. Through them he had a separate building (a temple or hall) put up, had sculptures carved inside and outside, and had the 'eternal stone' cut and inscribed. The Turk ruler plainly credits Chinese craftsmen with the stonework and the temple beside his brother's grave; his cousin Yollugh Tegin wrote the text.
p.q: De chez le kagan des Chinois j'ai fait venir des sculpteurs et je (leur) ai (fait) sculpter. On n'a pas rejeté mon invitation, mais on a envoyé les sculpteurs intérieurs (c.-à-d. attachés à la maison) du kagan. Je leur ai fait ériger à part l'édifice (le temple, la salle), et tailler à part les sculptures à l'intérieur et à l'extérieur, et je leur ai fait tailler la pierre.
p.s: Bilge Qaghan (inscription composed by Yollugh Tegin), Kul Tegin inscription, 732, in Vilhelm Thomsen's French translation (1896)
p.pe: Turks (Kok Turk) and Tang Chinese craftsmen
p.t: From the khagan of the Chinese I brought sculptors and had them carve. My invitation was not refused: they sent the khagan's inner (household) sculptors. I had them put up a separate building (the temple, the hall), carve sculptures inside and outside, and cut the stone.
p.c: Thomsen's translation of this passage has several question marks in the surrounding lines; the Chinese annals confirm that the emperor sent artists.

p.h: A night in a Tatar house
p.g: Lodged by a village head man, Jesse describes a room with a divan running all round it, no tables or chairs, a three-legged low table for meals, and a fireplace so big that six or eight people could stand inside the chimney. p.h: Not the ruins of a departed race
p.g: Sergeant Andreyev reported in 1763 a ruined timber 'fortress' on the Bear Islands, its beams seemingly cut with stone tools, built by 'what other nation cannot now be determined'. A German writer, von Berg, later saw such ruins as signs of great changes over many centuries. Wrangel disagrees in a footnote: these half-buried wooden huts are just like those still used in the region and are far too flimsy to have survived for centuries. This passage is not about Tartars, but it is an early, direct warning against reading ordinary ruins as relics of a lost people.
p.q: A hasty glance at these half-subterranean WOODEN jurti is quite enough to convince any one, that they are not the remains of any remote antiquity, but merely huts resembling those still in use among the population of these regions, and of too slight a construction, and too perishable a material, to permit of their having remained for centuries as the monuments of a departed race.
p.s: Ferdinand von Wrangel (English translation by Mrs Sabine, 1840), footnote
p.c: Andreyev's description is quoted from his 1763 journal (pages n99 to n100); Wrangel's own survey in 1820 found no trace of the fortress.
p.tg: ruins timber lost race interpretation

p.h: The Khan's palace: 'an assemblage of wooden houses'
p.g: Adèle defends the palace of the Crimean khans against visitors who sneered that it was only a cluster of wooden houses with crude paintings, divans and carpets. She agrees that is what it is made of, but says its charm lies in feeling, not materials. It is a useful witness to how the Tatar capital's palace was actually built: timber, painted walls, fountains and gardens.
p.q: " How," said they, " can any one apply the name of palace to that assemblage of wooden houses, daubed with coarse paintings, and furnished only with divans and carpets?" And these people were right in their way.
p.s: Adèle Hommaire de Hell (English translation, 1847)
p.c: The palace had been restored under Tsar Alexander I, as the authors say on p.363, so not everything seen was original.

p.h: A hundred leagues of wall, with mountains in the gaps
p.g: Cruz reports that the Chinese have a wall of a hundred leagues (some say more) between themselves and the Tartars, always garrisoned against Tartar raids. He reasons that it cannot be continuous but must use mountains to fill the gaps, because a Persian lord told him Persia had similar walls broken by hills. The Wall is credited plainly to the Chinese, built against the Tartars.

Pode se crer que este muro nam he cõtinuado se nam q̃ se antremetem algũs mõtes ou serras, porq̃ me afirmou hũ señor da Persia que auia semelhantes obras nalgũas partes da persia, cõ se antremeterẽ outeiros ou serras.
p.s: Gaspar da Cruz, O.P. (Tractado, Évora 1569)
p.t: as I have said, the Chinese have a hundred leagues of wall (others say it is more) between themselves and them, where there are always garrisons to defend against the incursions of the Tartars. It may be believed that this wall is not continuous, but that some mountains or ranges come in between, because a lord of Persia assured me that there were similar works in some parts of Persia, with hills or ranges coming in between.

p.h: Houses of mud, wood and mats, and a roofed bazaar
p.g: Behind its famous mosques, Bukhara was built of humble materials. Most houses had one storey, a few more than two, made of mud, wood and mats. The great roofed bazaar built by the late king, with its long straight line of shops hung with Chinese porcelain and Russian bottles, impressed him most.
p.q: The houses are mostly of one story high; some of them of more than two; they are neatly constructed of mud, wood, and mats, which prevent the falling of the dust from the roof. … The large bazar, which is roofed, has a very striking appearance.
p.s: Mohan Lal (1846 edition)

p.h: Oak walls twenty-eight feet thick
p.g: Using Professor Surovzov's 1778 study of the chronicles and of old gate sites, Erman reconstructs the Tatar city before 1552. It was nearly as big as the Kazan of his own day. Its walls were two parallel fences of very thick oak timbers, twenty-five feet apart, with the space between filled with stones and clay, and it had thirteen gates with towers.
p.q: The walls round the town measured in thickness twenty-eight feet, and were formed of two parallel wooden fences twenty-five feet asunder, and having the space between them filled up with stones and clay. The wooden fences, as well as the towers over the gates, were formed of oak timbers of extraordinary thickness. The gates, with their towers, were thirteen in number
p.s: Adolph Erman (translated by W. D. Cooley, 1848), after G. S. Surovzov (1778)
p.c: Reconstructed from chronicles and excavations of gate sites, not seen by Erman.

p.h: Cave houses dug by Chinese settlers
p.g: Caught in a freezing storm in the Ordos, the priests found a ravine lined with man-made caves, neatly plastered, with windows, stoves and heated beds (kang). Huc explains that Chinese settlers in Tartary dig such homes into hard hillsides. A Mongol sheltering in the next cave told them he had known the Chinese families who dug them, and that the local Mongols had driven them out two years before for encroaching and stealing.
p.q: not simple caves formed by nature, but fine, spacious apartments excavated by the hand of man. … When the Chinese establish themselves anywhere in Tartary, if they find mountains, the earth of which is hard and solid, they excavate caverns in their sides. These habitations are cheaper than houses, and less exposed to the irregularity of the seasons.
p.s: Évariste Huc (translated by William Hazlitt, 1852)
p.tg: cave dwellings yaodong chinese settlers ordos

p.h: Stone statues on the steppe that today's Tartars know nothing about
p.g: She examined upright stone figures scattered over the steppe, each carved with a man's or woman's bust. From their dress and faces she judges them 'Tartar workmanship' of Kalmyk or Hun type, but notes that the living Tatars know nothing of them and she cannot tell whether they marked graves or grazing bounds. Matthew Guthrie adds a whole appendix on them.
p.q: They are standing perpendicularly in the ground, bearing each the bust of a man or woman tolerably sculptured for Tartar workmanship; which there can be no doubt of their being, from the particular dress in which they are represented, and the marked features of the Calmouks, or Huns. But whether these rude monuments of antiquity (for the present race of Tartars know nothing about them,)…
p.s: Maria Guthrie (letter, translated by Matthew Guthrie, 1802)
p.pl: Nogai steppe east of the Dnieper
p.c: Attribution by dress and 'features' is guesswork; these stone figures (kamennye baby) belong to several earlier steppe peoples.
p.tg: stone statues kamennye baby monuments steppe

p.h: Not caves but shining tents of waxed silk
p.g: The Chinese, bitter enemies of the Niuche Tartars, mock them as cave-dwellers, but the text calls this false: they live in fine tents used instead of houses, made of silk or cloth coated with clear wax so they shine like mirrors and shed the rain. Great men have several tents joined so they look like one, for wives, servants and kitchen.
p.q: De Sinezen, die met recht op de Tarters van Niuche zeer gebeeten zijn; verdichten en drijven hen tot spot na, datze in holen en onderaartsche kuilen woonen; 't welk valsch is: want zy onthouden zich in zeer schoone en cierlijke Tenten … uit zijde stoffen of lakens, die met helder en doorschijnend wasch zoo aartigh en kunstig bestreeken zijn, datze in de Zon glinsteren en blinken als een spiegel
p.s: Johan Nieuhof, general description of China (Dutch, 1665); this part is compiled, largely from Martino Martini
p.t: The Chinese, who with good reason are very bitter against the Tartars of Niuche, invent and mock them by saying that they live in caves and underground pits; which is false: for they keep themselves in very fine and handsome tents … of silk stuffs or cloths, so neatly and artfully coated with bright, translucent wax that they glitter and shine in the sun like a mirror
p.n: OCR normalized; the two printed columns, interleaved in the OCR, are read in order.
p.tg: tents silk wax caves

p.h: Kuchum's empty capital and the mosque the Tatars still kept
p.g: Just up the Irtysh from Tobolsk, by a stream called Sibirka that he thought gave all Siberia its name, Spafarii notes the empty little town and earthworks of Kuchum, the Tatar khan who ruled when Yermak's Cossacks came. The site was naturally strong, an island, but deserted. Only the Tobolsk Tatars still renewed a mosque there and came to worship. The editor adds that the historian Müller later described these ruins.
p.q: близъ рѣчки лежитъ пустой городокъ и шанцы Кучюма царя Сибирского, который владѣлъ въ то время, какъ приходилъ Ермакъ въ Сибирь; и мѣсто то самое крѣпкое: островъ есть, однакожъ нынѣ лежитъ пусто, толко Тоболскія Татары для воспоминанія нечистые ихъ вѣры магмецкіе обновили прежъ сего и нынѣ обновляютъ мечеть, въ которой по ихъ нечистой вѣрѣ приходяще дѣйствуютъ.
p.s: Nikolai Spafarii (ed. Yu. V. Arsenyev, 1882)
p.pe: Siberian Tatars (Tobolsk Tatars, former subjects of Khan Kuchum)
p.t: near the stream lies the empty little town and earthworks of Kuchum, tsar of Siberia, who ruled at the time when Yermak came into Siberia; and the place is very strong: it is an island, yet now it lies empty, only the Tobolsk Tatars, in remembrance of their unclean Mahometan faith, renewed a mosque before this and renew it now, in which they come and perform their rites according to their unclean faith.
p.c: Spafarii does not say he visited the site, which lies a short way upriver from Tobolsk where he stayed; 'unclean faith' is his Orthodox hostility to Islam.
p.tg: kuchum isker ruins mosque earthworks

p.h: Stone stairs of a palace no Manchu built
p.g: Near Ningguta the Jesuits found ruined cities, one reachable only by a narrow causeway through water, with great stone staircases and palace remains finer than anything in Ningguta itself. They concluded these were the work not of the present Manchus but of the twelfth-century Kin (Jurchen), who ruled north China, built towns and palaces, and were then destroyed by the Mongols and the Chinese.
p.q: Here are also found great Stone Stair-cases, with some other Remains of a Palace … So that it is very probable, all the Monuments of Antiquity in Eastern Tartary were not the Work of the present Manchews, but of those of the 12th Century, who, under the Name of Kin chau, were Masters of the North of China
p.s: Jesuit map-makers of 1709 to 1711 (Régis, Jartoux, Fridelli and others), compiled by Du Halde (English translation, 1738)
p.pe: Jurchen (Kin) of the 12th century, ancestors of the Manchus
p.tg: ruins jurchen jin dynasty palace stone

p.h: Genoese forts razed by Tatars, rebuilt by Turks
p.g: Zuev credits the Crimean fortresses to three builders: the Genoese fortified the towns, the Tatars razed the walls when they took them, and the Turks later restored the fortifications at Kefa, Kerch and Kozlov and built Arabat and Perekop. At Perekop a broad, deep, stone-lined ditch cut the isthmus from sea to sea behind an earth rampart, while the fortress itself had become heaps of brick, bombs and cannonballs.
p.q: Alle diese Oerter waren, so lange die Genueser sie beherrschten, wohl befestigt, die Tatarn schleiften aber, bey der Einnahme derselben, die Festungswerke. Wie sie nachher den Türken unterwürfig wurden, stellten selbige in Kefa, Kertsch und Koslow die Festungswerke wieder her, und legten die Festung Arabat … wie auch Perekop an
p.s: Vasily Zuev (Sujef), 'Nachrichten von der Krim', in Neue Nordische Beyträge vol. 4 (1783), edited by P. S. Pallas
p.t: All these places were well fortified as long as the Genoese ruled them, but the Tatars razed the fortifications when they took them. When they later became subject to the Turks, these restored the fortifications at Kefa, Kerch and Kozlov and built the fortress of Arabat … as well as Perekop
p.tg: fortifications genoese ottomans perekop builders

p.h: Brick-lined graves of the Astrakhan Tatars
p.g: Around Astrakhan Hanway found settled farmers 'of the race of the Crim Tartars', tributary to Russia. He contrasts their burial with the Kalmyks': they dig deep graves, line them with sun-dried bricks and whitewash them, build a cover over them, and raise mud walls around the tomb topped with white flags. The same page describes their marriage custom of the white tent (see below).
p.q: They dig their graves very deep, and after lining them with bricks dried in the sun, and whitewashing them in the inside, they build a cover over them. They also raise thick walls of mud round each tomb, on the top of which are fixed one or more white flags, according to the character of the deceased.
p.s: Jonas Hanway (Historical Account, 1753)
p.pe: Tatars of Crimean descent settled around Astrakhan
p.tg: graves mud brick tombs islam astrakhan

p.h: Building a house the Tartar way
p.g: Facing winter in a poor hut at the khan's capital, de Tott rebuilt it himself 'without departing from the method of building pursued by the Tartars'. On the next page he explains the method: a timber frame of posts, closely set uprights woven with hazel rods like a basket, packed with pounded earth and chopped straw, then plastered with lime and hair and painted. He thought it more solid and healthy than European peasant houses.
p.q: I drew the plan, I collected the materials, and superintended the work, without departing from the method of building pursued by the Tartars… I shall take this opportunity of describing the structure of the houses in Crimea; but these details, or the architecture of the Tartars, will be of more service to the lovers of oeconomy, than to disciples of Vitruvius.
p.s: Baron de Tott (English translation, 1785)
p.tg: wattle and daub timber houses building methods

p.h: The Khans' graves upset a traveller's ideas
p.g: Kohl had been taught to think of the Khans as destroyers who burned Moscow and terrorised Vilna and Warsaw. In their burial ground he found neat white marble monuments among vines, shrubs and flowers, with thoughtful inscriptions, and he concluded that 'the records of history' were imperfect.
p.q: In the burial-place of the Khans I found many memorials strikingly at variance with our notions of these barbarians; so many traces of humanity and piety, that I felt more strongly than ever, how imperfect are the records of history.
p.s: J. G. Kohl (English abridged translation, 1844)
p.tg: tombs marble khans prejudice

p.h: Chinese-style roof tiles in a marmot burrow
p.g: Heikel describes the mound beside the Kul Tegin monument. Marmots had dug into it, and from one of their holes he pulled a quantity of half-round roof tiles 'such as are still used in China to cover the roofs of houses', with more scattered on the hill. He concluded the mound was a fallen building, a temple put up when the monument was erected. It is a first-hand archaeological observation that fits the inscription's statement about Chinese builders.
p.q: Je retirai d'un des trous faits par ces animaux une quantité de tuiles demi-rondes, telles qu'on les emploie encore généralement en Chine pour couvrir les toits des maisons. Il y en avait plusieurs autres semblables éparpillées sur la colline et aux alentours.
p.s: Axel Heikel, Inscriptions de l'Orkhon (Helsingfors 1892), report of the Finnish expedition of 1890
p.t: From one of the holes made by these animals I pulled out a quantity of half-round tiles, such as are still generally used in China to cover the roofs of houses. There were several others like them scattered over the hill and round about.
p.n: Checked against the page image.
p.tg: roof tiles temple archaeology marmots chinese style

p.h: Steppe cemeteries of stone and clay: pyramids, towers, a khan's domed tomb
p.g: Levshin calls a Kazakh cemetery one of the most curious sights for a traveller: after the empty steppe the eye rests on pyramids, towers and high enclosures built of stone and clay, spears hung with horsehair and ribbons, yurt lattices, stone or wooden turbans, a saddle, bow and arrows on a famous rider's grave. Over the grave of Abulkhair Khan stood a square vaulted building. The Kazakhs, a nomadic people, built lasting monuments for their dead.
p.q: глаза останавливаются или подъ тѣнью дерева, или на складенныхъ изъ камней и глины пирамидахъ, башняхъ и высокихъ оградахъ. Въ одномъ мѣстѣ видитъ онъ копья съ развѣвающимися на нихъ конскими гривами, лентами и платками; въ другомъ рѣшетки, служившія стѣнами кибиткѣ … Надъ гробомъ Хана Абуль-хайра на рѣчкѣ Улкіакѣ … было построено квадратное зданіе со сводомъ
p.s: Aleksei Levshin (1832)
p.pl: Kazakh steppe; Olkeyek river (tomb of Abulkhair Khan)
p.t: the eyes come to rest either in the shade of a tree, or on pyramids, towers and high enclosures built of stones and clay. In one place he sees spears with horse manes, ribbons and kerchiefs fluttering from them; in another, the lattices that served as the walls of a kibitka … Over the grave of Abulkhair Khan on the Olkeyek stream … a square vaulted building was built
p.tg: cemeteries tombs abulkhair stone and clay grave markers

p.h: Pit houses of the Baraba Tatars
p.g: Crossing the Baraba steppe between Tara and Tomsk, Lorenz Lange's party met the Baraba Tatars, whom he calls heathens living wretchedly. Their winter dwellings were dug into the ground, raised about an ell above it with stakes and roofed with straw; inside each stood a small wooden idol in human shape, dressed in rags, called Shaitan, to whom they promised a cap or collar in return for good hunting.
p.q: Im Winter bewohnet diese Wüsteney eine Horde von Tartaren, welche von denen Russen Barabinsky Tartaren genennet werden … In ihren Wohnungen, welche in der Erde gegraben, und oberhalb ungefehr eine Elle mit Staqueten erhöhet, und mit Stroh bedecket sind, halten sie einen kleinen aus Holz geschnittenen Abgott, in der Gestalt eines Menschen.
p.s: Lorenz Lange (journal of his 1715 journey to China, printed by Weber)
p.pe: Baraba Tatars (Siberian Tatars between Tara and Tomsk)
p.t: In winter this wilderness is inhabited by a horde of Tartars whom the Russians call Baraba Tartars … In their dwellings, which are dug into the earth and raised about an ell above it with stakes and covered with straw, they keep a small idol carved from wood in the shape of a man.
p.c: Cited from the 1744 reissue, which reprints the 1721 text page for page with clearer OCR.
p.tg: pit houses idols shaitan baraba

p.h: 'The wanderer builds no farmsteads and no palaces'
p.g: A line of the poem, quoted in Vambery's glossary under the word for 'nomad', says that the person who moves from place to place does not build farmsteads or palaces. The poet is contrasting nomad life with the settled court life of Kashgar, where palaces (saray) were built. It is an eleventh-century Turkic writer's own view that nomads and palace-builders were different ways of living.
p.q: köcükli kisi etmes urtu saraj. Der von einem Orte zum andern ziehet, bauet keine Gehöfte und Schlösser. (87)
p.s: Yusuf Khass Hajib, Kutadgu Bilig (1069 to 1070), verse quoted with German translation in Vambery's glossary (1870)
p.pe: Turkic nomads of the Qarakhanid realm
p.t: köchükli kishi etmes urtu saray: he who moves from one place to another builds no farmsteads and no palaces. (chapter 87)
p.c: A moral saying about the uncertainty of worldly life rather than an ethnographic report; Vambery's readings are now outdated (Arat 1947).
p.n: Checked against the page image.

p.h: The minaret of Bolgar, built by a vanished people
p.g: Haxthausen climbed the surviving minaret at Bolgar, which he credits to the old Bulgarian state destroyed by the Mongols and Tatars. The ruins stand beside a Russian church, Kazan Tatars still make pilgrimages to the saints' tombs there, and Alexander von Humboldt had scratched his name on the minaret wall.
p.q: The powerful and civilized Bulgarian people who founded this important city have quite disappeared, and the Russians, Tatars, Tchuvash, etc. have taken their place ; all trace of their physiognomy, customs, and language is lost. … We ascended the lofty minaret, which commands an extensive view over boundless forests.
p.s: August von Haxthausen (translated by Robert Farie, 1856)
p.c: His claim that the Bulgars left no trace is his own opinion; the Kazan Tatars themselves (see his p.323) were often described as partly descended from them.

p.h: The 'Silver Hill': a buried brick fortress
p.g: What looked like a hill on the coast turned out to be the sand-covered shell of a huge fired-brick building with a wall about 600 feet long. Muraviev dug for coins and found Muslim-style graves and broken glass. The local Turkmens told him it had been built by the Russians, and a translator's footnote links it to an ancient wall along the Gorgan River.
p.q: The Silver Hill is, as above mentioned, only the shell of some huge building or fortress, which has been covered with sand from the eastern side ; nevertheless within those walls I found tombs, and, indeed, got at some human remains, buried after the Mahomedan fashion … The great wall is about 600 feet long and over 12 feet in height. It consists of beautiful burnt bricks
p.s: Nikolai Muraviev (translated by W. S. A. Lockhart, 1871)
p.pl: Gorgan River mouth, southeast Caspian coast
p.pe: Yomut Turkmens (living around it); builders unknown
p.c: The site lies at the western end of the brick barrier now called the Great Wall of Gorgan, usually dated to the Sasanian period. The claim that Russians built it is local belief, and the footnote rejects it.
p.tg: ruins fired brick fortress gorgan wall turkmen

p.h: Ruins of an imperial city, its stones carried off to build Astrakhan
p.g: Near Tsaritsyn Struys passed the ruins of Czaresgorod, the 'Imperial City', which he says Tamerlane destroyed. It had been built of hard stone, some remains of which could still be seen, but most of it had been carried off to Astrakhan to build that city. This matches the known reuse of brick and stone from the ruined Golden Horde capital, though Struys does not say who built it.
p.q: nous passâmes prés des ruines de Czaresgorod ou Ville Impériale, qui fut détruite par Tamerlan pendant la guerre dont nous avons ci-dessus parlé. Elle étoit bâtie de pierres dures dont on voit encore quelques restes, mais la plupart furent portées à Astracan, & servirent à la construire.
p.s: Jan Struys (French translation by Glanius, Amsterdam 1681)
p.pl: Tsarev, lower Volga (probably the Golden Horde capital, New Sarai)
p.t: we passed near the ruins of Czaresgorod, or Imperial City, which was destroyed by Tamerlane during the war we spoke of above. It was built of hard stones, of which some remains are still seen, but most were carried to Astrakhan and served to build it.
p.c: Struys saw ruins from the river; the Tamerlane story and the stone reuse he had from others.
p.tg: sarai ruins stone astrakhan tamerlane

p.h: A tent for two thousand people at Güyük's election
p.g: At the assembly that elected Güyük Great Khan, Carpini found a huge tent of white purple cloth which he reckoned could hold more than two thousand people, ringed by a wooden palisade painted with figures. The chiefs changed the colour of their robes each day. A few pages on he describes another tent, the 'Golden Horde', on pillars covered with gold plates fixed with gold nails.
p.q: Nous trouuames là vne tente de pourpre blanc tres-grande, voire telle, à nostre aduis, qu'elle estoit capable de tenir plus de deux mil personnes. A l'entour d'icelle on auoit fait esleuer vn eschaffaut ou palissade de bois, remply de diuerses figures & peintures.
p.s: John of Plano Carpini (French translation by Pierre Bergeron, 1634)
p.t: There we found a very large tent of white purple, so large, in our opinion, that it could hold more than two thousand people. Around it they had set up a scaffold or palisade of wood, covered with various figures and paintings.

p.h: Round reed huts for summer, other houses for winter
p.g: Three versts from Kuznetsk Gmelin visited a village of Teleut Tatars with two kinds of houses, one for summer and one for winter. The summer huts were round and pointed, about three fathoms across, with a small door on the east side, a smoke hole at the top, benches all round and a cooking hollow in the middle. They were built of reeds woven onto thin poles, with birch bark tucked in against the rain.
p.q: Das Dorf bestehet aus zweyerley Art Häusern, in der einen wohnen sie des Sommers, in der andern des Winters. … Die Sommerhütten sind von Figur rund, und oben zugespitzt … Der Bauzeug dieser Häuser ist Schilf, welches an die inwendig zusammen verbundenen dünnen Stöcke angeflochten
p.s: Johann Georg Gmelin (German original, Göttingen, 1751)
p.t: The village consists of two kinds of houses: in the one they live in summer, in the other in winter... The summer huts are round in shape and pointed at the top... The building material of these houses is reed, woven onto thin poles bound together on the inside

p.h: A queen's travelling mosque, left at the border
p.g: Ibn Battuta escorted Uzbek Khan's Byzantine wife on a visit to her father in Constantinople. Like her husband, she carried a mosque (evidently a tent) that was set up at every halt for daily prayers. At the first Byzantine fortress she left it behind, and from then on, he says with some dismay, the call to prayer stopped and wine appeared at her table.
p.q: The Queen had with her a mosque, which she set up at every stage, just as her husband used to do. In this she had daily prayers. She left it, however, at the fortress. After this the office of the Moazin ceased : wine was brought into the banquet and of this she drank.
p.s: Ibn Battuta (translated by Samuel Lee, 1829)
p.pl: Balkans, on the road to Constantinople
p.tg: mosque tent portable islam khatun byzantium

p.h: The round felt tent used 'over all Tartary'
p.g: Elphinstone contrasts two ways of living among the Uzbeks. Their houses, villages and towns look just like Afghan ones, but their tent is the round lattice tent covered with felt (the yurt), which he calls the kirgah and says is used across all of Tartary. On the same page he adds that it is warmer than the Afghan black tent and hardly harder to carry.
p.q: Their houses, villages, and towns, exactly resemble those of the Afghauns, but their tents are widely different The Uzbek tent is of the kind called Kirgah, which appears to be in use over all Tartary, in part of Persia, and even in part of China. It is round, and formed of lattice work … covered with black or grey felts.
p.s: Mountstuart Elphinstone (1815)
p.c: From informants; Elphinstone did not visit Uzbek country.
p.tg: yurt kirgah felt lattice houses

p.h: Who built the ruins of the steppe? 'Not our ancestors'
p.g: Levshin's chapter on ruins begins by admitting that it is hard to say who built them, because they are of different kinds: some are Buddhist temples plainly built by Mongols or Dzungars, some look like mosques, some are ordinary Asian dwellings, some are too ruined to judge. Materials differ too: big stones, brick, clay. The Kazakhs, he says, only agree that the buildings were not their ancestors', and they call old graves and a few ruins 'Nogai'.
p.q: Трудно и даже едва ли возможно опредѣлить, какой народъ строилъ сіи зданія: ибо они разныхъ родовъ. Одни, сохранивъ признаки капищъ, Ламайскому служенію посвященныхъ, очевидно принадлежатъ Мунгаламъ, или Зюнгарамъ; другія похожи на Магометанскія мечети; третьи суть остатки обыкновенныхъ Азіатскихъ жилищъ … Нынѣшніе Киргизъ-Казаки вообще не говорятъ объ нихъ ничего правдоподобнаго, кромѣ того, что они не принадлежатъ ихъ предкамъ
p.s: Aleksei Levshin (1832)
p.pe: Kazakhs; Mongols and Dzungars; unknown earlier peoples
p.t: It is hard, and hardly even possible, to determine what people built these buildings, for they are of various kinds. Some, keeping signs of temples devoted to Lamaist worship, clearly belong to the Mongols or Dzungars; others resemble Muslim mosques; a third kind are remains of ordinary Asian dwellings … The present Kirghiz-Kazakhs in general say nothing plausible about them, except that they do not belong to their ancestors
p.tg: ruins builders buddhist temples mosques stone and brick

p.h: Nomads who fear that houses will fall on them
p.g: Soopoon Choomboo told Turner that the wandering people beyond the desert disliked entering houses. Turner passes on the explanation he heard (fear that houses would fall, perhaps from earthquakes) and adds his own guess: that the ability to flee smallpox made a mobile life attractive. Either way, he says, large hordes still live in tents with their herds.
p.q: This prejudice is said to have its foundation in a dread of their falling; an apprehension which may perhaps have originated, in remote times, from the calamitous effects of earthquakes … Thus large hordes of Tartars are still found to dwell in tents, tending upon cattle, and placing their chief dependance upon their herds
p.s: Samuel Turner (1800)
p.c: Both explanations are guesses; the second (smallpox) is Turner's own.
p.tg: tents houses nomads earthquakes smallpox

p.h: Stone houses and mud-brick ovens in Little Bukharia
p.g: The anonymous author, who says he lived in Little Bukharia, describes its townspeople's houses as built of stone and fairly good, with few furnishings: no tables or chairs, only Chinese chests on which mattresses were laid. Slaves bought from the Kalmyks, Russians and others cooked in iron pots set into a hearth, and some houses had small ovens of clay or unbaked brick, like their walls.
p.q: Les maisons des Bouchars sont de pierre, & passablement bonnes. Leurs meubles sont en petit nombre, & de peu d'ornement. Ils n'ont ni tables ni chaises. … Il y en a qui ont aussi de petits fours, qui se font, comme le reste de leurs murailles, de terre grasse ou de briques crues.
p.s: Anonymous author of the 'Relation de la Boucharie'
p.pe: Bukharans (townspeople of Little Bukharia) under Kalmyk rule
p.t: The houses of the Bukharans are of stone and passably good. Their furniture is scanty and plain. They have neither tables nor chairs. … Some also have small ovens, which are made, like the rest of their walls, of clay or of unbaked bricks.
p.c: The text says both stone houses and walls of clay or mud brick; which was usual is not clear.

p.h: The khan's stone palaces and clay-daubed wooden houses
p.g: The khan had two residences, one at Bakhchysarai and one on the Alma. At Bakhchysarai the khan's 'palaty' (chambers), kitchens and stables were of stone, set low under a hill, with a church of the Virgin two versts away served by Greeks. The Alma court had one stone chamber and wooden houses plastered with clay, standing in a vineyard. It is a rare early note on Crimean Tatar building materials.
p.q: А въ Бакчисараѣ палаты Царевы, поварни и конюшни, каменныя, а стоитъ подъ горою ниско; да за Царевымъ дворомъ версты съ 2, церковь Пречистыя Богородицы въ солончакахъ, а служатъ у нее Гречане. А которой дворъ на рѣкѣ на Алмѣ, и въ томъ дворѣ одна палата, да избы деревянныя, обмазанныя глиною, а стоитъ на берегу въ виноградѣ.
p.s: Book of the Great Map (1627), ed. Yazykov (1838)
p.t: And in Bakhchysarai the tsar's chambers, kitchens and stables are of stone, and it stands low beneath a hill; and about 2 versts beyond the tsar's court is a church of the Most Pure Mother of God in the salt flats, and Greeks serve in it. And the court on the river Alma has one stone chamber, and wooden houses daubed with clay, and it stands on the bank in a vineyard.
p.c: The church is probably the Uspensky cave monastery near Bakhchysarai; 'palata' in 17th-century Russian usually means a masonry building.

p.h: Mud and dung huts in winter, round houses on carts in summer
p.g: Broniewski, the Polish envoy who spent nine months in the Crimean khanate, describes Tatar winter villages called 'ulus': huts of very thin wood daubed with mud and animal dung and roofed with reed. In April the Tatars leave them with wives, children and slaves, carrying round felt-covered houses that barely hold four or five people on two-wheeled carts drawn by camels or oxen, and return in October.
p.q: tugurijs Tartaricis, quæ vulgo vlnsi à Barbaris nominantur, ac vt pagi ex tenuissimis lignis, limo vel cœno stercoribusque pecorum seu animalium obliti, facti, & arundine tecti sunt … Verùm æstate & in autumno Tartari in eis tugurijs non degunt, nam in Aprili cum vxoribus, liberis, familia, mancipijs ac domibus, quæ rotundæ penulis obsitæ quatuor vel quinque hominibus ad degendum vix commodæ sunt, & in carris rotis duabus sustentatis … vehũtur.
p.s: Marcin Broniewski (Martin Broniovius), Tartariae descriptio (written 1579), printed in the 1595 Cologne edition of Possevino's Moscovia
p.t: Tartar huts, which the barbarians commonly call 'vlnsi' (evidently ulus, a misprint), made like villages of very thin wood, plastered with mud or muck and the dung of cattle or animals, and roofed with reed ... But in summer and autumn the Tartars do not live in these huts, for in April, with wives, children, household and slaves, they are carried with their houses, which are round, covered with penulae (felt coverings), and scarcely roomy enough for four or five people to live in, on carts resting on two wheels ...

p.h: Alushta: terraced roofs and a mosque of wood and clay
p.g: Webster describes the Tatar village of Alushta built in terraces up the hillside, so that each house's flat roof served as the street or promenade for the one above. Its mosque, under huge walnut trees, was a 'rude structure of wood and clay' with a projecting roof. It is a precise picture of vernacular Tatar building materials.
p.q: Alushta is built on a sort of terrace, so that the flat roof of one house serves as a promenade to the people of the upper one. There are seven or eight rows of these houses, none having more than one flat, and that very low, with a portico in front … The mosque is embowered among old and immense walnut trees. It is a rude structure of wood and clay
p.s: James Webster
p.pe: Crimean Tatars of the south coast
p.c: 'One flat' here means one storey.

p.h: Circassian houses of earth and boughs, and no walled towns
p.g: At Terki the Tsar kept garrisons in all the towns, leaving the Circassians only open towns and villages under their own lords. Their houses were poor ones of earth and branches, plastered inside with clay. Olearius adds that they spoke the common Tartar language and were Muslims in name, though without Koran or priests.
p.q: he hath put Garrisons into all the Cities, leaving the Circassian Tartars, for their habitations, but only open Towns and Villages … Their houses are but poor ones, built, for the most part, of earth and boughs of trees, and within, plaister'd over with Clay.
p.s: Adam Olearius (English translation by John Davies, 1669)
p.pl: Terki, on the Terek river, North Caucasus
p.pe: 'Circassian Tartars' (Kabardians of the Terek) under Russian rule

p.h: A Muslim saint-khan's tomb, and the wrestling match that converted his people
p.g: The Tobolsk Bukharans in Unkovsky's party told him of the tomb of 'Temer khan', a ruler of the Ili who, they said, had worshipped idols until a Muslim merchant threw his strongest wrestler three times. The khan then converted, his people were circumcised and threw the tassels from their caps into the Borotala river, damming it. Muslims built chambers over his grave and still brought offerings. Unkovsky wanted to see it but was not allowed. The tomb is generally identified with the mausoleum of the Chagatai khan Tughluq Timur near Khorgos.
p.q: Того ради Темерханъ принялъ Махометской законъ, и всѣ его владѣнія люди обрѣзались и съ шапокъ залы (или кисти) въ рѣку Борталъ побросали, и будто оными рѣку запрудили. И для вышеозначенного махометане оного Темерхана, святымъ почитаютъ, а надъ гробомъ его полаты построены и приносятъ доднесь махометане приносы на гробъ его, и сторожи при томъ гробѣ имѣются.
p.s: Ivan Unkovsky, reporting what the Tobolsk Bukharans told him (ed. N. I. Veselovsky, 1887)
p.pe: Chagatai Mongols (Temer khan) and Muslim Bukharans
p.w: told on 9 November 1722; events c. 1388 by the Bukharans' reckoning
p.t: For that reason Temer khan accepted the Muhammadan law, and all the people of his realm were circumcised and threw the tassels from their caps into the river Borotala, and supposedly dammed the river with them. And for this the Muhammadans revere Temer khan as a saint, and chambers have been built over his tomb, and to this day the Muhammadans bring offerings to his tomb, and there are guards at that tomb.
p.c: A conversion legend passed on by Muslim merchants; Unkovsky did not see the tomb. The identification with Tughluq Timur is a modern one, not Unkovsky's.

p.h: A Kazakh tent of folding trellis
p.g: On the steppe four miles from Omsk, Holman and an interpreter visited a family of Kazakhs in their tent. He learned that the frame was made of neat trellis-work that folded up small for moving, covered with thick matting, with woollen beds round half the wall separated by fine cane screens. A pit dug near the centre kept the lambs warm, while sheep and horses had tents of their own. The family let him examine whatever he liked.
p.q: The frame of the tent was made of neat trellis-work, so constructed as to admit of being folded up into a small compass, for the convenience of conveyance, whenever they think proper to change their habitations; this was surrounded by thick matting; around one half of the inner circumference of the tent were placed beds of a coarse woollen stuff
p.s: James Holman (1825)
p.c: Holman was blind; his description comes from touch and from what his interpreter told him.

p.h: The silver tree made by a Paris goldsmith
p.g: At Karakorum Mongke had a large walled court beside the town wall with a great palace where he held drinking feasts twice a year. Because it was unseemly to carry skins of milk and drink into the hall, Master William of Paris, a goldsmith captured in Hungary and working for the khan, made at the entrance a great silver tree with four silver lions at its roots, from which mare's milk flowed through a pipe.
p.q: Ipse Mangu habet apud Caracarum magnam curiam juxta muros ville … Ibi est unum magnum palatium, in quo tenet potationem suam bis in anno … In introitu illius magni palatii, quia turpe erat ibi inferre utres cum lacte et aliis potibus, fecit ei magister Willielmus parisiensis unam magnam arborem argenteam, ad cujus radices sunt quatuor leones argentei, habentes unum cannale, et vomentes omnes lac album jumenti.
p.s: William of Rubruck
p.pe: Mongke Khan's court; the Parisian goldsmith William Buchier
p.t: Mongke himself has at Karakorum a great court next to the town walls … There is a great palace in which he holds his drinking feast twice a year … At the entrance of this great palace, since it was unseemly to bring in skins of milk and other drinks, Master William of Paris made him a great silver tree, at whose roots are four silver lions with a pipe, all spouting white mare's milk.
p.c: Rubruck names the maker as a Parisian captive craftsman; the Mongols' showpiece was European and Chinese workmanship.

p.h: A wall of brushwood built by captives at Esztergom
p.g: Esztergom, the richest city in Hungary, had fortified itself with ditches, walls and wooden towers. Roger says the Tartars had their captives carry bundles of branches and pile them into a high wall along the edge of the ditch in a single effort, then set thirty stone-throwing machines behind it and pounded the city and its wooden towers day and night. The builders of this siege work, he notes, were the prisoners.
p.q: Strigonienses interim se cum fossatis muris et turribus ligneis fortissime munierant. … Ecce una dierum ciuitatem Tartari circumdederunt, et captiui qui cum eis erant tot ramorum fasciculos portauerunt, quibus in una parte ciuitatis supra fossati supercilium altum murum simul et semel de fasciculis construxerunt, et statim post murum illum dictas triginta machinas posuerunt
p.s: Master Roger (Rogerius), Carmen miserabile, in the 1885 Budapest edition (Chronica minora)
p.t: Meanwhile the people of Esztergom had fortified themselves very strongly with ditches, walls and wooden towers. … Then one day the Tartars surrounded the city, and the captives who were with them carried so many bundles of branches that on one side of the city, on the brink of the ditch, they built a high wall of the bundles all at once, and immediately behind that wall they set the thirty machines already mentioned
p.c: Roger was not at Esztergom; he reports the siege from others.

p.h: Who dug the old graves and mines of Siberia?
p.g: Russians called the old graves and ancient mine shafts found across Siberia 'Chudic', and some scholars built on the word a theory of a highly civilised Chud people who once worked the Altai mines. Klaproth answers that the adjective simply means 'foreign' or 'unknown', as vague as 'Scythian' or 'barbarian', and links the theory to Bailly's dreams of a civilised plateau of Tatary, which he says does not exist.
p.q: Il y a même eu des savans qui croyaient qu'une partie de la Sibérie avait été autrefois habitée par des Tchoudes, que ce peuple était très-civilisé, qu'il exploitait les mines des montagnes d'Altai et autres. Toutes ces hypothèses ne sont fondées que sur l'adjectif tchoudique, dont on se sert en Russie et en Sibérie pour désigner les anciens tombeaux et les galeries de mines
p.s: Julius Klaproth
p.pe: the 'Chud', a vague name for unknown ancient peoples
p.t: There have even been scholars who believed that part of Siberia had once been inhabited by Chuds, that this people was highly civilised, and that it worked the mines of the Altai and other mountains. All these hypotheses rest only on the adjective 'Chudic', which is used in Russia and Siberia to designate the ancient tombs and mine galleries

p.h: A stone minaret and a khan's tomb at Kasimov
p.g: In the Tatar quarter Pallas measured a tall round tower (a minaret, which he calls Misgir) of dressed limestone, all that stood of a ruined mosque (Metsched) built of large bricks. On the next page he describes the plain stone mausoleum of the khans with a small prayer room, and reports that the owner of the land had pulled down the carved gate and the khan's house and burned much of the stone for lime.
p.q: stehet noch izt in dem höchsten Theil der Stadt, ein hoher und starker, rund aufgeführter Thurn oder Misgir, von einem zerstöhrten Bethause… Das alte Bethaus, oder Metsched, hat aus Ziegeln bestanden, welche über 13 Zoll groß sind; der Thurn aber ist aus lauter glattgehauenen und ziemlich grossen Baustücken… erbaut.
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (Reise, first edition, St Petersburg 1771-1776)
p.t: there still stands in the highest part of the town a tall, strong, round-built tower or Misgir, from a ruined house of prayer… The old house of prayer, or Metsched, was of bricks more than 13 inches long; but the tower is built entirely of smoothly dressed and fairly large blocks of stone.
