p.h: Log houses roofed with birch bark
p.g: Klaproth translates the Chinese encyclopedist Ma Duanlin on a northern people called the Piebald Horses. They built houses of logs laid one on another like the curb of a well, roofed them with birch bark, slept on hay, did not ride but drank mare's milk and fattened black-maned horses to eat. Klaproth notes that Ostyaks and Samoyeds still build this way and thinks the people were one of those tribes.
p.q: Leurs habitations sont faites avec des arbres posés les uns sur les autres, comme on fait les clôtures des puits. Le toit est couvert d'écorce de bouleau. La terre, le bois, l'herbe ou la paille leur servent de tapis, et l'endroit où ils dorment est couvert de foin. D'autres n'ont pas de demeure fixe.
p.s: Ma Duanlin (Chinese encyclopedist, c. 1300), translated by Julius Klaproth
p.pe: Boma, the 'Piebald Horse' people of southern Siberia
p.t: Their dwellings are made of trees laid one upon another, as the curbs of wells are made. The roof is covered with birch bark. Earth, wood, grass or straw serve them as carpets, and the place where they sleep is covered with hay. Others have no fixed dwelling.
p.c: The link Klaproth draws between these Piebald Horses and the later 'piebald horde' of Siberia is his own suggestion.
p.tg: log houses birch bark siberia chinese sources

p.h: The Kalmyk kibitka: a felt house two camels can carry
p.g: A precise description of the felt tent (kibitka) from people who stayed in them: a cylinder as high as a man's shoulder, a conical roof open at the top for smoke, a wooden ring held up by many spars. The whole thing comes apart and can be carried by two camels. On the next page they add that the felts kept out the fiercest storms, as they learned from experience.
p.q: Their dwellings are felt tents, called kibitkas by the Russians. They are four or five yards in diameter, cylindrical to the height of a man's shoulder, with a conical top, open at the apex to let the smoke escape. The frame is light, and can be taken asunder for the convenience of carriage.
p.s: Xavier and Adèle Hommaire de Hell (English translation, 1847)

p.h: Madzhar's brick buildings, described in 1772
p.g: Klaproth quotes the naturalist S. G. Gmelin, who saw the ruins in 1772 when they were best preserved: a great city on a plateau, with fortified mansions at the edge. The bricks were like those Astrakhan Tatars still made; walls were bonded mostly with clay and plastered and whitewashed inside; buildings were square, octagonal or round, up to nine fathoms high and topped by pyramids or domes.
p.q: The bricks resemble those still made by the Tartars of Astrachan, that is to say, they are broader and thicker than ours. In the external walls, a mortar composed of lime and sand is used only here and there, the cement generally employed being clay alone… The figure of the buildings yet preserved is square, octagonal, and circular.
p.s: Samuel Gottlieb Gmelin (visit of 1772), in Klaproth's extract (English translation, 1814)
p.c: Gmelin called it 'a magnificent Scythian city'; Klaproth corrects the attribution to the Golden Horde.

p.h: The craftsmen of Damascus marched off to Samarkand
p.g: When Timur took Damascus in 1401, Ibn Arabshah says he carried off its learned men and craftsmen, 'everyone skilled in any art': weavers, tailors, stone-cutters, carpenters, cap-makers, farriers, tent-makers, painters and decorators, bow-makers and falconers. They were shared out among the army commanders, who were ordered to deliver them to Samarkand. Ibn Arabshah, then a boy, was himself taken from Damascus to Samarkand.
p.q: واخذ من دمشق ارباب الفضل واهل الصنائع وكل ماهر في فن من الفنون بارع من النساجين والخياطين والحجارين والنجارين والاقباعية والبياطرة والخيميه والنقاشين والقواسين والبازداريه وفي الجملة اهل اي فن كان … وفرق هؤلاء الطوائف على رؤوس الجند وامرهم ان يوصلوهم الى سمرقند
p.s: Ahmad ibn Arabshah (Arabic text, print catalogued 1842)
p.pe: Timur's army and the craftsmen of Damascus
p.t: He took from Damascus the men of learning and the craftsmen, everyone skilled and outstanding in any art: weavers and tailors, stone-cutters and carpenters, cap-makers and farriers, tent-makers, painters and bow-makers, and falconers; in short, the people of every craft whatever … He divided these groups among the heads of the army and ordered them to deliver them to Samarkand.
p.c: Ibn Arabshah was among the captives, but wrote some thirty years later and with deep hostility to Timur.

p.h: Khiva: walls of earth and houses of mud
p.g: The British factors Hogg and Thompson reached Khiva in 1740. They describe it as the khan's seat on rising ground, defended by a very thick earth wall higher than the houses, with turrets and a wet ditch. The houses are low, mostly mud-built, with flat roofs covered in earth. On the same page they note that the Khivans live in towns while their Kazakh neighbours live in tents.
p.q: It is situated on a rising ground, has three gates, and is defended by a strong wall of earth, very thick, and much higher than the houses: it has turrets at small distances, and a broad deep ditch full of water. The place is large, but the houses are low, the greatest part of them being built with mud; the roofs are flat, and covered with earth.
p.s: British factors Reynold Hogg and George Thompson, their 1740 journal as printed by Jonas Hanway (1753)

p.h: Tombs of the khans and a monument to a Christian wife
p.g: In the palace courtyard she sees two domed rotundas holding the remains of generations of khans, and a small mausoleum said to honour a khan's beloved Christian wife, probably a captive. Inside, a marble vestibule has three fountains, and vine-and-rose bowers fill a small garden.
p.q: Near the handsome mosque in the court of Batcheferai palace, mentioned in my last, we perceived a couple of pretty rotundos, in which repose the ashes of a long line of Chans; but what most attracted our eyes… was a pretty little mausoleum, dedicated “To Conjugal Fidelity and Attachment,” erected by one of the Crimean Chans on losing a beloved christian wife, probably a fair captive
p.s: Maria Guthrie (letter, translated by Matthew Guthrie, 1802)
p.c: The story of the Christian wife is what she was told; 'probably a fair captive' is her guess.

p.h: An emperor who preferred a tent to a palace
p.g: The Qianlong emperor received the British envoy not in a hall of his summer palace but in a great tent in the garden, with small round tents pitched in front for the tributary princes. Staunton explains the choice: the Manchu rulers had adopted Chinese customs but kept a fondness for their old movable dwellings when they were on 'Tartar ground'.
p.q: The Tartar dynasty, in conforming in most instances, to the customs of a much more numerous and more civilized, tho vanquished nation, retained still a predilection for its own ancient manners, in which occasionally, and upon Tartar ground, it took a pleasure in indulging. The moveable dwelling of a tent was, more than a permanent palace of stone and timber, the favourite residence of a Tartar sovereign.
p.s: George Leonard Staunton
p.c: The explanation of the emperor's motive is Staunton's interpretation.

p.h: Ruins 'all of Tartar origin', and a palace the Kalmyks would not live in
p.g: In his appendix Matthew Guthrie lists brick ruins on the Akhtuba, at Madzhary on the Kuma (32 buildings in 1780, only four by 1793) and near the Terek, which Pallas had drawn, and calls them all of Tartar origin from their shape, construction and inscriptions. He follows Pallas in thinking them tombs or shrines, because Mongols so loved camp life that the Kalmyk princes of his day would not live in a palace Russia built for them.
p.q: all of Tartar origin, as is evident from several kinds of proof, viz. shape, construction, and inscriptions… I am of Pallas's opinion with regard to the sepulchral or religious destination of all those ruins, from the known attachment of the Monguls to a camp residence, which to this day prevents their descendants, the Calmuc princes, from inhabiting a palace built for them by the crown of Russia
p.s: Matthew Guthrie (editor's Appendix, 1802)
p.c: Second-hand from Pallas; Klaproth (W056) later argued Madzhary was a real town, not just a cemetery.

p.h: The khan's palace, 'perfectly in ruins', regilded for the Empress
p.g: Craven lodged in the khans' palace. She describes an irregular building mostly of one floor raised on pillars of painted and gilded wood, a finely proportioned doorway with a gilt inscription, courts within courts, a harem higher than the rest, and marble-paved rooms with fountains playing. She was told it had been in ruins until the Russian governor had it repaired, regilded and repainted for Catherine II's coming visit.
p.q: The Khan's palace is an irregular building, the greatest part of it is one floor raised upon pillars of wood painted and gilt in a fanciful and lively manner
p.s: Elizabeth Craven (letters published London, 1789)
p.c: What she saw was a Russian restoration of 1786, not the palace as the khans left it.

p.h: A khan who lived in a felt tent
p.g: Muraviev says the Khan of Khiva lived in a felt tent all year round and kept his houses only for his wives, spending most of his time hawking and hunting on the steppe. He also notes the Khan had banned alcohol and tobacco on pain of having one's mouth slit.
p.q: His mode of living is quite nomadic, for he occupies a felt tent all the year round, keeping his houses for his wives only. The greater part of his time is passed in the steppe, hawking or hunting, snipe and wild goats being his favourite game.
p.s: Nikolai Muraviev (translated by W. S. A. Lockhart, 1871)

p.h: Birch-bark cone for the kumis festival
p.g: Each June, Yakut chiefs held a feast to bless their herds. Mare's milk was fermented into kumis in large leather bags, and a summer hut was raised on a meadow: a cone of thin poles covered with birch bark, decorated inside and out with birch branches, with a hearth in the middle. Guests of any nation were welcome; the shamans took the head seats. The shaman then poured kumis on the fire to each of the gods.
p.q: A summer hut is built of thin poles of a conical form, covered with the inner bark of birch, on some extensive meadow. It is ornamented inside and out with branches of the birch-tree, and a hearth is made in the centre. Relations and acquaintances are invited to the banquet; but all guests are welcome of every nation indiscriminately.
p.s: Martin Sauer (1802)
p.c: Presented as general custom; Sauer does not say he attended a festival himself.

p.h: Prayer walls you must always pass on the right
p.g: Gerard describes mani walls: long dykes of loose, uncemented stone, topped with slates carved with the prayer 'Om mani padme hum'. The Tartars always keep them on the right hand, even if it means a detour of a quarter of a mile. On nearby pages he describes chortens, prayer flags on every house, and prayer wheels turned by water and wind.
p.q: the most common are tumuli, named Mane, consisting of a dyke of different lengths from ten to two hundred feet, two broad, and three or four high; they are constructed of loose stones without cement, and upon their tops are numerous pieces of slate of all shapes and sizes, carved with sentences in the Oochen or sacred character.
p.s: Alexander Gerard (ed. George Lloyd, 1841)
p.tg: mani wall stone buddhism inscriptions

p.h: A 500-league wall against the Tartars, mostly mountains
p.g: Mendoza reports a wall 500 leagues long running west to east, built by a king 'Tzintzom' (Qin Shi Huang) to protect himself from the Tartars, 'and so the wall takes in the whole frontier of Tartary'. But, he adds, 400 of those leagues are made by nature, very high closed mountains; only the remaining hundred were built by the king, of very strong stone, seven fathoms wide at the base.
p.q: Hallase en este Reyno vna cerca, o muralla, que tiene quinientas leguas de largo … Hizo la vn Rey llamado Tzintzom, por ampararse de los Tartaros, con quien tenia guerra, y assi toma la muralla toda la frontera de Tartaria. Pero ha se de entender, que las 400. leguas que tiene la dicha muralla, son hechas por la naturaleza, por que son vnas sierras altissimas muy cerradas.
p.s: Juan González de Mendoza (Historia del gran Reyno de la China, Rome 1585)
p.pe: Chinese builders; Tartars (Mongols) as the enemy
p.t: There is in this kingdom an enclosure or wall five hundred leagues long ... A king called Tzintzom made it to protect himself from the Tartars, with whom he was at war, and so the wall takes in the whole frontier of Tartary. But it must be understood that 400 of the leagues of the said wall are made by nature, for they are very high, very close-set mountains.
p.c: Mendoza never saw it; he relies on Gaspar da Cruz, Rada and Chinese books. The natural-barrier claim comes from those sources.

p.h: 'Their houses are only of cords and canvas'
p.g: As Timur approached Syria, the Mamluk governors rejected advice to make peace. Yazdi gives them a proud speech: other kingdoms fell because their towns were mud and brick, but Syria's fortresses are cut from solid rock. The Tartars, they sneer, live in homes and walls of rope and canvas, meaning tents. The boast was followed by defeat.
p.q: Their towns were built only of mud and brick ; but ours are all of solid stone, cut out of the almost impenetrable rock ;… The houses and walls of these Tartars are only of cords and canvas ; while we live in good fortresses, which are of hewn stone
p.s: Speech Sharaf al-Din Ali Yazdi puts in the mouths of the Mamluk emirs (English of 1723, via Pétis de la Croix)
p.pe: Timur's Tartar army, described by the Mamluk council of Syria
p.c: A speech composed by a court historian for enemies of his patron's grandfather, not a transcript.

p.h: Homes on eight-foot wheels
p.g: When the camp moves, Perry says, women and children ride in covered carriages on two great wheels about eight feet across, high enough to ford small rivers, and they live in these as well as in their tents 'like as in Houses'. Bactrian camels ('dromedaries') pull them. People of rank have several such carriages for baggage and servants.
p.q: …Wives and their Children are drawn on covered Machines fixed on two large Wheels of about 8 Foot diameter, … so that they can easily ford over small Rivers; in which, as well as their Tents, they live like as in Houses; and Persons of Distinction have several of these for their Baggage and Retinue. They are drawn by Dromedaries,
p.s: Captain John Perry (The State of Russia, 1716)

p.h: Domed tombs of the Khans
p.g: Beside the palace mosque, the Khans lay in a small burial ground of Turkish-style tombs, some of marble, and in two domed octagonal mausoleums about thirty feet across. Inside were wooden coffins draped in black cloth and topped with the turbans of the dead. Webster also describes the town's one-storey houses and streets of shops grouped by trade.
p.q: There are two large octagons, with domes, of about thirty feet diameter, which contain the bodies and monuments of many Khans. In the first are ten or twelve wooden coffins, covered with black cloth, and having at the top the turbans of the deceased.
p.s: James Webster

p.h: Kazan's earth-filled timber ramparts
p.g: During the siege Ivan IV's clerk Ivan Vyrodkov built a siege tower six sazhens high opposite Kazan's Tsar's Gate and mounted guns on it. The chronicle explains how the Kazan defenders survived: at every gate beyond the moat they had great 'tarasy', timber cribs filled with earth, and they dug holes and burrows under the gates and walls and fought from them 'like snakes'. Kazan's defences were timber and earth, not stone.
p.q: Погани же крыющеся въ ямы и рвы копающе подъ врата градцкые и подъ стѣну и рыюще норы подъ тарасы, бѣ бо у нихъ у всякыхъ воротъ за рвомъ тарасы велики, землею насыпаны, изъ-за тарасовъ біющеся по вся дни и изъ норъ, якоже змѣи
p.s: Nikon Chronicle, PSRL vol. 13, part 1 (1904)
p.t: And the pagans hid, digging pits and ditches under the city gates and under the wall, and burrowing holes under the tarasy (for at every gate, beyond the moat, they had great tarasy filled with earth), fighting every day from behind the tarasy and from the holes, like snakes

p.h: Bukhara burned because it was built of wood
p.g: Retelling the Mongol sack of Bukhara from Persian historians, Pétis explains why the fire was so complete: most buildings were of wood, because stone was hard to get around Bukhara. Only public buildings such as the mosques and caravanserais, built of brick, escaped. It is a clear statement of what one of Central Asia's great cities was built from.
p.q: all Parts of the Town were strait on fire, the greatest part of the Building being made of Wood, because of the difficulty of getting Stone in the Country round Bocara. … and all the Houses became a Prey to the Flames, except some publick Buildings, such as the Mosques and Caravansera's, which were made of Bricks.
p.s: François Pétis de la Croix (English translation, 1722), citing Fadlallah (Rashid al-Din) and others
p.c: Marginal source notes are mixed into the OCR here and have been dropped. Compiled five centuries after the event.

p.h: No houses, only portable huts of wicker and reeds on carts
p.g: Michalo describes the Tatars' pastoral life: they follow their herds across the plains, have no enclosures and no houses except portable tents made of wicker and reeds covered with felt and rush mats, which they carry on carts full of wives and children. They do not farm even rich land, live on milk without bread or beer, and own nothing fixed except wells shared by the clan.
p.q: Septa nulla habent, nec domos, praeter tabernacula gestatoria, ex viminibus & arundinibus compactis, cilicijs velata storeis, & mattis scirpeis munita, quae uxoribus & pueris referta, vectant secum in plaustris.
p.s: Michalo the Lithuanian, De moribus Tartarorum, Lituanorum et Moschorum, fragment 1 (c. 1550; Basel, 1615)
p.pl: Crimea and the Black Sea steppe
p.t: They have no enclosures and no houses, only portable tents of wicker and reeds joined together, covered with felts and mats and made fast with rush matting, which, filled with wives and children, they carry with them on carts.
p.c: Michalo generalises; the Crimean khanate also had towns such as Bakhchysarai and Kaffa (under the Ottomans), which he mentions elsewhere.
p.tg: tents wagons felt nomads pastoralism

p.h: Felt tents on carts, as in Herodotus
p.g: Leaving the Crimea, the party came on a few nomad tents: round, about four feet high and eight feet across, covered in rushes and thick felt, with a smoke-hole and a banner marking the horde. She notes they ride on carts called kibitkas, just like the cart-dwelling Scythians of Herodotus, and that women live in separate tents.
p.q: the very tents that I have been describing, called Kabitkies, are placed on carts of the same name, and drawn with their inhabitants from one grazing ground to another, as the difference of season, or a want of pasture for their numerous flocks, demands a change of place. The women are kept in separate tents pitched near those of the men
p.s: Maria Guthrie (letter, translated by Matthew Guthrie, 1802)
p.c: The link to Herodotus's Scythians is a learned comparison, not evidence of descent.

p.h: The 'Seven Palaces' in the steppe
p.g: Bell did not visit this building on the upper Irtysh, but reports what he was told: a regular brick or stone edifice of seven rooms under one roof, standing alone in the steppe. Local Tartars credited it to Tamerlane or to Genghis Khan. Its rooms were full of scrolls in the writing of the 'Tongusts, or Kalmucks' (probably meaning Tanguts, that is Tibetans, or Kalmyks); Bell bought a bundle from a soldier in Tobolsk and gave some to Sir Hans Sloane. The Tibetan or Kalmyk writing suggests a Kalmyk (Oirat) Buddhist building rather than a work of Tamerlane, and the ruin, 'Sem Palaty', later gave the city of Semipalatinsk (Semey) its name.
p.q: It is very surprising to find such a regular edifice in the middle of a desert. Some of the Tartars say it was built by Tamerlane, called by the Tartars Temyr-Ack-Sack or Lame-Temyr; others by Gingeez-Chan. The building, according to the best information I could obtain, is of brick or stone, well finished, and continues still entire. It consists of seven apartments under one roof,
p.s: John Bell (Travels, 1763)
p.c: Hearsay: Bell never saw the building, and the Tamerlane and Genghis Khan attributions are local legend.

p.h: Ruined walls from mountain to mountain: 'Alexander's barriers'
p.g: A day beyond Derbent Rubruck crossed a valley where the foundations of walls ran from one mountain to the next. He identifies them with the barriers of Alexander meant to hold back 'wild peoples', and explains these rationally as the shepherds of the wilderness kept out of the farmland and cities. He adds that he could learn nothing certain about the other barriers where Jews were said to be enclosed.
p.q: In crastino transivimus per vallem quamdam, in qua apparebant fundamenta murorum de uno monte ad alium, et per summitates montium nulla erat via. Ista solebant esse claustra Alexandri, feras gentes chohibentia, hoc est, pastores de solitudine, ut non possent ingredi super terras cultas et civitates.
p.s: William of Rubruck
p.t: The next day we crossed a valley in which the foundations of walls could be seen running from one mountain to another, and over the mountain tops there was no road. These used to be the barriers of Alexander, holding back the wild peoples, that is, the shepherds of the wilderness, so that they could not come into the cultivated lands and the cities.
p.c: The walls were real, probably part of the Sasanian (6th-century) defences around Derbent; crediting them to Alexander is legend, which Rubruck repeats.
p.tg: alexander's gates walls gog and magog ruins

p.g: Describing Grueber's engraving of a Kalmyk dwelling (Figure A), Kircher explains the felt tent: a framework of small folding rods inside, covered outside with a coarse woollen material bound with ropes. This is the yurt, with its collapsible lattice wall, as reported by an eyewitness.
p.q: Habitationem eorum Figura A. exprimit, estque tentorium Tartaricum intrinsecùs ex parvis plicatilibus bacillis confectum, exterius verò rudi ex certæ lanæ materia funibusque constricta contectum.
p.s: Athanasius Kircher, S.J. (China illustrata, Amsterdam 1667), from the oral report and drawings of Johann Grueber and Albert Dorville
p.t: Figure A shows their dwelling: it is a Tartar tent made on the inside of small folding rods, and covered on the outside with a rough material of a kind of wool, bound tight with ropes.
p.c: Based on Grueber's sketch and account; the engraving was redrawn in Amsterdam.

p.h: Tall carts carrying round felt houses
p.g: Barbaro watched the whole horde pass Tana and describes its vehicles: two-wheeled carts taller than Italian ones, closed with reed mats and covered with felt or cloth depending on rank. Some carried a house built on a timber ring with half-hoops above, filled with reed mats and covered in felt, which was lifted off when they camped.
p.q: This people carie with them innumerable cartes of twoo wheeles higher than ours be, which are closed with mattes made of reades, and parte covered with felte, parte with clothe … Some of these cartes carie their houses vpon them which are made on this wise. They take a cercle of tymber, whose dyameter is a pase and an halfe, crossed within foorthe with other halfe cercles
p.s: Giosafat Barbaro (Tudor translation by William Thomas, c. 1550)
p.pe: Tatars of the Golden Horde (the camp of Küchük Muhammad)

p.h: Stone houses that turn their backs to the street
p.g: In her general letter on the 'Crim Tartars' she says their houses are single-storey stone buildings bonded with limy clay and roofed with tiles. They have no street windows: the fronts face an inner courtyard so that the women can take the air unseen behind muslin screens.
p.q: The Tartar houses are of one story, constructed of stone, cemented together by a calcareous clay, and covered with tiles. Toward the street they have no windows; polygamy, and its natural consequence, jealousy, having turned the facade of Tauric dwellings to the inner court, where the women may breathe the fresh air through muslin blinds.
p.s: Maria Guthrie (letter, translated by Matthew Guthrie, 1802)

p.h: A Yakut prince's winter house of timber and earth
p.g: A Yakut prince at Amga, owner of two thousand horses, showed Lesseps his 'yurt'. Its walls were upright logs set side by side and plastered with clay, leaning inwards to carry a low-pitched roof. One half housed the family in bunk-like compartments, the other was a byre for cows and calves, with a round wooden hearth in the middle.
p.q: Des poutres posées debout les unes à côté des autres, & recouvertes de terre grasse, en forment les murs, qui ne s'élèvent point perpendiculairement comme les nôtres. Plus rapprochés vers le haut, ils supportent un toit dont l'inclinaison est peu rapide … De l'autre côté de la yourte demeurent les bêtes, les vaches, les veaux, c'est tout simplement une étable.
p.s: Jean-Baptiste Barthelemy de Lesseps
p.t: Beams set upright side by side and covered with clay form its walls, which do not rise vertically like ours. Drawing closer together towards the top, they carry a roof with a gentle slope … On the other side of the yurt live the animals, the cows and calves; it is quite simply a byre.
p.c: The Yakuts are a Turkic people, but Lesseps does not call them Tartars.
p.tg: yurt timber clay yakuts winter house

p.h: Timur's tomb, stripped of its gold
p.g: Izzet Ullah visited the Gur-i Amir, the tomb of Timur (Tamerlane), whose court history calls his army 'the Tartars'. He saw the great dome, the famous dark green stone slab and the inscribed plate, and was told the gilding had been stripped off by the Bukharan ruler Shah Murad. The poor attendants asked him whether any descendants of Timur still lived in India who might help them.
p.q: the seat of the sepulchre of Amir Timur ; a lofty building with an immense cupola : within it is a remarkable slab of a brilliant green stone, and above it is a plate with an inscription, with the name of Timur engraved on it. Formerly the dome was gilt, but Shah Murad Be stripped off the gilding, and took it away ;
p.s: Mir Izzet Ullah (translated by H. H. Wilson)
p.pe: Uzbeks of Bukhara; tomb of Timur
p.c: The story of the stripped gilding is what he was told.

p.h: Stone statues and ruined cities he never saw
p.g: In a footnote Strahlenberg records that Russian regiments going up the Irtysh in 1720 found antiquities and 'Temples of Idols', and that Tobolsk Tatars and Russians told him of many stone figures of men and beasts and the ruins of several cities in the little-visited steppe between the Tobol and Ishim. He links them to obelisks said to have been set up by Tamerlane and to the seat of Oghuz Khan, and regrets he could never go to see them.
p.q: …and I have also been told, by the Tobolskian Tartars and Russians, that, from this River, farther towards the West, South, and South-west from the City of Tobolsky, between the Sources of the Rivers Toboll and Ischim, whither very few People frequented, there were to be found great Numbers of Images, cut in Stone, of Men and Beasts; and that the Ruins of several Cities were discernible in those Desarts.
p.s: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg, author's footnote (English translation, 1738)
p.pl: Between the Tobol and Ishim rivers, south of Tobolsk
p.c: Pure hearsay: he says himself he never had the chance to visit. The Tamerlane and Oghuz Khan links come from his reading.

p.h: Log huts with windows made of ice
p.g: Travelling up the Irtysh in midwinter, Bell's party passes many Tatar villages and sleeps in their huts. He describes one- or two-room log houses chinked with moss, a broad bench for sitting and sleeping, and, in place of glass, a pane of ice cut to fit the window. The next page adds that these Tatars are very clean and use open hearths rather than Russian stoves.
p.q: These houses consist generally of one or two rooms, according to the ability of the landlord. … The walls are built of wood and moss, consisting of large beams, laid one above another, with a layer of moss between every two beams. All the roofs are raised. A square-hole is cut out for a window, and to supply the want of glass, a piece of ice
p.s: John Bell (Travels, 1763)
p.pl: Irtysh valley between Tobolsk and Tara

p.h: A palace for Altan Khan, and a beam that fell
p.g: After Qiu Fu's death Zhao Quan became more powerful among the Mongols. He honoured Altan Khan as an emperor and built him a palace, but on the day the ridge-beam was raised a great wind blew it down, injuring several men, and Altan was too frightened to live there. The Mongol ruler's palace was a Chinese project, built by Chinese hands.
p.q: 時邱富死趙全在敵中益用事尊諳達為帝治宫殿期日上棟忽大風棟墜傷數人諳達懼不敢復居
p.s: Zhang Tingyu and the Qing history office, History of the Ming (Siku quanshu Wenyuange copy, Kanseki Repository transcription)
p.pe: Tumed Mongols under Altan Khan; Chinese deserters
p.t: At that time Qiu Fu had died, and Zhao Quan, among the enemy, grew ever more powerful. He honoured Anda (Altan Khan) as emperor and built palaces for him. On the day set for raising the ridge-beam a great wind suddenly blew, the beam fell and injured several men, and Anda was afraid and did not dare to live there.
p.c: Told as an omen story by a hostile Chinese source; the Siku copy writes 諳達 for 俺答 (Altan).

p.h: A khan's burial mound heaped up with helmets and shields
p.g: Sailing down the Volga below Simbirsk in May 1703, the traveller saw a high, almost treeless round hill called Sariolkiergan. Russians told him it was the tomb of a Tatar king named Mamon (Mamai), who had come up the Volga with seventy Tatar princes to conquer Russia, and that his soldiers had carried the earth for the mound in their helmets and shields. It is a local legend about a kurgan, reported as hearsay.
p.q: Die Russen berichteten uns, daß daselbst das Begräbniß eines Tartarischen Königs oder Kaysers, Namens Mamon, wäre, welcher mit siebenzig andern Tartarischen Prinzen die Wolga herauf gekommen, in der Absicht, sich von ganz Rußland zu bemeistern. Weil aber dieser Prinz hier gestorben, hätten seine in grosser Menge mitgebrachte Soldaten ihm zu Ehren dieses Grabmahl errichtet, und in ihren Sturm-Hauben und Schildern die Erde zu diesem Berge angetragen.
p.s: Journal of an unnamed painter-traveller (evidently Cornelis de Bruyn, 1703) printed in Weber, Das veränderte Russland
p.t: The Russians told us that there lay the tomb of a Tartar king or emperor named Mamon, who had come up the Volga with seventy other Tartar princes, intending to make himself master of all Russia. But because this prince died here, the soldiers he had brought in great numbers raised this tomb in his honour, and carried the earth to this hill in their helmets and shields.
p.c: Cited from the 1744 reissue, which reprints the 1721 text page for page with clearer OCR. A legend told by Russians; no Mamai burial is known there.
p.tg: kurgan mamai legend volga

p.h: The defeated Mongols build a moated fort
p.g: After the Kashmiri army routed the Tibetans near Basgo, the Mongol army fled to Tashigang, where, the chronicle says, they built a fort, surrounded it with a wall and ringed it with water, and stayed inside, secure against assault. The builders in this passage are the Mongols themselves.
p.q: the Mongol army in its flight [eventually] reached Bkra-sis-sgan. There they built a fort, shut it in with a wall, and surrounded it with water. Inside they made it secure against an assault of armies, and there they abode.
p.s: Chronicles of Ladakh (La dvags rgyal rabs), translated by A. H. Francke (1926)

p.h: How a Tatar cottage was built
p.g: Holderness gives a builder's-eye account of the ordinary Tatar house: oak stakes driven upright into the ground, woven through with branches, plastered inside and out and whitewashed, with an earth or marl roof, or tiles for richer families. Farm buildings used the same stakes and wattle, plastered with cow dung. This is about as far from 'lost stone cities' as it gets, and she saw it every day.
p.q: The cottages of the Tatar peasants, for cheapness of construction, rapidity of building, and simplicity of materials, are perhaps unrivalled … They are constructed of oaken stakes, whose ends are driven perpendicularly into the ground … into these, liggers are entwined, and the whole are well plastered within and without, and white-washed when dry.
p.s: Mary Holderness
p.c: 'Liggers' are pliant rods or branches used as wattle.

p.h: Summer tents of boiled birch bark
p.g: The Yakuts had two kinds of home. For summer they used the urasa, a light round tent of poles covered with sheets of birch bark that were boiled to soften them and then sewn together. White outside and yellow inside, they looked from a distance like canvas tents. The herders moved with them to the best pastures while they cut hay for the winter.
p.q: In summer they use Urossy, which are light circular tents formed of poles, and covered with birch-bark, which they strip from the trees in large pieces. These strips are first softened by boiling, and are then sewed together; the outside being white, and the inside yellow, the Urossy have a very pleasing appearance, and at a distance resemble large white canvas tents.
p.s: Ferdinand von Wrangel (English translation by Mrs Sabine, 1840)

p.h: Summer huts, winter log cabins, and fields of barley
p.g: The Ides section describes the Baraba people between Tara and the Ob. They live in villages, in light huts in summer and good wooden cabins in winter, 'like the Tartars of Siberia', and they plough and sow oats, barley and buckwheat. The same page says they drink a spirit distilled from mare's milk called kumis and carry a wooden idol, their 'Saitan', on the hunt.
p.q: C'est un peuple malin & belliqueux, qui habite dans des cabanes de bois, comme les Tartares de Syberie … Ils habitent dans des especes de villages, sous des huttes legeres en été, & en de bonnes cabanes de bois en hyver. Le labourage est en usage parmi eux, & ils sement de l'avoine, de l'orge, du sarazin &c.
p.s: Evert Ysbrants Ides's route to China (1692-1695), summarized by the editors of the 1718 French edition of Le Brun and inserted in it
p.pl: Baraba steppe, between the Irtysh and the Ob
p.pe: Barabinsky (Baraba Tatars), called a kind of Kalmyk
p.t: They are a cunning and warlike people, who live in wooden cabins like the Tartars of Siberia … They live in kinds of villages, in light huts in summer and in good wooden cabins in winter. Ploughing is practised among them, and they sow oats, barley, buckwheat and so on.
p.c: From the Ides material; the book calls them 'a kind of Kalmyk', though they are now counted as Siberian Tatars.
p.tg: log cabins huts farming baraba

p.h: Kurgans raised by each mourner's handful of earth
p.g: After watching a kurgan being opened at Kerch, Spencer reflects on the countless mounds of the region. He reports the tradition of 'descendants of the aboriginal inhabitants' in the Crimean mountains: when a great warrior or king died, every admirer carried a portion of earth and threw it on his grave. On the next page he calls this 'the tradition of the Tartars' and compares it to Scottish cairns.
p.q: these tumuli were voluntarily erected by the people ; as when any of their great warriors or kings expired, his ashes were placed in the tomb, and every man who admired his virtues carried a portion of earth and threw it over his grave.
p.s: Edmund Spencer
p.pe: Crimean Tatars and older mountain peoples (as tradition-keepers)
p.c: A local tradition; the Kerch kurgans are mostly Greek and Scythian burials many centuries older than the Tatars. Spencer credits the builders to 'a great and powerful people' of antiquity, not to the Tatars.

p.h: A Mongol tent 'like the roof of a round tower'
p.g: On his first journey beyond the Great Wall with the Qing embassy to the Russians, the Jesuit Gerbillon went into a Mongol tent 'the better to know how they were built'. He describes a round cage of small sticks about 13 or 14 feet across and 8 or 9 feet high, with a pointed roof, covered with felt ('woollen stuff, not woven, but mill'd'). Inside: a plank bed, a bench, a cupboard and wooden bowls.
p.q: It is a sort of Cage, made of pretty small Sticks, round, and about 13 or 14 Foot Diameter. … the Roofing begins at about four Foot from the Ground, and ends in a Point like the Roof of a Round Tower, or Pigeon-house: They are covered with Pieces of Woollen Stuff, not woven, but mill'd.
p.s: Jean-François Gerbillon, Jesuit (journal compiled by Du Halde, English translation, 1738)
p.pl: Inner Mongolia, north of the Great Wall

p.h: Beyond the pass: felt tents and felt carts
p.g: Travelling north from Beijing, Zhang Dehui crossed the pass beyond Xuande and found that from here on every post station belonged to a Mongol clan and was named after its holder. Climbing the ridge he saw for the first time the felt tents and felt carts of herders who moved with water and grass. For him this line marked the end of the Chinese world.
p.q: 自是以北諸驛皆蒙古部族所分主也毎驛各以主者之名名之由嶺而上則東北行始見毳幕氊車逐水草畜牧而巳非復中原之風土也
p.s: Zhang Dehui, Record of a Journey (Qiujian ji juan 100 = Yutang jiahua juan 8; Sibu congkan text, Kanseki Repository transcription)
p.t: From here northward, all the post stations are held as shares by Mongol clans, and each station is named after its holder. Going up from the ridge, we travelled northeast and for the first time saw felt tents and felt carts; [people] follow water and grass and herd their animals, and that is all. This is no longer the land and custom of the Central Plain.

p.h: Mongol felt tents versus Manchu canvas tents
p.g: Grosier compares the two kinds of Tartar tent. Manchu tents are just single or double canvas, like European army tents. Mongol tents are round, shaped like a cut-off cone, covered in white or grey felt, with a smoke hole above a central fire; warm while the fire burns, freezing at night, stifling in summer. Three pages earlier he states flatly that the Mongols have 'neither towns, villages, nor houses', only wandering hordes living under tents.
p.q: These tents are however more commodious than the common tents of the Mantchews, which are composed only of double or single canvass, almost like those of our troops; these of the Moguls are circular, in form of the frustum of a cone, and covered with a large piece of white or gray felt. A round hole in the top gives a passage to the smoke,
p.s: Jean-Baptiste Grosier (English translation, 1788)
p.c: Compiled from Jesuit travellers, probably Gerbillon; Grosier did not see these tents.
p.tg: yurts felt tents manchus mongols

p.h: Cuman grave mounds, statues and brick towers on the steppe
p.g: Crossing the steppe, Rubruck describes the tombs of the Cumans, the Turkic people the Mongols had conquered there. They raised a mound over the dead with a statue facing east holding a cup; for the rich they built little pointed houses, and he saw great brick towers and stone houses in a land without stone. The same page notes that nobody knew where Chinggis Khan was buried.
p.q: Pour les Comans, ils ont coustume d'esleuer vne motte ou tertre sur la sepulture du mort, & luy dressent vne statuë la face tournée à l'Orient … Aux riches & Grands ils dressent des pyramides, ou petites maisons pointuës, & ay veu en des endroits de grandes tours de brique, & en d'autres des maisons basties de pierres; encores qu'en ces quartiers là on n'y trouue point de pierres.
p.s: William of Rubruck (French translation by Pierre Bergeron, 1634)
p.t: As for the Cumans, they are accustomed to raise a mound over the grave of the dead man and set up a statue for him facing east … For the rich and great they put up pyramids, or little pointed houses, and in some places I saw great towers of brick, and in others houses built of stone, although no stone is found in those parts.
p.c: These are Cuman (Qipchaq) monuments, not Mongol ones; Rubruck does not say who built the brick towers.

p.h: The khans' palace: painted walls and a fountain
p.g: Alexander found the palace of the former khans in good repair, though he had been told it was a ruin. He describes gaudily painted walls, minarets and tall pointed chimneys, an oblong courtyard with a marble fountain said to honour a khan's Christian wife, and a mosque by the gate. Inside were painted ceilings, stained-glass windows and brocade divans; he calls it 'a most interesting specimen of Tartaric magnificence' and notes that no Russians were allowed to live in the town.
p.q: It is a most grotesque pile : the walls are gaudily painted, and above the roofs rise minarets and numerous tall sharp-pointed chimnies. The buildings of the palace inclose an oblong court, in which is a marble fountain, erected to the memory of the Christian wife of a khan ; on the left of the gateway is a mosque
p.s: James Edward Alexander (1830)
p.c: He does not say who built it. The Christian-wife story is the local legend behind the 'Fountain of Tears'.

p.h: Itil: a city of felt huts with one brick palace
p.g: Yaqut's excerpt describes the Khazar capital Itil on the lower Volga as two towns on either bank. The western part, where the king lived, was walled and about a parasang long, but its buildings were mostly huts of felt, with a few of clay, plus markets and baths. On the next page (n27) it says the king's palace, away from the river, was of fired brick, and that the king let nobody else build in brick.
p.q: Haec pars occidentalis in parasangae longitudinem extenditur, muro cincta, sed eo quidem sparsae raraeve structurae. Eorum autem aedificia sunt casae (seu mapalia) ex panno coactili confectae, paucis exceptis, quae e luto constructa. Sunt iis fora et balnea.
p.s: Ibn Fadlan as quoted by Yaqut (Latin translation by C. M. Frähn, De Chasaris, 1822)
p.t: This western part stretches for a parasang in length and is enclosed by a wall, but its buildings are scattered and few. Their dwellings are huts (or tents) made of felt, apart from a few built of clay. They have markets and baths.
p.c: Yaqut attributes this to Ibn Fadlan, but much of it matches the geographer al-Istakhri, and Ibn Fadlan probably did not visit Itil.

p.h: The khan's palace, once 'entirely in the Chinese' style
p.g: De Tott describes the palace of the Crimean khans at the edge of Bakhchysarai, ringed by rocks and fed by streams channelled into kiosks and gardens. He says it was first built in a 'Chinese' manner and later repaired in Turkish fashion. On the same page he claims crime was rarer in Tartary than anywhere, so the capital had no guards but the khan's.
p.q: The Palace he inhabits, formerly built entirely in the Chinese, but repaired in the Turkish fashion, still retains some of the beauties of its former stile of construction. It is placed at one of the extremities of the town, and is surrounded by very high rocks, from whence flows an abundance of streams, which are conveyed into the kiosks and gardens in a most delightful manner.
p.s: Baron de Tott (English translation, 1785)
p.c: 'Chinese' is de Tott's impression of the painted, wide-eaved style; he gives no source for who built it.
p.tg: palace khan gardens fountains chinese style

p.h: Felt tents, and boats of wicker and raw hide
p.g: Thomas says almost no river could stop them, since they swam their horses across. If a river was too deep, they at once wove wicker baskets like small boats, stretched raw animal hides over them, loaded their baggage and crossed without fear. They lived in tents of felt and of leather. This is the whole of what he says about their dwellings: portable felt and leather, not buildings.
p.q: si qua vero immeabilis unda occurrit, continuo in modum lemborum ex viminibus cistas intexunt, superducentes crudas animalium cutes, quibus sarcinas inferentes intrant, & transeunt absque metu, Tentoriis utuntur filtrinis, & ex coriis factis
p.s: Thomas, archdeacon of Split, Historia Salonitana, in the first edition by Ivan Lučić (Lucius), Amsterdam 1666
p.t: but if an impassable stream meets them, they at once weave baskets of wicker in the manner of skiffs, stretching raw animal hides over them; putting their baggage in, they get in and cross without fear. They use tents of felt and tents made of hides

p.h: The silver tree that poured four drinks at Karakorum
p.g: Beside Möngke's palace at Karakorum stood a great silver tree made by a captive Parisian goldsmith, Master Guillaume. Four silver lions at its foot and pipes hidden in the trunk delivered wine, kumiss, honey-mead and rice beer, and a silver angel on top blew a trumpet (worked by a man hidden inside) to call the servers. It is a vivid case of a Mongol showpiece built by a foreign craftsman.
p.q: ce M. Guillaume luy auoit fait vn grand arbre d'argent, au pied duquel estoient quatre lyons aussi d'argent, ayans chacun vne pipe ou canal d'où sortoit du lait de iument. Les quatre pipes estoient cachées dans l'arbre, montans iusqu'au sommet, & de là s'escoulans en bas. Sur chacun de ces muids ou canaux y auoit des serpens dorez dont les queuës venoient à enuironner le corps de l'arbre.
p.s: William of Rubruck (French translation by Pierre Bergeron, 1634)
p.pe: Mongols (court of Möngke Khan); Guillaume Boucher, a Parisian goldsmith
p.t: this Master Guillaume had made him a great silver tree, at whose foot were four lions, also of silver, each with a pipe or channel from which mare's milk flowed. The four pipes were hidden in the tree, rising to the top and flowing down from there. On each of these conduits were gilded serpents whose tails wound round the trunk of the tree.

p.h: A brick tower said to be Genghis Khan's
p.g: Among the ruins of Old Urgench Abbott saw a tall, tapering brick column that he says was put up by Genghis Khan, decorated only with bands of patterned brick and leaning from the wind. Nearby he describes a saint's tomb with a conical roof of coloured tiles on a 24-sided base, and a tiled tomb said to have been built by a lady of Genghis Khan's family for her lover.
p.q: On the north of the site, (I speak at hazard,) stands a brick column, erected by Chenghis Khaun. It is the frustrum of an extremely taper cone, surmounted by a cylinder, and is very sufficiently ugly. It has no base, and its sole ornaments have been zones of bricks, of alternating patterns.
p.s: James Abbott
p.c: The attribution to Genghis Khan is what Abbott was told or assumed; the tall minaret standing at Konye-Urgench today is usually dated to the 14th century.

p.h: Ruined Tatar towns along the Volga
p.g: On the left bank of the Volga, Haxthausen says, the Tatars were not only nomads: they had fixed towns and farms, as shown by ruins and by place names. The Akhtuba valley where Sarai stood is covered with ruins for about 85 versts (roughly 90 km). When the Horde broke up, the towns were destroyed and the settlers driven off by Kirghiz and Bashkir raiders, leaving only ruins and broken mosques.
p.q: This is evident not merely from the ruins of cities (the whole district on the Akhtuba, where Sarai stood, for eighty-five versts, is covered with ruins), but the names of nearly all denote that the Tatars had fixed settlements here. When the Mongol-Tatar empire was dissolved, the cities were destroyed … only here and there a ruin or dilapidated mosque bore witness to their former existence.
p.s: August von Haxthausen (translated by Robert Farie, 1856)
p.pl: Lower Volga (Akhtuba valley, Kazan to Astrakhan)
p.c: He reports this from local knowledge and place names while passing through the Saratov region; he did not visit the Akhtuba ruins himself.
p.tg: ruins sarai akhtuba mosques golden horde

p.h: Steppe full of ancient graves of the 'Chud', an unknown people
p.g: Crossing the 'Tatar steppe' to the Abakansk fort on the Yenisei, the botanist Sievers found the whole area full of ancient grave monuments of a people still unknown, whom Siberians simply called Chud. He saw no inscriptions on the many standing stones. Nearby, he notes, Abakansk had been built in the previous century with palisades and five small cannon against raids by Tatars and Kirgiz.
p.q: Auf der ganzen tatarischen Steppe und hier herum ist alles voll von uralten Grabmälern von einer bis jetzt unbekannten Nation, die nur schlechthin in Sibirien Tschudi genannt werden. An den vielen aufgerichteten Steinen sah ich nirgends Inschriften.
p.s: Johann Sievers, letters from Siberia, in Neueste Nordische Beyträge vol. 7 (1796), edited by P. S. Pallas
p.pe: Unknown ancient builders ('Chud'); Sagai and other steppe Tatars living there now
p.t: On the whole Tatar steppe and round about here everything is full of very ancient grave monuments of a nation unknown until now, which in Siberia are simply called Chud. On the many standing stones I saw inscriptions nowhere.

p.h: How a Mongol tent is built
p.g: Huc visited Mongol families and describes their tent exactly: a cylinder about three feet high topped by a cone, a folding lattice of crossed bars below, a ring of poles meeting at the top like umbrella ribs, a thick covering, and a low folding door with a beam across the bottom. The next page describes the smoke-hole flap of felt and the men's and women's sides inside.
p.q: The Mongol tent, for about three feet from the ground, is cylindrical in form. It then becomes conical, like a pointed hat. The woodwork of the tent is composed below of a trellis-work of crossed bars, which fold up and expand at pleasure. Above these, a circle of poles, fixed in the trellis-work, meets at the top, like the sticks of an umbrella.
p.s: Évariste Huc (translated by William Hazlitt, 1852)
p.tg: ger yurt felt tent lattice

p.h: 'No towns, no edifices' in the land of grass
p.g: Crossing the prairies of the Chakhar, Huc sums up what makes Tartary unlike anywhere else: no towns, no buildings, no crafts, no farming and no forests, only endless grassland, lakes, rivers and mountains. A page later he describes encampments of tents appearing and vanishing as herders moved to fresh pasture.
p.q: There are no towns, no edifices, no arts, no industry, no cultivation, no forests; everywhere it is prairie, sometimes interrupted by immense lakes, by majestic rivers, by rugged and imposing mountains; sometimes spreading out into vast limitless plains.
p.s: Évariste Huc (translated by William Hazlitt, 1852)
p.c: A literary generalisation; elsewhere Huc describes lamaseries, trading towns and ruins in the same region.
p.tg: steppe no cities nomads grassland

p.h: Kalmyk leather huts shaped like a hooped petticoat
p.g: Weber's informant Poussett described the Kalmyk caravan that came to trade at Astrakhan each year, grazing its way along the Volga. They carried leather huts called 'Kubiten' (kibitkas), which looked like a whalebone hooped petticoat; they raised them on poles, cooked inside, and closed the top hole when the fire was out to keep warm at night. Each morning the houses were loaded back onto the pack animals.
p.q: Sie hätten eine Art Hütten von Leder, die einer jupe de baleine ähnlich sähen, und Kubiten genennet würden, diese stelleten sie mit Stangen auf, machten Feuer und Essen darinn, und stopfeten wenn das Feuer ausgebrannt, oben das Loch zu, und wärmeten sich auf solche Art des Nachts. Des Morgens lüden sie ihre Häuser auf die Last-Thiere und jagten weiter fort.
p.s: Friedrich Christian Weber (Das veränderte Russland), reporting Poussett of Astrakhan
p.t: They had a kind of leather huts, which looked like a whalebone petticoat and were called Kubiten; these they set up with poles, made fire and food inside, and when the fire had burned out stopped up the hole at the top, and so kept warm at night. In the morning they loaded their houses onto the pack animals and moved on.
p.c: Cited from the 1744 reissue, which reprints the 1721 text page for page with clearer OCR.

p.h: Felt-walled tents and wooden doors
p.g: When Chinggis made his adopted brother Sigi Qutuqu chief judge, he told him to divide the whole population into those living in felt-walled tents and those living in dwellings with wooden doors, that is nomads and settled folk. Sigi Qutuqu then asked as his reward for people from the towns with walls of pounded earth. The Mongols thus sorted their world by house type, and counted walled-town people as a separate prize.
p.q: Splitting up those that live in felt-walled tents, Separating those that live in dwellings with wooden doors. … let him decide in favour of granting me the people from the towns that have walls of pounded earth.
p.s: Anonymous author of the Secret History, words given to Chinggis Qa'an and Sigi Qutuqu (translated by Igor de Rachewiltz, 2015)
p.pe: Mongols and the peoples under them
p.c: The editor's footnote glosses the pairing as 'nomadic or settled populations'.

p.h: Tartar towns of wood and sun-dried brick
p.g: Explaining why old place names in Marco Polo and Rubruck cannot be found on the ground, Strahlenberg says that most Tartar peoples roamed, their khans never stayed long in one place, and their towns were built of wood or sun-dried brick. Centuries of wars, he says, destroyed them so thoroughly that not even ruins remain. This is his general judgement, not a report of a particular site.
p.q: …because most of the Tartarian Nations roving about, and the Residences of their Chams being never fix'd long in one Place, their Cities and Towns being also compos'd of Houses or Huts, built either of Wood or Bricks, slightly dry'd in the Sun, it is, therefore, no Wonder that … their Cities and Towns have been so destroy'd, that even the Ruins of them are no more to be seen.
p.s: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (English translation, 1738)

p.h: Wooden houses 'in the Turkish style', and crafts left to slaves and foreigners
p.g: The Tatars build wooden houses much in the Turkish manner, but they themselves very rarely practise crafts. Whatever merchants or artisans are found in the towns are Christian slaves or Turks, Armenians, Jews, Circassians and Roma. Fields are worked by captive Hungarians, Russians, Muscovites and Moldavians. This is a direct statement of who built and made things in the khanate.
p.q: Aedificia & domus ligneas similes admodum Turcico more ædificant … mechanicas autem artes rarissimi exercent, & quicunq; mercatores vel artifices ibi reperiuntur, vel Christianorum mancipia, vel Turcæ, Armeni, Iudæi, Cercesij, Petigorenses, qui Christiani sunt, Phylistini vel Cyngani obscurę & extremæ conditionis homines sunt.
p.s: Marcin Broniewski (Martin Broniovius), Tartariae descriptio (written 1579), printed in the 1595 Cologne edition of Possevino's Moscovia
p.pe: Crimean Tatars; Christian slaves, Turks, Armenians, Jews, Circassians, Roma
p.t: They build wooden buildings and houses very much in the Turkish manner ... but they very rarely practise the mechanical arts, and whatever merchants or artisans are found there are either Christian slaves, or Turks, Armenians, Jews, Circassians, Piatigorians who are Christians, 'Philistines' or Gypsies, men of obscure and the lowest condition.
p.c: A diplomat's generalisation; it ignores Tatar artisans who certainly existed in towns like Bakhchisaray.

p.h: The stone cathedral that became a furnace
p.g: When the new town fell, the bishop, the grand prince's wife, daughters-in-law, grandchildren, boyars and townspeople shut themselves in the stone Cathedral of the Mother of God, built by the Suzdal princes. The Tatars set it on fire. Then they forced the doors, killed the survivors and stripped the wonder-working icon of its gold, silver and gems. The passage shows a Rus-built stone church and who ruined it.
p.q: Татарове же силою отвориша двери церковныя, и видѣша овы огнемъ скончавшася, овы же оружьемъ до конца смерти предаша; святую Богородицю разграбиша, чюдную икону одраша, украшену златомъ и серебромъ и каменьемъ драгымъ

p.h: Felt houses thirty feet wide, pulled by 22 oxen
p.g: Rubruck describes the Mongol felt houses built on a frame of rods and carried whole on carts. He measured one cart's wheel track at 20 feet, with the house overhanging by at least 5 feet each side, and counted 22 oxen pulling one house, in two rows of eleven, with an axle as big as a ship's mast and a driver standing in the doorway.
p.q: Et faciunt tales domus ita magnas quod habent aliquando triginta pedes in latitudine. Ego enim mensuravi semel latitudinem inter vestigia rotarum unius bige .xx. pedum, et quando domus erat super bigam excedebat extra rotas in utroque latere .v. pedibus ad minus. Ego numeravi in una biga .xxij. boves trahentes unam domum, undecim in uno ordine secundum latitudinem bige, et alios .xj. ante illos.
p.s: William of Rubruck
p.t: And they make these houses so large that they are sometimes thirty feet across. I once measured the width between the wheel tracks of one cart at 20 feet, and when the house was on the cart it overhung the wheels on each side by at least 5 feet. I counted 22 oxen drawing one house on one cart, eleven in a row across the width of the cart and another eleven in front of them.

p.h: A Kalmyk princess in a silk-lined felt tent
p.g: Sent to treat the widowed Kalmyk princess, held under Russian guard in a dispute over the khanate, Cook entered a very large beehive-shaped tent covered with felt and lined with Persian silk. She lay on a down bed covered with silk, with priests and chiefs standing round. He decided her illness was confinement and grief.
p.q: In company with the major, the governor's only son, I went to a very large tent, in form of a bee-hive, covered with felt, and lined with Persian silk. When I entered into the tent, the Princess was lying on a bed of down covered with silk; her face was from us. Many Kalmucks well dressed were standing with great decorum
p.s: John Cook (published 1770)

p.h: A Kazak camp of felt tents and reed huts
p.g: Just across the Oxus, Moorcroft passed through a Kazak owal (aul, a tent village) of khirgahs (felt tents) and kappahs, round huts of mats and reeds with conical tops. Saddled horses waited at the doors, and the cattle were stabled in pits dug in the ground and roofed with branches, grass and sand.

Horses stood saddled at the doors of the tents, and mares and foals, and many camels, were grazing in the adjoining jangal. The cows were stabled in holes made in the ground, roofed with branches of trees and grass, and covered with sand and bushes.

p.h: A ruined palace city with a giant stone Buddha
p.g: Quoting the diary of Gao Shiqi, who accompanied the Kangxi emperor to Manchuria in 1682, the gazetteer describes Huorong city: a walled site over forty li around with an inner forbidden city, the foundations of three halls strewn with broken green-glazed tiles, and outside it a great stone Buddha about three zhang high on a lotus base, with a leaning stone pagoda. Gao took it for the Jin (Jurchen) upper capital; the gazetteer's editors then use the Jin river name Anchuhu (which they equate with the Alchuka) and Song travellers' distances to argue that the Jin capital lay further west, toward the Sungari.
p.q: 沙林東南十五里曰火茸城金之上京㑹寧府也廣四十餘里中間禁城可里餘三殿基址皆在碎碧瓦棊布其上禁城外有大石佛髙可三丈許蓮花承之前有石塔向東小欹
p.s: Agui, Liu Jinzhi and the Qianlong commission, Imperially Commissioned Gazetteer of Shengjing (1784 recension; Siku quanshu Wenyuange copy, Kanseki Repository transcription), quoting Gao Shiqi's diary of 1682
p.pe: Builders of an earlier dynasty (identified as Jin; now known as Bohai)
p.t: [Gao Shiqi's diary:] Fifteen li southeast of Shalin is Huorong city, the upper capital Huining prefecture of the Jin. It is more than forty li around; in the middle is a forbidden city about a li across, where the foundations of three halls all survive, with broken green tiles scattered over them like chess pieces. Outside the forbidden city is a great stone Buddha about three zhang high, resting on a lotus, and in front of it a stone pagoda leaning a little to the east.
p.c: Gao's identification is doubted in the gazetteer itself. Modern archaeology identifies the ruins near Ningguta, with their stone Buddha and stone lantern, as Shangjing, capital of the Bohai kingdom (8th to 10th centuries).

p.g: Broniewski notes very deep wells cut by the old Greeks or the ancient peoples who lived in Crimea before them, and frequent, very large Greek ruins of castles, cities, churches and monasteries in the mountains and forests. They had stood empty so long that their names were lost. He does not credit these ruins to the Tatars.
p.q: fontes seu putei altissimi mira profunditate & difficultate à veteribus Græcis seu populis illis antiquissimis & maximis, qui eam Peninsulam ante Græcorum tempora incolebant, quondam excisi & facti … arcium, ciuitatum, templorũ, monasteriorumq; antiquissimæ & maximæ Græcæ ruinæ frequentissimæ admodum reperiuntur, quæ cum multo sęculo habitatoribus caruêre propter antiquitatem temporũ cognomina sua amiserũt.

p.h: Two-storey tiled houses in the valleys
p.g: Jesse notices that Tatar houses in the inland valleys were better built than the flat-roofed coastal ones: still low, but often two storeys with an outside gallery, raised tiled roofs and carved wooden ceilings. At the village inn of Uzenbash a Tatar barber gave him an expert shave.

p.h: A silver bowl from a riverbank grave, and who could have made it
p.g: When the Irtysh undercut its bank near Samarovsky Yam in 1688, a wooden coffin with old bones, silver arm-rings, a silver necklace and a silver bowl fell out. The governor of Siberia, Fyodor Golovin, later gave the bowl to Witsen. Witsen asks who made such silverwork, found in several graves there, since the present inhabitants do not know how to work silver.

p.s: Nicolaes Witsen
p.t: a grave, or wooden coffin, with the bones of a man long dead, together with some silverwork of arm-rings and a silver necklace … It deserves notice where, and by whom, this silver vessel, whose like is found more often in that region in some burial places, may have been made, because in these parts the art of working silver is not known among the natives today.

p.h: Twenty-two oxen to pull one house
p.g: Rubruck took a tape to a Mongol wagon-house. He measured one at twenty feet between the wheels, with the house overhanging them, and counted twenty-two oxen, eleven abreast on each side, hauling it, with an axle as thick as a ship's mast. On the same page he says the felt roof was painted and the door-felt embroidered with vines, trees, birds and beasts.

p.h: A Nogai cottage of sun-dried brick and reeds
p.g: Settled by Russian officials only a generation earlier, the Nogais now built their own cottages. The walls are sun-dried brick, whitewashed yearly; the roof is rafters covered with reeds and branches loaded with earth and ashes. Inside are two rooms, and a man with two wives builds a separate room for each.
p.q: The Nogai constructs his own cottage with bricks dried in the sun, and whitewashes it regularly once a year within and without. Its dimensions are scarcely more than two or three-and-thirty feet by thirteen. The roof consists of a few rafters on which are laid reeds and branches of trees loaded with earth and ashes.
p.s: Xavier Hommaire de Hell (English translation, 1847)

p.h: Kalmuk Tatars with 'portable cities'
p.g: The appendix summarises the letters of the Jesuit Johann Grueber, who crossed from China to Lhasa in 1661. Past the Yellow River his party entered the Kalmuk desert, whose people raided caravans and 'at certain seasons settle with their portable cities' on riverbanks. Their houses were tents of plaited sticks covered with coarse woollen cloth tied with cords, and the Jesuits sketched the people they met.
p.q: they immediately entered that vast and barren desert of Kalmuk, inhabited by the Kalmuk Tatars (the Eluths or Tatars of Koko-nor), who rove up and down it to rob the caravans, and at certain seasons settle with their portable cities on the banks of the rivers. … Their habitations are tents made with small sticks twisted or plaited together, and covered with a coarse woollen stuff bound together with cords.
p.s: Account of Johann Grueber's travels, from Astley's Collection of Voyages (reprinted in Markham's appendix)
p.c: A compiler's paraphrase of Grueber's letters as abstracted by Athanasius Kircher; the bracketed gloss is part of the printed text.

p.h: Proof that Madzhar was built by Kipchak Tatars
p.g: Klaproth sets out his evidence that Madzhar was a Tatar town: the shape of its buildings and burial chapels, which match a Tatar cemetery near Tbilisi; walls decorated with coloured glazed tiles, a Tatar and Mongol fashion; Arabic gravestones; coins of the Golden Horde; and mentions in Asian histories. He also opened a brick vault himself and found a wooden coffin.
p.q: The following facts, however, afford incontestable proofs that Madshar was a town built and inhabited by Ckipdshack Tartars. I. The form of the buildings and sepulchral chapels is characteristic of Southern Asia… The fashion of adorning the walls with tiles, which are glazed on one side with different colours, is also Tartar and Mongol.
p.s: Julius Klaproth (English translation, 1814)

p.h: Kalmyk felt tents at a Volga horse fair
p.g: Crossing the Volga at Saratov to a great horse market held by the Kalmyks, Bell describes their tents step by step: leaning poles fixed into a smoke-hole ring, a frame of light rods tied with thongs, and a covering of felt. On the next page he adds that the felt is coarse wool and hair, that the tents fold up quickly, and that one camel can carry five or six of them.
p.q: These tents are of a conical figure; there are several long poles erected, inclining to one another, which are fixed at the top into something like a hoop, that forms the circumference of an aperture for letting out the smoak, or admitting the light; across the poles are laid some small rods… this frame is covered with pieces of felt,
p.s: John Bell (Travels, 1763)

p.h: Brick temples and clay houses on the Irtysh
p.g: On the way up the Irtysh Baikov noted a Kalmyk 'mosque' (a Buddhist temple) of burnt brick, then a Kalmyk lama with two large 'Burkhan' halls, also of burnt brick, and clay houses to live in. The fields around grew wheat and millet, but the ploughing was done by Bukharans, the settled Central Asian farmers who worked for the Oirats.
p.q: а въ Кабанъ-Гусанѣ поставлена мечеть Калмыцкая: кирпичь жженой … А живетъ тутъ Калмыцкой Лама подлѣ Иртыша на лѣвой сторонѣ. А поставлены у того Ламы двѣ палаты Бурханные велики: кирпичь жженой; а избы у нихъ, въ которыхъ живутъ, глиняные; а хлѣба родится у того Ламы пшеницы и проса много, а пашутъ Бухарцы.
p.s: Fyodor Baikov (1788 Novikov printing)
p.pe: Kalmyks (Oirats), a Buddhist lama, Bukharan farmers
p.t: and at Kaban-Gusan a Kalmyk mosque has been built: of burnt brick … And a Kalmyk lama lives here beside the Irtysh on the left bank. Two great Burkhan (Buddha) halls have been built for that lama, of burnt brick; and the houses they live in are of clay; and much wheat and millet grows for that lama, and Bukharans do the ploughing.
p.c: 'Mosque' is Baikov's word for a non-Christian temple; Burkhan is the Mongol word for Buddha.

p.h: 'May you stay in one place like a Christian'
p.g: Herberstein reports that the roving Tartars thought staying put was a misfortune, and that their worst curse on a child was to wish it a fixed home like a Christian's. He is careful to add that Tartars who live in towns and cities live differently, so he is describing the herders, not all Tartars.
p.q: They never stay for any length of time in one spot, for they consider it a great calamity to be obliged to remain long in the same place ; hence, when they are angry with their children, and wish to utter a heavy imprecation against them, they are accustomed to say, " may you abide in one place continually like a Christian, and inhale your own stink !"
p.s: Sigismund von Herberstein (translated by R. H. Major, 1851-52)
p.c: A saying reported secondhand; the next lines note that Tartars in towns and cities live otherwise.

p.h: Opened burial mounds all over the steppe: whose were they?
p.g: On the way home Unkovsky saw many burial mounds dug open 'like cellars' across the steppe. The Dzungar envoy Darzha said the dead were of his own people. Unkovsky objected that by their religion Kalmyks burn their dead or give them to dogs and birds, and never bury them with gold, so the mound-builders must have been someone else. An early recorded argument about who built the kurgans.
p.q: Ѣдучи въ пути степью, видѣли множество разрытыхъ бугровъ … яко погребы раскрытые, по всей степи видны. … Спрошено у него: Какіе люди тутъ погребены были? Оной сказалъ, будто ихъ народу. На сіе сказано ему, что по ихъ вѣрѣ умершихъ людей жгутъ и въ воду бросаютъ, собакамъ и птицамъ на кормъ отдаютъ, а съ золотомъ и ни съ какимъ богатствомъ не погребаютъ.
p.s: Ivan Unkovsky (ed. N. I. Veselovsky, 1887)
p.pl: Irtysh steppe between Semey (Semipalatinsk) and Yamyshevo
p.t: Travelling across the steppe we saw a great many dug-open mounds … like opened cellars, visible all over the steppe. … He was asked: what people were buried here? He said: supposedly of their own people. To this he was told that by their faith they burn their dead and throw them in the water, give them to dogs and birds for food, and do not bury them with gold or with any wealth at all.
p.c: Unkovsky saw the robbed mounds; his account of Kalmyk funeral custom is a generalisation made to win an argument.

p.h: How a Turkmen tent is built
p.g: Fraser says no one had yet described exactly how the 'portable wooden houses' of the Turkmens are made, and does so: a folding lattice of thin laths pinned with rawhide that opens out like a child's toy, curved roof poles, black felt (numud) coverings, a reed screen outside and a broad woven band holding it all together.
p.q: The frame is curiously constructed of light wood, disposed in laths of about an inch broad, by three quarters thick, crossing one another diagonally … and pinned at each crossing with thongs of raw hide, so as to be moveable ; … over which is thrown a covering of black numud, leaving in the center a large hole to give vent to the smoke, and light to the dwelling
p.s: James Baillie Fraser

p.h: Glazed brick and blue mosaic at Sarai
p.g: From the same ruins Zwick describes walls of glazed, pointed brick decorated with coloured mosaic on a deep blue ground, which he compares to the building styles of the Turks and Saracens from the Near East to Egypt and Spain. He says the same was true at 'Seray' further up the river. On the next page he describes a six-foot panel of this work, with a white inscription 'in the Tartarian language', reused in the wall of a peasant's cottage.
p.q: We perceived, from the ruins of this city, that here as well as at Seray, … walls were built of glazed brick and pointed, and mosaic work of various colours was employed in decoration here, as throughout the ancient Turkish, Tartar, and Saracen tribes, in the East, in Egypt, and Spain. The ground is usually deep blue, with other colours let in.
p.s: Heinrich August Zwick (English edition, 1831)
p.c: The omitted words call Seray the capital of an empire whose name is garbled in the OCR.

p.h: Xanadu: a marble palace and a portable palace of cane
p.g: At his summer capital Kublai had a marble palace with gilded, painted rooms inside a sixteen-mile walled park. He also had a second palace made of bamboo cane: gilded, roofed with split-cane tiles, held up by gilt dragon columns, and designed to be taken down and moved, with more than 200 silk cords to hold it against the wind. It is the steppe tent reimagined as palace architecture. This passage later inspired Coleridge's 'Kubla Khan'.
p.q: The construction of the Palace is so devised that it can be taken down and put up again with great celerity ; and it can all be taken to pieces and removed whithersoever the Emperor may command. When erected, it is stayed [against mishaps from the wind] by more than 200 cords of silk.
p.s: Marco Polo (translated by Henry Yule, 1871; bracketed words from other manuscripts)
p.c: The marble palace and the park are described on the previous page (p.263).

p.h: No towns, only houses on wheels
p.g: Fletcher says the Tartars build no towns or standing buildings. They live in wheeled 'walking houses' which they park in rows to form streets and the shape of a town, and even the khan's capital is a moving 'town of wood'. They reportedly think fixed buildings unhealthy.
p.q: Townes they plant none, nor other standing buildings, but have walking houses, which the Latines call veii, built upon wheeles like a shepheards cottage. … And when they come to their stage or standing place, they plant their cart houses very orderly in a ranke ; and so make the forme of streetes and of a large towne.
p.s: Giles Fletcher (1591; ed. E. A. Bond, 1856)
p.c: This echoes medieval accounts of the 13th-century Mongols; the Crimean khans of Fletcher's day actually ruled from the town of Bakhchysarai, which Fletcher never visited.

p.h: Crimea's ruined Greek cities with a thousand churches
p.g: Michalo says the Crimea was once so densely peopled by Greeks that single cities had a thousand churches, and that some cities, though ruined, still show by their walls and ruins how grand they were: Solkhat (called Krym by the Muscovites and once Theodosia by the Greeks) and old Chersonesos (Korsun), where the Rus' were baptised. He is clear about who built them: the Greeks, not the Tatars, who came later as settlers.
p.q: Atque nunc etiam urbes ibi nonnullae quamvis pessundatae, amplitudine tamen ambituum suorum & ruinarum, superbae olim fuisse apparent, & praesertim quae a nobis Solhoth; a Moscis Krym; a Graecis Theodosia appellabatur quondam, & metropolis vetusta Korsunij, quae genti Ruthenorum princeps dedit baptisma
p.s: Michalo the Lithuanian, De moribus Tartarorum, Lituanorum et Moschorum, fragment 1 (c. 1550; Basel, 1615)
p.pe: Crimean Tatars; earlier Greek Christian inhabitants
p.t: And even now some cities there, though ruined, show by the size of their circuits and of their ruins that they were once splendid, above all the one we call Solkhat, the Muscovites Krym, and the Greeks once called Theodosia, and the ancient metropolis of Korsun, which first gave baptism to the Ruthenian people
p.c: Michalo confuses Solkhat (Staryi Krym) with Theodosia (Kaffa); the 'thousand churches' is a traditional boast he repeats ('it is recorded').

p.h: Felt houses on wheels, drawn by thirty oxen
p.g: Describing the great assembly Genghis held on the plain of Toncat, Pétis explains that most lords brought their 'moveable houses' on wheels. They had wooden floors, lattice walls, a dome with a smoke hole, and felt covers rubbed with sheep's milk, or among the rich plastered with tallow, to shed the rain. Some were so heavy with furniture that thirty oxen pulled one, and every door faced south.
p.q: Some were cover'd with Felt rubbed with Sheep's Milk, so that the Rain might run off without penetrating it. … they are sometimes so heavy, by reason of the Furniture they contain, that they are obliged to put to one of them thirty Oxen to draw it along.
p.s: François Pétis de la Croix (English translation, 1722)
p.c: The details closely follow Rubruck's eyewitness description of 1253 and Carpini's; Pétis applies them to Genghis's assembly.

p.h: An Oirat prince builds a town with craftsmen from China
p.g: Travelling with the camp of the Oirat prince Ablai taisha, Baikov found him building a town on the Beshka stream between stone hills. Baikov could not tell whether it would be of stone or wood, but saw lots of timber cut, and was told the master builders had been sent from China. It is a precise, first-hand note of a steppe ruler commissioning a fixed town from foreign craftsmen.
p.q: А на той рѣчкѣ Бешкѣ Аблай-Тайша дѣлаетъ городъ; а про то подлинно не вѣдомо, каменной ли, или деревянной; а лѣсу нарожено много: лѣсъ сосновой тонокъ … а ставитъ тотъ городъ промежь горъ каменныхъ; а мастеры къ нему присланы изъ Китайскаго Царства
p.s: Fyodor Baikov (1788 Novikov printing)
p.t: And on that stream, the Beshka, Ablai taisha is building a town; whether of stone or of wood is not known for certain, but much timber has been felled, thin pine … and he is putting that town up between stony hills; and the master builders for it were sent from the Chinese Tsardom.
p.c: Baikov saw the works under way; the origin of the craftsmen is what he was told. Historians identify this with the Buddhist monastery-town later known as Ablai-kit, whose ruins survive.

p.h: Reed huts shaped like chicken coops, outside Astrakhan's walls
p.g: At Astrakhan the Tatars were not allowed to live inside the Russian-held city or to build walled towns. They lived in round huts of reeds or canes about twelve feet across, with a smoke hole and a cloth flap turned to the wind. In summer they loaded the huts onto carts and followed the pasture, which is why, Olearius says, the Russians called them wanderers.
p.q: The Inhabitants of the Country, who are the Tartars of Crim and Nagaia, are not permitted to live within the City … because they are not suffer'd to build Cities, nor to fortify their Towns nor Villages with walls. Their Huts are made either with Bull-rushes or Canes, being about twelve foot diameter, round, and towards the top, like the Coops wherein Chickens are kept in Europe.
p.s: Adam Olearius (English translation by John Davies, 1669)
p.pe: Nogai and Crimean Tatars under Russian rule

p.h: A round mound raised over the burned ship
p.g: After the ship cremation, Ibn Fadlan watched the Rus raise something like a round hill over the spot, set a large post of beech wood in the middle, and write on it the dead man's name and the name of the Rus king. It is a rare eyewitness account of a burial mound (kurgan) being built on the Volga.
p.q: Darauf führten sie über dem Orte, wo das aus dem Flusse gezogene Schiff gestanden, etwas einem runden Hügel ähnliches auf, errichteten in dessen Mitte ein großes buchen Holz und schrieben darauf den Namen des Verstorbenen, nebst dem des Königs der Russen.
p.s: Ibn Fadlan as quoted by Yaqut (German translation by C. M. Frähn, 1823)
p.t: Then, over the place where the ship drawn out of the river had stood, they built something like a round hill, set up in its middle a large post of beech wood, and wrote on it the name of the dead man together with that of the king of the Rus.
p.c: 'Büchen Holz' is read here as 'beechwood post'; other translators render the wood as birch (khadank).
