p.h: A palisade of wooden stakes around Liaodong
p.g: On the imperial map survey of Tartary, Pierre Jartoux found the ginseng country walled off from the province of Liaodong by a barrier of wooden stakes (the Willow Palisade), patrolled by guards to keep Chinese from slipping out to dig the precious root. He adds that two or three thousand still sneaked through, risking their freedom.
p.q: Les endroits où croît le gin-seng, sont tout-à-fait séparés de la province de Canton, appelée Leaotong dans nos anciennes cartes, par une barrière de pieux de bois qui renferme toute cette Province, et aux environs de laquelle des Gardes rôdent continuellement pour empêcher les Chinois d'en sortir, et d'aller chercher cette racine.
p.s: Pierre Jartoux, letter from Peking, 12 April 1711
p.t: The places where ginseng grows are entirely separated from the province of 'Canton', called Liaodong on our old maps, by a barrier of wooden stakes that encloses the whole province, around which guards patrol constantly to prevent the Chinese from leaving it and going to look for this root.
p.c: 'Canton' is an error in this reprint (the province meant is Guandong, i.e. Liaodong, not Canton in the south). The volume is a later Toulouse reprint.

p.h: A people who seem to hate every city and building
p.g: Riccoldo's first sight of the Tartars, inside 'Turchia' (Seljuk Anatolia under Mongol rule). He describes broad faces, narrow eyes and thin beards, and then claims they 'seem to hate every city and every dwelling building', destroying nearly all the towns, castles and houses they meet. For a source on who built what in 'Tartary', this is a blunt statement from a man who lived among them that the Tartars were destroyers, not builders.
p.q: sed videntur odire omnem ciuitatem et omne edificium habitacionis. Nam quasi omnes ciuitates et castra et habitaciones et edificia destruunt, et illum magis ledunt, qui se magis illis humiliat
p.s: Riccoldo of Monte Croce, Liber peregrinationis, ed. J. C. M. Laurent (Leipzig, 1864)
p.t: but they seem to hate every city and every dwelling building. For they destroy almost all cities and castles and dwellings and buildings, and they harm most the one who humbles himself most before them
p.c: A hostile missionary generalisation; he says they 'seem' to hate cities, and his own later chapters show Tartars ruling from Tabriz and Baghdad.

p.h: A land without a single house
p.g: Waiting at Selenginsk on the Mongolian border, Bell sums up Mongol life: in all of Mongolia there is not one house, and even the prince and the high lama live in tents that move with the herds. He adds that they do not plough at all, and admits that he finds this simple life pleasant in so dry a climate. The prince's camp at Urga, he explains a few pages later, is a moving city of several thousand tents.
p.q: …of Mongalia, there is not so much as a single house to be seen. All the people, even the prince and high priest, live constantly in tents; and remove, with their cattle, from place to place, as conveniency requires. These people do not trouble themselves with ploughing, or digging the ground in any fashion;
p.s: John Bell (Travels, 1763)

p.h: No cities, no villages, not even a house
p.g: Verbiest states plainly that in the whole of 'Western Tartary' he found only mountains, rocks and valleys, with no towns and no houses at all. The people lived in tents and moved them from valley to valley as the grazing required, keeping cattle, horses and camels but no pigs or poultry.
p.q: there is nothing to be found but Mountains, Rocks, and Vallies, there are neither Cities, Towns, nor Villages, nor so much as any Houses. The Inhabitants Lodge under Tents, pitched on all sides in the open Feilds. They are for the most part Grasiers, and transport their Tents from one Vally to another, according as the Pastures are better.
p.s: Ferdinand Verbiest (English translation, 1686)
p.c: He is describing the part of Mongolia the imperial hunt crossed, not all of Mongolia.

p.h: Ruined brick temples of a Mongol prince
p.g: Invited by their Mongol guide Idam, members of the mission rode out to a hillside covered with ruins of stone buildings about two versts long. Idam said a Mongol prince called Sain Koung had lived there about 300 years earlier and that the buildings were temples. Timkovsky records the materials exactly: granite foundations, walls of sun-dried brick, and clay mixed with gravel instead of mortar. On the next page he adds stone cornices, vaulted niches, a stone-paved court and broken green tiles, and says the Mongols now rarely visit these 'monuments of their former splendour'.
p.q: we reached a mountain, the declivity of which was covered with ruins of stone-buildings, about two wersts in extent. … The buildings, of which the ruins lay before us, were temples. … The foundations were of granite, like that of the neighbouring mountain; the walls are of bricks, dried in the sun.
p.s: George Timkowski (English translation, 1827)
p.c: The date and builder come from the guide Idam's oral tradition; Timkovsky could not check them.

p.h: Beds on the ground, horses in the house, beautiful tents
p.g: In a sketch of how the Tartars trained for war, Martini describes their great ring hunts and their camp habits. They sleep on the ground on a horse-cloth and care nothing for houses; if they must live in houses they keep their horses inside and knock holes in the walls. Their tents, he says, are very beautiful and put up and struck so skilfully that they never slow an army's march.
p.q: The earth covered with their Horse-cloath is their Bed ; for they care not for Houses, and Chambers ; but if they be forced to dwell in Houses, their Horses must lodge with them, and they must have many holes beaten in the Walls; but yet their Tents are most beautiful, which they fix and remove with such Art and dexterity,
p.s: Martino Martini (English translation, London 1654)
p.c: A general portrait; the 'holes in the walls' detail may be hearsay.

p.h: Kazan's wooden fortress burns
p.g: During a Russian campaign against Kazan, bribed Russians set fire to the Tartar fortress, which was built of wood, and it burned to the ground in sight of the Russian army. Herberstein, relying on soldiers' reports, scorns the Russian commander for letting the Tartars rebuild it. It is a clear statement that the Khanate's fortress in the 1520s was timber, not stone.
p.q: In the meanwhile the fortress of Kazan, which was built of wood, was set on fire by some of the Russians who had been bribed for that purpose, and was burnt to the ground under the eyes of the Russian army.
p.s: Sigismund von Herberstein (translated by R. H. Major, 1851-52)

p.h: Underground huts and a village in a circle
p.g: South of Perekop the post stations were sometimes in deserted Tatar villages, and sometimes the stable-keeper lived in a hut dug underground, which she calls common in this treeless, sun-baked country. At sunset she reached a Tatar village of huts straggling in a circle with no fence, while herds of horses, cows and sheep drifted home across the downs: 'a simple and majestic landscape'. A few lines earlier she had called Perekop's Tatar village the dirtiest place she ever saw.
p.q: The posts were sometimes in a deserted Tartarian village, and sometimes the only habitation for the stable-keeper was a hut made under ground, a common habitation in this country, where the sun is so extremely hot, and there is no shade of any sort.
p.s: Elizabeth Craven (letters published London, 1789)
p.pl: Northern Crimea, between Perekop and Karasubazar
p.c: Villages were emptied by emigration after the Russian annexation of 1783; Craven does not say why these were deserted.
p.tg: underground huts village steppe deserted villages

p.h: The 'Seven Palaces' were mud-brick and Bukharan
p.g: The fortress of Semipalatinsk ('seven palaces') on the Irtysh was named after ruins twelve versts upstream, famous in earlier travel books. Pallas went to see them: the remains of a few buildings of slate slabs set in clay and of unburnt brick, one a windowless hut, laid out without order. He judged the work poor and plainly Bukharan, and counted the seven 'palaces' only by including rubble heaps.
p.q: Gegenwärtig ist nur noch von dreyen Gebäuden verfallenes Mauerwerk vorhanden; die Lage der übrigen läst sich nur noch aus dem Schutt schliessen; die Bauart ist schlecht und leicht vor Bucharisch zu erkennen, auch sind die Gebäude ohne einige Ordnung angelegt gewesen.
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (Reise, first edition, St Petersburg 1771-1776)
p.t: At present only decayed masonry of three buildings remains; the position of the rest can only be inferred from the rubble; the building style is poor and easily recognised as Bukharan, and the buildings were laid out without any order.
p.c: The identification as Bukharan is Pallas's judgement from the building style; modern scholars link the site to a Zunghar (Oirat) Buddhist monastery.
p.tg: seven palaces mud brick bukharans ruins

p.h: The Great Wall, built by a Chinese emperor against the Tartars
p.g: Verbiest crossed the Great Wall several times and says all seven wonders of the world together could not match it. He credits it to an ancient Chinese emperor who built it as a bulwark against the Western Tartars, and was amazed that water, brick and mortar had been hauled up dry mountains. He measured one stretch with an instrument at 1,037 geometrical feet above the horizon.
p.q: 'twas to make a Bulwork against their Incursions, that a Chinese Emperor in Antient times caused this great Wall to be Built, which seperates China from their Countrey. I have passed it several times, and have considered it very attentively, And I can say without Hyperbolizing, that all the seven Wonders of the World put together, are not comparable to this worke.
p.s: Ferdinand Verbiest (English translation, 1686)
p.c: The OCR reads 'fewer times', which seems to be a misreading of 'several times'.
p.tg: great wall brick mortar fortification china

p.h: Kurgan graves of 'a race now extinct'
p.g: At Krasnoyarsk Erman studied a collection of bronze objects dug from the kurgans (burial mounds) of the Minusinsk district, including round mirrors decorated with animals. The local Tatars told him the mounds belonged to 'a race now extinct, and totally different from theirs'. Erman noted that similar mirrors were still used in Buryat Buddhist rites, and wondered whether the builders were really so different from living Siberians.
p.q: The most important consideration, however, is, that these mirrors are found in graves which, as the present Tatar inhabitants of the circle maintain, belong to a race now extinct, and totally different from theirs.
p.s: Adolph Erman (translated by W. D. Cooley, 1848)
p.pe: Tatars of the Minusinsk basin (Khakas); unknown ancient builders
p.c: Erman saw the objects in a private collection, not the graves; the 'extinct race' is local Tatar belief. Modern archaeology links most Minusinsk bronzes to Bronze and Iron Age cultures (such as Tagar) long before the Turkic-speaking Khakas.
p.tg: kurgans bronze mirrors builders lost race

p.h: 'Tartar houses' with a window of ice
p.g: Travelling up the Chusovaya toward the Urals, the embassy stayed in villages of the Voguls, whom Brand calls the first Siberian Tartars. He says they live in Tartar houses with a fireplace, and once the wood has burned down to coals the smoke hole in the roof is closed with a sheet of ice that lets in the daylight. They sit and sleep cross-legged on a broad bench running round the room.
p.q: welche die ersten Siberischen Tartarn so Wogultski genennet werden, und ein Heydnisches, aber dabey sehr superstitiöses Volck … wie sie denn auch in solchen tartarischen Häusern wohnen, die doch mit einem Camin gemacht, das Rauch-Loch, welches oben im Dach ist, wird so bald das Holtz zu Kohlen gebrennet ist, mit einer Decke von Eiß zu gedecket, wodurch das Tages-Licht hinein fället
p.s: Adam Brand (Neu-vermehrte Beschreibung, Lübeck 1734)
p.pe: Voguls (Mansi), whom Brand calls the first Siberian Tartars
p.t: who are the first Siberian Tartars, called Wogultski, and a heathen but very superstitious people … and they also live in such Tartar houses, which are however made with a fireplace; the smoke hole at the top of the roof is covered, as soon as the wood has burned to coals, with a cover of ice, through which the daylight falls in
p.tg: houses ice window smoke hole voguls

p.h: Tartars in huts, now made to build villages
p.g: Describing the lands between Beijing and the Russian frontier, Careri says the vast 'Imperial Tartary' owned by the emperor of China was uncultivated and wooded, and its 'poor Tartars' lived in huts without walled houses, like the ancient nomads with portable dwellings. But the present emperor was now 'civilising' them, beginning to have villages built and gathering them in, with forty tributary princes including the Khalkha.
p.q: vivendovi que' poveri Tartari sotto capanne, senza case murate, a modo degli antichi Numidi, o Hamaxobiti, che tutti intesi alla vita pastorale, nè men case avevano, ma con loro portatili mapali, ove più concio era, andavano ad abitare. Ma l'Imperador odierno della Tartaria, bene al presente dirozzandogli comincia a far loro fabbricare Ville, e raccorgli entro a quelle in comunanza
p.s: Giovanni Francesco Gemelli Careri (Giro del Mondo, part IV, Naples 1700)
p.pe: Mongols under Qing rule ('poor Tartars'; Khalkha)
p.t: those poor Tartars living there under huts, without walled houses, in the manner of the ancient Numidians or Hamaxobians, who, all given to the pastoral life, did not even have houses but went to live wherever it was most convenient with their portable huts. But the present Emperor of Tartary, now civilising them well, is beginning to have villages built for them and to gather them into these in communities
p.c: Careri did not travel there; this comes from Jesuits at court (Grimaldi, Gerbillon, Pereira). The classical comparison is his own.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image; long s normalized.
p.tg: huts nomads qing villages mongols khalkha

p.h: Kholm's church: carved heads, Roman glass, a floor like a mirror
p.g: The chronicler describes Daniil's Church of St John in Kholm in unusual detail: vaults resting on four carved human heads, windows glazed with 'Roman' glass, a floor cast of copper and pure tin that shone like a mirror, and doors trimmed with white Galician and green Kholm stone, carved by 'a certain craftsman Avdei'. Nearby stood a tower on a stone base 15 ells high, built of hewn timber and whitewashed. The builders are Rus, and the materials are named.
p.q: комары, съ каждого угла преводъ, и стоянье ихъ на четырехъ головахъ человѣцскихъ изваяно отъ нѣкоего хытреца; окна украшена стеклы Римьскими … внутрьній же ей помостъ бѣ слитъ отъ мѣди и отъ олова чиста, яко блещатися яко зерцалу; двери же ей двоя украшены каменьемъ Галичкымъ бѣлымъ и зеленымъ Холмъскымъ, тесанымъ
p.s: Hypatian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 2 (1843)
p.pe: Prince Daniil of Galicia and his craftsmen (one named Avdei)
p.t: vaults, with an arch from each corner, and their supports on four human heads carved by a certain craftsman; the windows adorned with Roman glass … its floor inside was cast of copper and pure tin, so that it shone like a mirror; its two doors were adorned with hewn stone, white Galician and green Kholm stone
p.c: The chronicler writes that the church later burned; the description is of a building he knew.
p.tg: kholm stone church glass carving tower timber

p.h: A prefabricated wooden town floated down the Volga
p.g: To besiege Kazan, Ivan IV had a whole timber town made in advance upriver, carried it down the Volga on big Beloozero boats, and set it up quickly on a hill at the mouth of the Sviyaga, 15 versts from Kazan. The chronicle adds that churches, monasteries and houses were built inside. The fortress that ended the Kazan khanate was Russian-built and timber.
p.q: везущи съ собою готовы градъ древяны на великихъ лодіяхъ Белозерскихъ, тово же лѣта новъ, хитръ сотворенъ. И плывше … придоша въ землю Казанскую на рѣку Свіягу, на мѣсто указное имъ
p.s: Anonymous author of the History of the Kazan Tsardom, PSRL vol. 19 (1903)
p.pe: Ivan IV's builders; Shah Ali of Kasimov and Muscovite voevodas
p.t: carrying with them a ready-made wooden town on great Beloozero boats, new that same year and skilfully made. And sailing … they came into the Kazan land to the river Sviyaga, to the place appointed for them
p.tg: sviyazhsk prefabricated timber fortress volga

p.h: Treasure-hunters in the grave mounds
p.g: South of Tomsk lie many burial mounds of earth and stones. Bell was told that Russians went out every summer to dig them for gold, silver and weapons, and he saw some of the finds himself, including a brass horseman and gold deer figures. From the horse bones and weapons he concludes that great men were buried with their horse and servant, a custom he says the Kalmyks still keep; the Kalmyks, who hate disturbing the dead, sometimes robbed the grave-robbers. His Baraba Tartar informants credited the battles to Tamerlane.
p.q: Many persons go from Tomsky, and other parts, every summer, to these graves; which they dig up, and find, among the ashes of the dead, considerable quantities of gold, silver, brass… Whence it appears, that when any general or person of distinction, was interred, all his arms, his favourite horse and servant, were buried with him in the same grave;
p.s: John Bell (Travels, 1763)
p.pl: Upper Tom and Ob steppe, south of Tomsk
p.pe: ancient steppe peoples; Kalmyks and other Tartars
p.c: The digging is reported by informants; Bell saw only objects brought back. The link to Tamerlane is a local tradition.
p.tg: kurgans grave robbing gold burial tomsk

p.h: At Nanjing the conquerors live in huts; the Chinese keep the stone city
p.g: Describing the ruined Ming imperial palace at Nanjing, Nieuhof notes that the Tartar garrison settled near a temple and built themselves huts, leaving the Chinese to live and trade in the city. The palace buildings, of hard stone painted yellow, were Chinese work. On the same page he says the Tartars destroyed the palace out of hatred for the Ming family.
p.q: The Tartars seated themselves near to an Idol Temple called Paolinxi, where they built themselves several Hutts, leaving the Chineses to dwell in the City, and there to drive their Trade. The buildings are all of a hard sort of Stone, which the Natives have most curiously Painted with a Yellow Colour, that when the Sun reflects on them, they shine like Gold.
p.s: Johan Nieuhof (English translation by John Ogilby, 1669)
p.tg: huts nanjing palace stone

p.h: Balkh's great mosque, broken open by Genghis Khan for treasure
p.g: Balkh lay in ruins, never rebuilt since Genghis Khan destroyed it; only the outline of the city could be traced. Its mosque had been one of the finest in the world, and Genghis had three of its pillars torn down because he was told treasure was hidden beneath them. Ibn Battuta then tells the legend behind that rumour: a governor's wife built the mosque from the price of a jewelled robe and buried a third of the money under a pillar for repairs.
p.q: It has not been rebuilt since its destruction by the cursed Jengiz Khan. … Its mosque was one of the largest and handsomest in the world. Its pillars were incomparable : three of which were destroyed by Jengiz Khan, because it had been told him, that the wealth of the mosque lay concealed
p.s: Ibn Battuta (translated by Samuel Lee, 1829)
p.c: He saw the ruins; the story of the pillars and the treasure is local tradition.
p.tg: balkh mosque ruins genghis khan treasure

p.h: Old walls of 'the former dynasty' and earth-roofed huts on the Kerulen
p.g: Zhang passed the ruined base of a long wall stretching out of sight, which he credits to 'the former dynasty', meaning the Jurchen Jin, as their outer rampart. On the Kerulen he found a mixed population of 'barbarians' and Chinese living in a few houses roofed with earth and growing a little hemp and wheat.
p.q: 四驛有長城䫋址望之綿延不盡亦前朝所築之外堡也…瀕河之民雜以蕃漢稍有屋室皆以土冐之亦頗有種藝麻麥而巳
p.s: Zhang Dehui, Record of a Journey (Qiujian ji juan 100 = Yutang jiahua juan 8; Sibu congkan text, Kanseki Repository transcription)
p.t: After four stages there is the ruined base of a long wall, stretching on endlessly as far as one can see; this too is an outer rampart built by the former dynasty... The people along the river are a mix of fan (steppe peoples) and Han Chinese. There are a few houses, all roofed with earth, and they also do some farming, of hemp and wheat, and that is all.
p.c: 'Former dynasty' (前朝) here means the Jin, whose border walls ran across Inner Mongolia.
p.tg: long wall jin earth roofs farming kerulen

p.h: Golden columns and a Green Mount in the Khan's palace
p.g: Odoric describes the palace: a raised basement, twenty-four golden columns, walls hung with red leather, and a giant jade jar hooped with gold and fed by conduits of drink. On the page before he describes an artificial hill planted with trees, the Green Mount, with a lake and bridge. Yule notes that the hill still stood inside the Peking palace walls in his day.
p.q: But his own palace in which he dwells is of vast size and splendour. The basement thereof is raised about two paces from the ground, and within there be four-and-twenty columns of gold ; and all the walls are hung with skins of red leather, said to be the finest in the world.
p.s: Friar Odoric of Pordenone (translated by Henry Yule, 1866)
p.pe: The Great Khan (Yuan emperor) and his court
p.c: Yule notes that Mongol palace arrangements followed older Chinese and Asian royal traditions.
p.tg: palace jade gold green mount yuan

p.h: Clay ruins in the steppe, credited to Bukharan farmers
p.g: South of Semipalatinsk the party saw the foundations of a house of six rooms, which Gmelin calls the former dwelling of a Kalmyk 'idol-worshipper'. Others had stood there, but weather had destroyed them because all were built only of clay. Irrigation channels in the fields he credits to Bukharans, since, he explains, the Kalmyks do no farming at all and even their ruler has no fixed seat but is always on the move.
p.q: allein das Wetter hatte sie ganz zernichtet, weil alle Gebäude bloß von Leim aufgeführet gewesen waren. Auf dem Felde dabey sahe man einige Rinnen in dem Erdreiche, in welche die Einwohner dieser Gegend, welche Bucharen gewesen seyn sollen, Wasser geleitet haben
p.s: Johann Georg Gmelin (German original, Göttingen, 1751)
p.pl: Irtysh steppe south of Semey (Semipalatinsk), Kazakhstan
p.t: but the weather had destroyed them entirely, because all the buildings had been made only of clay. In the field nearby one could see some channels in the ground, into which the inhabitants of this area, who are said to have been Bukharans, had led water
p.c: Who built the houses is Gmelin's inference from hearsay and from what he knew of Kalmyk life.
p.tg: ruins clay irrigation bukharans kalmyks

p.h: The Grand Canal: a Mongol work, or only a Mongol repair?
p.g: Barrow credits the successors of Genghis Khan with opening a waterway joining the two ends of the empire, praising it as the highest credit to the Mongol Tartars. He records the Chinese counter-claim that the Tartars only repaired older works. Elsewhere he says Kublai 'repaired' the canal.
p.q: the successors of Gengis-Khan were induced to open a direct communication between the two extremes of the empire, by means of the rivers and canals; an undertaking that reflects the highest credit on the Mongul Tartars, and which cannot fail to be regarded with admiration, as long as it shall continue to exist. The Chinese, however, say, that the Tartars only repaired the old works that were fallen into decay.
p.s: John Barrow
p.tg: grand canal mongols yuan builders

p.h: Russian towers built from Tatar rubble
p.g: The few towers still standing among the ruins were not Tatar work at all, Zwick decided, but early Russian forts. His reasons are practical: the towers are held together with clay, while the Tatar buildings used a hard mortar, and they were patched together from broken pieces of fine older buildings, with glazed tiles stuck in any which way.
p.q: In the first place, they are built with clay cement, whereas the Tartars used a durable mortar; in the next place, they are evidently piled up from the ruins of handsome buildings, as may be seen by the glazed tiles which are stuck on at random, without any respect to the glazed side.
p.s: Heinrich August Zwick (English edition, 1831)
p.pe: Golden Horde Tatars; early Russian settlers
p.c: The judgement that the towers are Russian is Zwick's own reading of the masonry.
p.tg: mortar spolia towers russian ruins

p.h: A round frame of sticks covered with white felt
p.g: Rubruck describes the Mongol dwelling (the yurt or ger): a circular frame of interlaced sticks meeting in a hoop at the top with a chimney collar, covered in felt. The felt is whitened with chalk, clay or bone powder and embroidered with vines, trees, birds and beasts. Rockhill's note adds Carpini's description of the same round felt tents.
p.q: converging into a little round hoop on the top, from which projects above a collar as a chimney, and this (framework) they cover over with white felt. Frequently they coat the felt with chalk, or white clay, or powdered bone, to make it appear whiter, and sometimes also (they make the felt) black.
p.s: William of Rubruck (translated by W. W. Rockhill, 1900)
p.tg: yurt felt tent dwelling

p.h: The khan's felt house inside a fence of reeds and willow
p.g: The ruler of the Dzungars received the Russian envoy in a 'felt house' (a large yurt), set inside an enclosure woven from reeds and willow withies, entered through a door made of six planks. Unkovsky had to lift the felt door flap himself. The detail shows the materials of a steppe palace: felt, reed, willow and a little timber.
p.q: Какъ дошли сажень за 6 до коши, которая вкругъ контайшиной войлошной избы изъ камыша и талнику сплетена, отворили двери, которыя изъ шести плахъ сплочены.
p.s: Ivan Unkovsky (ed. N. I. Veselovsky, 1887)
p.t: When we came within about 6 sazhens of the enclosure (kosha), which is woven of reed and willow around the Kontaisha's felt house, they opened the doors, which are joined from six planks.
p.tg: yurt felt reed willow palace

p.h: A Tartar house: one storey, cushions, and cupboards behind the panels
p.g: At Karasubazar Craven visited the wife of the kadi (judge). The house, she writes, was a very light building of a single storey with no wooden furniture at all, only large cushions round the room. What impressed her was that the panelling slid back to reveal storage space larger than the room itself, so that 'every necessary' was hidden behind the walls.
p.q: A Tartar house is a very slight building of one story only … no chair, table, or piece of furniture in wood to be seen … large cushions are ranged round the room, on which we sat or reclined
p.s: Elizabeth Craven (letters published London, 1789)
p.tg: house cushions interior wainscot

p.h: Inside a Kirghiz felt tent on the Pamirs
p.g: Wood and his party were invited into one of the best tents of a Kirghiz camp of 100 families. He describes its coarse dun felts held by broad white bands, the ice-bag by the door that served as the family's water supply, a Russian iron cauldron on a tripod over the fire, and the measurements of the tent.
p.q: Close to the door lay a bag filled with ice … the water of the family. On drawing aside the felt which screened the entrance, the air of tidiness and comfort that met our eyes was a most agreeable surprise. … The Kirgah had a diameter of fourteen feet, a height of eight, and was well lighted by a circular hole above the fire-place.
p.s: John Wood
p.tg: yurt kirgah felt kirghiz pamir

p.h: Conquerors who would rather live in tents and carts than towns
p.g: Hayton's summary of the Tartar character includes a line that answers the question of Tartar towns directly: they know how to conquer foreign lands but not how to keep them, because they prefer to live in tents and wagons rather than in towns. The Latin version says the same, that they 'do not know how to live in castles and cities'.
p.q: Les Tartars scevent bien conquerre les estranges terres, mès il ne les sevent garder, car miaus volent estre en tentes e en chars que habiter en villes.
p.s: Hayton of Corycus, La Flor des estoires de la terre d'Orient (French text, 1307), ed. Ch. Kohler (1906)
p.t: The Tartars know well how to conquer foreign lands, but they do not know how to keep them, for they would rather be in tents and in carts than live in towns.
p.tg: tents wagons nomads towns

p.h: How a Mongol yurt is built
p.g: Bichurin describes the yurt, 'which we call a kibitka': folding lattice walls tied with rawhide instead of nails, which can be widened or heightened, a domed roof of poles set like rays into two half-rings, covered with one layer of felt in summer and two or three in winter and bound with woollen bands. A smoke hole at the top, a felt or wooden door always facing south-east. He gives the sizes too: 12 to 20 feet across.
p.q: Монголы кочуютъ въ круглыхъ юртахъ, которыя у насъ иначе называютъ кибитками. … Состоятъ изъ рѣшетчатыхъ складныхъ стѣнокъ, скрѣпленныхъ вмѣсто гвоздиковъ сырымъ ремнемъ; съуживая можно повышать ихъ, разширяя понижать. Полукруглый наметъ, составляющій кровлю, состоитъ изъ двухъ полукружій, къ которымъ лучеобразно прикрѣплены палки, упираемыя въ рѣшетчатыя стѣнки. Сей остовъ оболокаютъ войлоками въ одинъ, а зимою въ два и три ряда
p.s: Iakinf (N. Ya. Bichurin), 1828
p.t: The Mongols live nomadically in round yurts, which among us are otherwise called kibitkas. … They consist of folding lattice walls fastened with rawhide instead of nails; by narrowing them one can make them higher, by widening them lower. The half-round canopy that forms the roof consists of two half-rings to which poles are fixed like rays, resting on the lattice walls. This frame they cover with felts in one layer, and in winter in two and three

p.tg: yurt felt lattice kibitka construction

p.h: A silver fountain-tree made by a captive Parisian goldsmith
p.g: At the entrance of Mongke Khan's palace stood a silver tree built by 'master William', a Paris goldsmith taken captive in Hungary. Four silver lions spouted mare's milk, and pipes in the tree poured wine, clarified kumiss, honey mead and rice wine when a hidden man blew a trumpet-blowing angel on top. On the next page Rubruck says the palace itself was laid out like a church with a nave and two rows of pillars.
p.q: master William the Parisian had made for him a great silver tree, and at its roots are four lions of silver, each with a conduit through it, and all belching forth white milk of mares. … And from one of these pipes flows wine, from another caracosmos, or clarified mare's milk, from another bal, a drink made with honey, and from another rice mead
p.s: William of Rubruck (translated by W. W. Rockhill, 1900)
p.pe: Mongke Khan's court; Guillaume Boucher of Paris
p.tg: silver tree karakorum palace captive craftsmen boucher

p.h: Steppe houses dug into the ground
p.g: On the treeless steppe, Holderness says, Tatar houses were often dug down into the earth so deeply that they needed only a roof. She notes they were warmer in winter and cooler in summer than the usual plastered wooden huts.
p.q: The houses of the Stepp Tatars are often dug in the ground, to such a depth as to require only roofing to complete them. These being impervious to the air, are warmer in winter, and cooler in summer, than the usual huts, which are built of wood and plastered.
p.s: Mary Holderness
p.tg: dugouts earth houses steppe climate

p.h: A Nogai village built on a Mennonite plan
p.g: Near the Mennonite colonies on the Molochna, Haxthausen visited a Nogai Tatar village that looked 'perfectly German'. The Mennonite farmer Johann Cornies had persuaded the formerly nomadic Nogais to build this way and, Haxthausen was told, had already settled 17,000 of them. Solid houses with chimneys, poplars, gardens and Mennonite ploughs had replaced the old steppe life.
p.q: The houses in this village were all built with regularity and solid structure ; they had chimneys and enclosed courtyards. In front of the house-doors generally stand two poplars, with small flower-beds on each side ; in the gardens I noticed a great many fruit-trees, and in the courtyard ploughs, harrows, and carts of Mennonite construction
p.s: August von Haxthausen (translated by Robert Farie, 1856)
p.c: The figure of 17,000 settled Tatars was told to him, not counted.
p.tg: nogai village mennonites settlement houses

p.h: 'Tartaric battlements' where no Tartars came
p.g: At Novgorod, Alexander saw citadel walls topped with what he calls 'Tartaric battlements', copied from the Kremlin's, and notes that the Tartars never reached Novgorod, so its church crosses have no crescent beneath them. He repeats the popular idea that a crescent under a cross marks the Tatar period, and calls Moscow's Kremlin battlements 'Tartaric' as well. He also uses the label for a tower in the Genoese fortress at Balaklava.
p.q: The walls of the citadel were surmounted by Tartaric battlements, in imitation of those of the Kremlin; yet the Tartars in their invasions never penetrated to Novogorod, and the crosses on the churches do not, therefore, surmount a crescent
p.s: James Edward Alexander (1830)
p.c: 'Tartaric' is his style label: the Moscow Kremlin's brick walls and swallow-tail merlons were built by Italian masters in the 1480s and 1490s. The crescent-under-the-cross explanation is a popular belief that most historians reject.
p.tg: battlements kremlin style label crescent

p.h: Ablai-kit: a brick temple full of books in the steppe
p.g: Gmelin did not go himself: he sent a corporal, soldiers and a scribe, with orders to measure the place and 'carry off everything'. They reported a rectangle walled with broken rock, buildings on a raised base, a hall with two bellied furnaces, a great clay idol with sixteen smaller ones, and heaps of Tibetan ('Tangut') and Kalmyk manuscripts and woodblocks; nearly twenty cartloads still lay there. Gmelin names it the idol temple of the Kalmyk prince Ablai of the Khoshut, driven out about 1671.
p.q: In eben diesem Gebäude war ein großer Schrank mit vielen Fächern, worin bey der ersten Entdeckung viele Schriften gelegen haben, die nun in dem ganzen Gebäude zerstreuet sind. … Alle diese Gebäude sind von gebackenen Ziegelsteinen aufgeführet
p.s: Johann Georg Gmelin (German original, Göttingen, 1751)
p.t: In this same building was a large cupboard with many compartments, in which many writings lay when the place was first discovered, and which are now scattered through the whole building... All these buildings are built of baked bricks
p.c: Second-hand: the description is the soldiers' and scribe's report. It also records the expedition removing manuscripts from the site.

p.h: The khan's palace at Bakhchysarai
p.g: Pallas walks the reader through the Crimean khans' palace, which he calls a jumble of dwellings and offices round several courtyards. Upstairs the rooms are Turkish in style, with carpets, divans, wall paintings and stained glass, partly redone in European taste for Catherine the Great's visit in 1787. He notes the rose garden and fountain, the decayed harem, and a cage-like kiosk where the khan kept his falcons.
p.q: The apartments and galleries above-stairs, are decorated totally after the Turkish manner, with carpets and divans, or low sofas, oriental landscapes, clumsy paintings on the walls, artificial flowers, chimney-pieces, and stained glass windows. The alterations we noticed in some of these apartments, were made for the reception of the Empress in 1787,
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (English translation, 1812 edition)

p.h: Tents 'round like a pigeon-house'
p.g: Perry, an English engineer, watched Kalmyk hordes camp across the Volga every summer while he dug the Volga to Don canal. He describes their tents as round lattice-work frames that fold into narrow panels, covered with thick felt ('wylock'), with a door, a smoke hole and a fire in the middle; with the door and hole shut, he says, the tent is 'as warm as a stove'. He adds that a chief's tent could be lined with Persian silk.
p.q: The common Tents, in which the Cullmicks and other forementioned Tartars live and move, with their Camps, from Place to Place, are made of small Lettice-Work, round like a Pidgeon-House, … and which when they strike, folds together in narrow Pannels. They cover them over with Wylock, … matted together like Felt or Hat-Work,
p.s: Captain John Perry (The State of Russia, 1716)
p.tg: yurts lattice felt kalmyks tents

p.h: A Kremlin wall 'built by the Tatars'
p.g: Erman describes Kazan's fort, or kremlin, on a steep tongue of land between the Kazanka and the Bulak, 'still surrounded by the stone wall built by the Tatars'. On the next page he adds that inside it stood 'ruins of Tatar edifices, very solidly constructed of brick', beside Russian barracks, prisons and the cathedral.
p.q: Close to the steepest part of the bank lies the fort, or kreml, which is still surrounded by the stone wall built by the Tatars.
p.s: Adolph Erman (translated by W. D. Cooley, 1848)
p.pe: Kazan Tatars (the former Khanate of Kazan)
p.c: Modern historians date Kazan's white-stone kremlin walls to after the Russian conquest of 1552, built by masons from Pskov; Erman's own account of the siege (T0013 n171) describes the Tatar walls as oak timber filled with stones and clay. The brick Tatar ruins he saw are more securely Tatar work.

p.h: Forty stone pillars and a house of Chinese porcelain
p.g: In the Garden of the Plain, Babur describes the Chehel Sutun (Forty Pillars), a two-storey hall built entirely on carved stone columns, twisted and fluted, and a throne cut from a single huge stone brought from far away. Nearby stood a pavilion whose walls were covered in Chinese porcelain, for which, he was told, someone had been sent to China.
p.q: In this garden, there is another state pavilion, the walls of which are overlaid with porcelain of China, whence it is called the Chinese House. It is said that a person was sent to Khita, for the purpose of bringing it.
p.s: Babur (translated by John Leyden and William Erskine, 1826)
p.c: That the porcelain was fetched from China is what Babur was told.

p.h: The Great Wall is brick, built against the Tartars
p.g: Careri rode out from Beijing and walked four miles up the mountains to see the Wall himself. It stood 15 to 20 feet high, higher and wider in the valleys, room for six horses abreast, built 'of large fire-baked bricks with few stones', with strong square towers two bowshots apart running to the sea. He credits the emperor 'Xi-hoamti' with building it more than 1800 years earlier 'as a defence against the raids of the Tartars'.
p.q: Egli è alto quel muro in alcune parti 15. e in altre 20. piedi; ma nelle valli è più alto assai, e più largo, potendovi agiatamente andar sei cavalli di fronte. La fabbrica è di grandi mattoni cotti al fuoco, con poche pietre: & ha di quando in quando le sue Torri bẽ forti, e quadrate, l'una lontana all'altra quanto due tratti di freccia
p.s: Giovanni Francesco Gemelli Careri (Giro del Mondo, part IV, Naples 1700)
p.pl: Great Wall of China (north of Beijing)
p.pe: Chinese builders; Tartars as the enemy it was built against
p.w: 1696 (visit); wall credited to Qin Shi Huang
p.t: That wall is 15 feet high in some parts and 20 in others; but in the valleys it is much higher and wider, so that six horses can comfortably go abreast on it. The construction is of large bricks baked in the fire, with few stones, and from time to time it has its towers, very strong and square, one as far from the next as two bowshots
p.c: The 1800-year date and builder are from Chinese tradition via Jesuit books; the brick section he saw is a Ming rebuild.

p.h: Ruined cities on the Volga, blamed on Tamerlane
p.g: Sailing below the Kama, the embassy passed rich, empty grassland where only the ruins of cities and villages could be seen. Olearius was told they had been destroyed by Tamerlane; nearby hills were named after vanished cities, and on the previous page he notes the site of a former 'City of Tartary' with a saint's tomb still visited by locals. A treasure stone with a joke inscription on its underside is told on the same page.
p.q: On the right hand, we had the view of a spacious and very delightful Champain Country, the ground very rich, with a high grass on it; but it was not inhabited, and there could be seen only the ruins of Cities and Villages, which had been heretofore destroy'd by Tamberlane.
p.s: Adam Olearius (English translation by John Davies, 1669)
p.pl: Middle Volga below the Kama mouth, near Tetyushi
p.pe: Former Tartar (Volga Bulgar and Golden Horde) towns
p.c: He saw the ruins from the ship; who destroyed them is local tradition.

p.h: Timur's stone mosque, built by stonecutters from India
p.g: Babur, who took Samarkand more than once, describes the buildings of his ancestor Timur: a four-storey palace, the Gok-serai, in the citadel, and a grand mosque of stone near the Iron Gate, whose Qur'an inscription could be read almost a kos away. He notes that the stonecutters were brought from Hindustan. Erskine's footnote adds that the historian Sharaf al-Din counted 200 masons from Azerbaijan, Fars and India.
p.q: There are many other magnificent edifices. One of these is the grand mosque, which is situated near the Iron-gate, within the walls of the city, and is built of stone. A number of stone-cutters were brought from Hindustan to work on it.
p.s: Babur (translated by John Leyden and William Erskine, 1826)

p.h: Baraba Tatars: houses dug into the earth
p.g: Between Tara and Tomsk lay the Baraba district, home to Tatars who had once paid fur tribute both to the tsar and to the Kalmyk prince Ablai, and now paid only the tsar. They spoke both Kalmyk and Tatar, lived in dwellings dug into the ground like cellars, had their own princelings and small 'dug' towns (earthworks), and lived by hunting of every kind.
p.q: и въ той Барабинской волости живутъ Татары, которые прежъ сего платили есакъ Великому Государю и Аблаю тайшѣ, а нынѣ только Великому Государю платятъ. И тѣ Татары говорятъ по калмыцки и по татарски, а жилище ихъ есть, копаютъ въ землѣ погребы, и князцы у нихъ есть, и городки копаные, и звѣриные промыслы всякіе промышляютъ
p.s: Nikolai Spafarii (ed. Yu. V. Arsenyev, 1882)
p.t: and in that Baraba district live Tatars who formerly paid tribute (yasak) to the Great Sovereign and to Ablai taisha, but now pay only to the Great Sovereign. And these Tatars speak Kalmyk and Tatar, and their dwelling is this: they dig cellars in the ground; and they have princelings, and dug-out little towns, and they carry on all kinds of hunting.
p.c: Baraba was off his route; this is Tobolsk knowledge, not his own observation.

p.h: Xanadu: a Chinese-style palace built on a drained lake
p.g: Rashid describes how Qubilai's summer palace near Kaiping-fu was built. On the previous page he says the khan consulted sages and engineers, who chose a lake in a meadow, and that they gathered a local stone burned instead of firewood (coal). Here the lake is filled with rubble and broken brick sealed with molten tin and lead, raised on a platform, and crowned with a palace built 'in the manner of Cathay', inside a marble wall. The builders' style is Chinese, the patron Mongol.
p.q: با چشمهٔ آن از حصا و آجرّ خرد کرده پر کردند و قلعی و ارزیز بسیار بر ان کداختند تا محکم شد و بمقدار مرد بالائی از زمین بر آوردند و صفّهٔ بر بالای آن ساختند … و بر سر آن صفّه قرشی بیانك ختای ساخته و پیرامون آن مرغزار از مرمر دیواری کشیده
p.s: Rashid al-Din (Persian text ed. E. Blochet, 1911)
p.t: [the lake] with its spring they filled with rubble and broken brick, and melted a great deal of tin and lead over it until it was firm; they raised it the height of a man above the ground and built a platform on top of it … and on top of that platform they built a palace in the Cathay [Chinese] manner, and round that meadow they drew a wall of marble.
p.c: Rashid never saw Shangdu; he relied on informants from Yuan China. The Persian word qarshi (palace) and the phrase 'Cathay manner' are explained in Blochet's notes.

p.h: Felt temples on the Volga, stone temples in Mongolia
p.g: Opening his chapter on Buddhist temples, Pallas contrasts the Volga Kalmyks, who because of their wandering life still kept their images in portable sacred felt tents, which he compares to the Tabernacle of the Israelites in the desert, with the Mongols under Chinese rule, who had long had permanent temples, some of stone. He adds that under the Mongol khans who ruled China, buildings for Lamaist worship were raised in the eastern Mongol steppes, but after the empire broke up the Mongols returned to a moving life.
p.q: die wolgischen Kalmücken aber halten, wegen ihrer unstäten Lebensart, ihren Götzendienst noch izt, so wie sonst auch die Mongolen thaten, in beweglichen heiligen Filzhütten, (Burchanin-Orgö) welche der Stiftshütte, bey denen in der Wüste, noch nomadisch lebenden Israeliten verglichen werden könten … Die Mongolen, welche unter China stehn, haben vorlängst an verschiednen Orten ihres Landes beständige und zum Theil von Stein erbaute Tempel gehabt
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (Sammlungen historischer Nachrichten über die mongolischen Völkerschaften, part 2, 1801)
p.pe: Volga Kalmyks; Khalkha and Inner Mongols
p.t: but the Volga Kalmyks, because of their unsettled way of life, still keep their idol worship, as the Mongols also formerly did, in movable sacred felt huts (Burchanin-Orgö), which could be compared to the Tabernacle of the Israelites still living as nomads in the wilderness … The Mongols who are under China have long had permanent temples in various places of their land, some of them built of stone

p.h: Ruined cities between Kazan and Astrakhan, their stones reused
p.g: Near Simbirsk de Bruyn was told of very old and important cities between Kazan and Astrakhan, among them 'Achtoeba'. Nothing of it remains, he says, because all its stones were carried away to build Astrakhan and other places. The name almost certainly points to the Akhtuba branch of the Volga, where the ruins of the Golden Horde capital lay; Struys (W249) reported the same stone-robbing in 1669.
p.q: Au reste on affirme qu'il y a des villes fort anciennes & fort considerables entre Casan & Astracan, & entr'autres Achtoeba … On sait aussi que la ville d'Achtoeba étoit située sur cette riviere, mais il n'en reste pas les moindres vestiges, toutes les pierres en aiant été transportées pour bâtir Astracan & quelques autres places.
p.s: Cornelis de Bruyn (French translation, Voyages de Corneille Le Brun, 1718)
p.pl: Akhtuba (the Volga branch where the Golden Horde capital Sarai lay)
p.t: Moreover, it is said that there are very ancient and very considerable cities between Kazan and Astrakhan, among others Achtoeba … It is also known that the town of Achtoeba stood on this river, but not the least trace of it remains, all the stones having been carried away to build Astrakhan and some other places.
p.c: Hearsay; de Bruyn says he could learn nothing certain about these cities.

p.h: A carved brick tower in a dead city
p.g: After days of travel without seeing a single house, the embassy passed two deserted walled cities. At the second, Taimingzingh, stood two towers, the larger an octagon faced in brick, with carved stone panels telling 'several Histories' set on all eight sides. The description fits the octagonal brick pagodas that still stand at ruined towns of the Khitan Liao dynasty (907-1125) in this part of Inner Mongolia, though Ides himself gives no date or builder.
p.q: we reached another old desolate City, called Taimingzingh, fortified with a square Wall, and necessary Bulwarks: There are in it two Towers or Turrets, one very high and the other less: The largest was an Octagon, whose Front was built with Brick, and about ten Fathom from the Ground there was on each of the eight sides Stones placed, in which were carved several Histories.
p.s: Evert Ysbrants Ides (English translation, 1706)
p.pe: Unknown builders (a 'Tartarian King' in Chinese tradition)
p.c: Linking the ruin to the Liao is a modern comparison, not something Ides says, and which ruined town he saw is uncertain.

p.h: Black felt tents and a room dug underground
p.g: Lost on a freezing night while hunting, young Timur and his companions saw black felt tents that at first looked like sand hills. The family took them for thieves, then gave them a room built underground, lit a fire, fed them soup and lent them flea-ridden blankets. Timur says that after becoming ruler he rewarded them.
p.q: About this time we saw some black (felt) tents or huts, upon which my companions said, " these are hillocks of sand and dust," … the inhabitants of which supposing I was a thief, hallooed out and prepared to attack me ; but when I told them all the circumstances, they were ashamed, and having cleared out a room which was constructed under ground, lighted a fire for us
p.s: Attributed to Timur (translated by Charles Stewart, 1830)
p.c: The word 'felt' is the translator's addition in brackets. The story may be literary.

p.h: Graves boxed in logs, like little houses
p.g: At the post village of Metyeshka, east of Kazan, Erman saw a Tatar burial ground. Each grave was covered by a man-length box about four feet high, filled with earth and built exactly like the dwelling houses, of rough-hewn logs laid one on another. The graves lay side by side, their long sides running east to west.
p.q: about the length of a man, and filled with earth. It is formed in the same manner as the dwelling houses, with rough-hewn posts laid one upon the other. The graves were in general parallel to one another, the longer sides lying nearly east and west.
p.s: Adolph Erman (translated by W. D. Cooley, 1848)
p.c: The sentence begins on the previous page (n177): 'On every grave there is a rectangular chest, raised about four feet above the ground'.

p.h: Portable Nogai huts of twigs and felt
p.g: Reuilly describes the seven or eight thousand Nogais roaming between the Berda and the Molochna. Their round huts, about eight feet across, have a wicker wall and dome covered with rush mats and brown felt, a smoke-hole and a tiny door; the furniture is a few cushions, a low table, pots and dishes. He adds that they were starting to build fixed houses and farm.
p.q: They encamp themselves in little cabins of felt; their tents, according to Thunmann, are a kind of portable huts, of a circular form, of about eight feet in diameter, made of lath-work or hurdles of twigs, about the size of a thumb, forming a sort of wall about four feet in height, upon which rests a dome or roof of the same structure
p.s: Jean Reuilly (English translation, 1807), citing Johann Thunmann
p.pe: Nogai Tatars (remnant of the Kuban Tatars)
p.c: The tent description is taken from Thunmann's earlier book, not Reuilly's own observation.

p.h: Inside a spotless Tatar house
p.g: After rejecting a filthy Russian post-house, Webster's party lodged with a Tatar family and were 'much surprised' by the cleanliness: double carpets, a row of cushions along the wall to sleep on, an open hearth in a big chimney, cushions piled to the roof and pots ranged on the rafters, all whitewashed. On the next page the host hints he hopes to be paid, unlike some Russian officers who answered with blows.
p.q: On entering, we were much surprised at the perfect cleanliness of the house. The room was doubly carpeted, and along the wall was a row of cushions, of sufficient breadth to admit of a traveller's stretching himself with perfect comfort. The fire was on the ground, in a large open chimney.
p.s: James Webster

p.h: Bukhara's houses of raw brick and timber
p.g: Fraser's informants described Bukhara's houses as two or three storeys of raw (unfired) brick strengthened with timber frames, with poorer houses of timber filled with mud and broken brick. The city's roughly eighty colleges, by contrast, were mostly of stone and lime.
p.q: The houses in Bockhara are in general two and even three stories high, built of raw brick, and often strengthened by wooden frame work ; those of inferior description are constructed of the same frames of timber, filled up with mud and fragments of brick.
p.s: James Baillie Fraser
p.c: Second-hand description.

p.h: Why 'Golden Horde': the khan's gilded tent
p.g: On Abu'l-Fida's remark that the horde of the Tartar prince of Berke's country comes as far as Ukek, Reinaud explains that horde (Turkish ordu) means tent: the Chinggisid khans moved with the seasons and wherever they pitched their tents was called the horde. He suggests the Russians called the dynasty the Golden Horde because the khan's tent stood on wooden posts plated with gold, citing Ibn Battuta.
p.q: Le mot horde, en arabe ordou, appartient à la langue turke et signifie tente. Les princes tartares de la race de Gengiskhan, qui régnèrent sur le Capichac, étaient dans l'usage de changer de demeure, suivant la saison, et le lieu où ils dressaient leurs tentes portait le nom de horde … probablement parce que la tente qu'occupait le khan était appuyée sur des pieux de bois recouverts de lames d'or
p.s: J. T. Reinaud (editor's footnote, 1848)
p.pe: Mongol khans of the Qipchaq steppe (Golden Horde)
p.t: The word horde, in Arabic ordu, belongs to the Turkish language and means tent. The Tartar princes of the race of Chinggis Khan who ruled the Qipchaq steppe used to change their residence with the seasons, and the place where they pitched their tents was called the horde … probably because the tent the khan occupied rested on wooden posts covered with plates of gold
p.c: An editor's explanation drawing on Rubruck, Ibn Battuta and Hammer-Purgstall, not Abu'l-Fida's own words.
p.tg: horde ordu tent golden horde etymology

p.h: Yurts of 'the former rulers of the country'
p.g: Near Tobolsk, on the steep bank of the Irtysh, Erman entered sooty Tatar yurts at Philatefsk. They were shaped like Ostyak (Khanty) huts but cleaner, with a clay hearth (chubal), a built-in cauldron, and woven cloth, Bukharan carpets or felt in the sleeping recesses. The families sat cross-legged round brick tea, with horse-flesh cooking. He calls them 'descendants of the former rulers of the country'.
p.q: The Ostyak mode of living cannot be confounded with that of these people, yet the yurts of both are shaped alike; but those of the Tatars have always the advantage in cleanliness, and, besides the chubal of beaten clay, there is also the well-set boiler: in the recesses, too, instead of skins there lies usually some woven fabric
p.s: Adolph Erman (translated by W. D. Cooley, 1848)
p.c: Here 'yurt' means a small fixed winter hut, not a felt tent.

p.h: Moscow's mosque, rebuilt by a Tatar merchant
p.g: Kohl visited Moscow's small mosque in the Tatar quarter. Its predecessor burned in the fire of 1812, and the poor congregation of about 120 Tatars could not rebuild until a wealthy Tatar paid for new walls. When Kohl saw it, it still had only a temporary roof and bare walls, and Russians had stolen one of its prized carpets.
p.q: The little building erected here to the honour of Allah … had a predecessor which in 1812 met with the same fate from the French fire, in which so many Russian churches shared. The flock were long unable to get together the necessary funds for a new temple, till about twelve years ago, when a wealthy Tartar erected the walls that are now standing.
p.s: J. G. Kohl (English abridged translation, 1844)

p.h: Tash Kurghan: domed houses of clay and sun-dried brick
p.g: Moorcroft describes the Uzbek-ruled market town of Tash Kurghan: about 20,000 one-storey houses of clay and sun-dried brick, domed 'in the usual fashion of the country', each in its own walled yard with fruit trees, along straight streets that crossed at right angles with water running down them.
p.q: Tash Kurghan is about three miles in circumference, and may comprise about twenty thousand houses. They are built of clay and sun-dried bricks, of one story, with domes in the usual fashion of the country, and each stands by itself in a walled enclosure, often containing fruit-trees.
p.s: William Moorcroft (edited by H. H. Wilson, 1841)

p.h: Leh: houses of unburnt brick and poplar beams
p.g: Moorcroft describes the walled capital of Ladakh: towers on the hills, a labyrinth of streets, and houses of one to three storeys built mostly of large unburnt bricks, a few of stone, whitewashed outside. p.q: The walls are in a few instances wholly, or in part of stone, but in general they are built with large unburnt bricks: they are whitened outside with lime, but remain of their original colour inside.

p.pe: Ladakhis (people of what Moorcroft called Hither Tatary)

p.g: Before they moved to Hungary, the Magyars lived on the steppe north of the Black Sea. Ibn Rusta calls them a race of the Turks, says their chief rides out with twenty thousand horsemen, and that they have tents (qibab) and move with the grass and pasture. p.s: Ibn Rusta (Arabic text ed. M. J. de Goeje, 1892)

p.h: The Golden Orda: a tent on gold-plated pillars
p.g: Carpini attended the enthronement of Guyuk near Karakorum. After a first great tent called the Sira Orda, the court moved to the Golden Orda, a tent whose pillars were plated in gold with gold nails and whose roof and sides were hung with precious cloth. Guyuk was then seated on the throne and everyone drank until evening.

p.h: A chapel mortared with a prince's ashes
p.g: The Kalmyks did build in stone and wood, for their dead nobles. Zwick visited a small memorial chapel (zaza) for the late Torgut prince Sandschi-Ubaschi: a wooden room about four paces square on a stone base, reached by steps, with a flat roof and a small tower. He was told that the prince's ashes had been mixed into its mortar and whitewash.
p.q: This chapel was erected to the memory of the late Torgud Prince Sandschi-Ubaschi, father of the Prince Zerren Ubaschi, and his ashes, as the Calmucs informed me, are mixed with the mortar which cements and whitens the building. The foundation of this edifice is of stone, upon which is erected a wooden chapel, with steps up to it.

p.h: Roadside buildings of the Mughal emperors
p.g: On the road west from Kunduz, Wood found a domed water cistern and a guard tower that he credits to the 'Mongol' emperors, meaning the Mughal dynasty of India founded by Babur. He admired them as public works for travellers, and notes that the emperors had kept post-houses all the way to Balkh.
p.q: At the bottom of their western slope stands a water-cistern, a dome-covered building, and a guard-tower … remnants of Mongol munificence, evincing, by their usefulness rather than their beauty, the philanthropic spirit of the monarch who erected them. … for during the palmy days of Baber's line the emperors of Hindustan had post-houses
p.s: John Wood

p.h: Kazan Tatars who 'live all in houses'
p.g: Bruce contrasts the Kazan Tatars with the nomads: they all lived in houses, farmed and supplied the south with food, which made them the most civilised of the Tartars in his eyes. He adds they were mostly Muslims, though many townspeople were Orthodox, and were forbidden to enter Russian fortifications. On the previous page he describes Kazan itself: wooden houses, a stone castle, and a population of Tatars and Russians.
p.q: The kingdom of Casan lies on the left side of the Wolga, and its inhabitants live all in houses, and subsist by agriculture : they supply the southern provinces with all sorts of provisions, and by this means they are the most civilized of all the Tartars.
p.s: Peter Henry Bruce (published 1782)

p.h: Fifteen hundred stonecutters on Babur's buildings in India
p.g: Babur was scornful of Indian architecture but impressed by India's supply of craftsmen. He compares Timur's famous stone mosque in Samarkand, built with 200 masons from several countries, to his own works: 680 stonecutters at Agra alone, and 1,491 across his building sites. The buildings of this Timurid ruler were raised by local Indian hands.
p.q: In Agra alone, and of stone-cutters belonging to that place only, I every day employed on my palaces six hundred and eighty persons; and in Agra, Sikri, Biana, Dhulpur, Gualiar, and Koel, there were every day employed on my works one thousand four hundred and ninety-one stone-cutters.
p.s: Babur (translated by John Leyden and William Erskine, 1826)
p.tg: stonecutters agra building labour

p.h: Unrobbed mounds, unlike those of Tartary
p.g: On the plain near Larissa Clarke saw many large tumuli in good condition, some with shepherds' huts built on top. He notes that, unlike the mounds of 'Tartary', they did not seem to have been dug open for treasure. The steppe kurgans were well known for being plundered for their gold.
p.q: They did not seem to have been opened and ransacked for the hidden treasure which it is possible some of them contain, as it has often happened in Tartary ; but, upon some of them, small huts had been constructed, as dwellings for the shepherds.
p.s: Edward Daniel Clarke (1816)
p.pe: (ancient Greek mound builders; comparison with the steppe)

p.h: A Buddhist monument of stone, clay and grey brick
p.g: On a walk near Urga the Russians climbed to a soubourgan (suburgan, a Buddhist stupa) built by a Mongol prince. Timkovsky notes how it was made: a square base of unhewn stone bound with clay and straw, grey brick walls, and a core of sand and stones. It shows Mongol nobles commissioning permanent religious buildings even while living in tents.
p.q: we ascended an eminence, on which stands a soubourgan, or sacred pyramid, of the disciples of Boudha, erected by a Mongol prince. The pedestal, which is of a square form, is made of unhewn stone, cemented with a composition made of clay and straw: the walls are made of gray bricks, and the interior filled with sand and stones.
p.s: George Timkowski (English translation, 1827)
p.tg: stupa suburgan brick clay buddhism

p.h: A solid brick tower thought to guard against Tartars
p.g: At Tong-choo-foo, the river port of Beijing, the embassy examined an old eleven-storey brick pagoda with no door or window in its solid lower stories. Nobody knew what it had been for; the guess Staunton reports is that it was an ancient watch tower against sudden Tartar raids.
p.q: It is built of brick, and in its exterior form resembles what are called in Europe Chinese pagodas … It is thought most probable that this building was erected prior to the existence of Tong-choo-foo, and perhaps of the great Chinese wall, and was intended for a watch tower, to guard against the sudden approach of the Tartar enemy.
p.s: George Leonard Staunton
p.c: Staunton admits the tower's 'original destination is not known with certainty'; the watch-tower idea is a conjecture, and many solid brick pagodas in north China were Buddhist relic towers.
p.tg: pagoda brick watch tower ruins

p.h: Akbar's red-brick rest-house on the road to Kashmir
p.g: On the old imperial road over the Pir Panjal, Vigne finds loose stones that are all that remain of a causeway laid by Akbar's pioneers, and a large brick serai (caravan rest-house) Akbar built for the imperial retinue. He credits the building plainly to the Mughal emperor and describes its material. He chose to sleep in a humbler house prepared for Ranjit Singh instead.
p.q: A large Serai built by him, of red brick, is conspicuously placed on the right bank of the stream, near Thana, and its quadrangle was well adapted to the reception of a cortege of a Mogul Emperor
p.s: Godfrey Thomas Vigne (1842)
p.tg: serai brick akbar road mughals

p.h: Mongols in tents of coarse felt; a timber stockade around Manchuria
p.g: Drawing on Gerbillon's 1688 journey, Davis says the Mongols and Kalkas are devoted to their Lamas, live in tents of coarse felt, eat half-raw meat and value livestock over money; Timkowski adds that brick tea is their currency. Two pages earlier he describes the Manchu homeland of Mukden, where the emperors are buried, fenced not by a wall but by a timber stockade about eight feet high, wrongly drawn on some European maps as part of the Great Wall.
p.q: Entirely devoted to their Lamas, whom even the Emperor of China honours, on account of their influence over the various tribes, the Mongols live in tents of coarse felt, eat nothing but flesh half raw, and exchange their sheep and cattle for a few of the necessaries of life, having no value for money.
p.s: John Francis Davis, summarising Gerbillon (1688)
p.pe: Mongol and Kalka Tartars; Manchu homeland
p.c: Second hand, from Jesuit and Russian travellers.
p.tg: felt tents lamas brick tea stockade mongols

p.h: A lama's castle of stone or brick, with no stairs or windows
p.g: Relaying Bogle, who lived five months with the Panchen Lama, Stewart describes one of the Lama's castles: stone or brick, many courts and halls, rooms finished in Chinese style with gilding and varnish. The surprise is what is missing: upper floors are reached by wooden or iron ladders, and light comes through covered holes in the ceilings. Stewart does not call this a Tartar building; it is the seat of the lama the Tartars revered.
p.q: The castle is of stone or brick, with many courts, lofty halls, terraces, and porticos ; and the apartments are in general roomy, and highly finished in the Chinese stile, with gilding, painting, and varnish. There are two conveniencies to which they are utter strangers, stair-cases and windows.
p.s: John Stewart, relaying George Bogle
p.c: Second hand, from Bogle's letters. The castle is Tibetan, not built by or for Tartars.
p.tg: castle stone brick chinese style ladders

p.h: Yarkand's new citadel and the old town dug up for treasure
p.g: Mirza Haidar describes how Aba Bakr made Yarkand his capital: he dug out the old town, finding much treasure, brought in water channels, laid out gardens and built a citadel thirty gaz high with six gateways guarded by paired towers. It is a local ruler's building programme described by a man who knew the city well.
p.q: The old town was dug out by Mirza Aba Bakr ; it was among the excavations [kazihka] which we have spoken about, and much treasure was found [in it]. … Mirza Aba Bakr built a citadel which, in most places, is thirty statute gaz in height.
p.s: Mirza Haidar Dughlat (translated by E. Denison Ross, 1895)
p.pe: Mirza Aba Bakr, Dughlat ruler of Kashgar
p.c: Mirza Haidar himself doubts the report of 12,000 gardens.

p.h: White marble tombs of Timur's descendants at Gazur Gah
p.g: At the shrine of the Sufi saint Khwaja Abdullah Ansari on the hills above Herat, Conolly walked through a walled garden where trees shaded 'several tombs of white marble built over the dust of the descendants of Timour-lung'. He adds that Timur's descendants built summer palaces and gardens on the same hill.
p.q: We deposited our slippers here, and then passed into a walled garden, the trees of which shaded several tombs of white marble built over the dust of the descendants of Timour-lung.
p.s: Arthur Conolly (1834)
p.tg: herat timurids tombs marble gardens

p.h: An Armenian monastery levelled by the Tartars and rebuilt in brick
p.g: At Etchmiadzin, seat of the Armenian patriarch, Chardin was told the first monastery was built by the patriarch Nerses and ruined by the Tartars, and that it had been levelled five times in all. What he saw was built of brick. Here Tartars appear as destroyers, not builders.
p.q: The first Monastery of this Church was built by Nierses the Twenty Ninth Patriarch of Armenia: This the Tartars ruin'd; and if we may believe the Chronology of the Place, it had been Five times levell'd with the Ground: It is at present built of Brick
p.s: Jean Chardin (English translation, London, 1691)
p.tg: etchmiadzin monastery brick destruction

p.h: Inside a Tatar mosque at Tobolsk
p.g: With the governor's help, Ides was allowed into a Tatar mosque, which he says outsiders were normally not shown. It was plain: large open windows and carpets on the floor, nothing more. Worshippers left their shoes at the door and sat in rows; the imam wore white calico and a white turban. He adds that the chief mullah was an Arab, and that anyone who could read Arabic was highly respected.
p.q: Metschets, called by other Authors Mosques, or Churches, had large Windows round them, all which were set open: The Floor was covered with Tapistry, besides which there was no other Ornament. All Persons at their entrance leave their Shoes or Slippers at the Door … The chief Priest sat there, in a white Calico Habit, and a white Turkish Turbant on his Head.
p.s: Evert Ysbrants Ides (English translation, 1706)

p.h: Terraced Tatar villages with clay roofs
p.g: In the mountain villages of Toklouk, Kooz and Otouz, Xavier found flat-roofed Tatar houses built against the valley sides, so that the roofs formed terraces where people worked and visited each other. The roofs are stout timber covered with a thick bed of clay. At evening whole villages gathered on them.
p.q: the terrace tops of their houses, where they regularly carry on their work, and which are formed of stout carpentry covered with a thick bed of clay. Nothing can be more picturesque than the appearance, at evening, of all these terraces rising in gradations one above the other.
p.s: Xavier Hommaire de Hell (English translation, 1847)

p.h: A nine-foot prayer wheel worked by a winch
p.g: At Soongnum Gerard saw three prayer cylinders kept turning by water, and at Nisung others turned by the wind. The largest, about nine feet high, stood in a square house with a wooden dome, lined with China silk, and needed two people to work it with ropes and a winch.
p.q: At Soongnum there are three cylinders kept constantly in motion by water, on the same principle as the water mills, and at Nisung several are turned by the wind.
p.s: Alexander Gerard (ed. George Lloyd, 1841)

p.h: Pyramids of poles covered with hides
p.g: The mine official Shangin, travelling in the high Altai, describes the local 'mountain Tatars' as herders who do no farming. Their huts, apart from the elders', are wretched: a few poles set up in a pyramid and covered with hair felts or, more often, animal hides, because they make no felt themselves. Since they move often with their herds, empty pole pyramids stand in many places.

p.s: Peter Ivanovich Shangin, journal of an Altai journey (translated by P. S. Pallas), Neue Nordische Beyträge vol. 5 (1793)
p.t: they set up a few poles … together and cover them with hair felts, but still more commonly with animal hides, since … make none themselves

p.h: Kuchum's hidden ford of stone and sand
p.g: Before Yermak's last night, the chronicle explains the trap: across a swampy stream near the Vagai, Kuchum had built a broad ford, wide enough for three or four carts abreast, in one spot only, packing it firmly with stones and sand; anyone who missed the spot drowned. A Tatar condemned to death was sent across it to spy on the sleeping Cossacks. It is one of the few Tatar-built works the chronicles describe.
p.q: понеже Кучюмъ учинилъ бродъ широкой, какъ въ три или въ четыре телѣги проѣхать въ одномъ мѣстѣ, каменьемъ и пескомъ засыпалъ плотно; а кто не угадаетъ, утопаетъ.
p.s: Kungur (Brief Siberian) Chronicle, Remezov tradition, 1880 edition
p.t: because Kuchum had made a broad ford, so that three or four carts could pass abreast, in one place, filled in firmly with stones and sand; and whoever did not hit upon it would drown.

p.h: A prince in exile sleeps in a felt tent of cross-poles
p.g: Driven out of his homeland, Babur set off for Khorasan with two or three hundred followers, most on foot. They had only two proper tents; Babur gave his to his mother and slept each night in a small felt tent on flexible poles. Erskine's note explains this alachuq was a felt-covered frame that folded up easily.
p.q: Such was our distress, that among us all we had only two tents. My own tent was pitched for my mother, and they erected for me at each stage a felt-tent of cross-poles, in which I used to take up my quarters.
p.s: Babur (translated by John Leyden and William Erskine, 1826)
p.tg: felt tent alachuq exile nomad dwelling

p.h: Bukhara's sun-dried brick and arched bazaars
p.g: Quoting Burnes's figures, Wolff describes Bukhara's massive buildings, the Khan's fortress-palace, houses of sun-dried brick, narrow dirty streets and lofty arched bazaars where each trade had its own section.
p.q: It has massive buildings, three hundred and sixty mosques, three hundred schools, the Khan's palace, or rather fortress ; houses built of bricks dried in the sun ; very narrow and dirty streets ; lofty arched bazaars, in which the different trades have their distinct sections ; and ponds and fountains for the supply of water.
p.s: Joseph Wolff, summarising Alexander Burnes
p.c: Taken from Burnes, as the page says.

p.h: Uzbek 'black houses' of felt
p.g: In his appendix on Bukhara, Fraser reports that the tents of the country Uzbeks were like those of the Turkmens: a lath frame under thick black felts, called kara-ui ('black house') or kirgah, with a lattice smoke hole that could be covered with felt when it rained.
p.q: The tents, or rather houses, of the Oozbecks resemble those of the Toorkomans, of which a description has already been given, a frame work of thin laths covered with thick, black felts, and they are called karaooees (black houses) or kirghahs. The floors of the rich are spread with carpets and numuds, those of the poor with a blanket or mat of camels' hair
p.s: James Baillie Fraser
p.pe: Nomadic Uzbeks of the emirate of Bukhara
p.c: From informants, not seen by Fraser.

p.h: The Xiongnu: no walled cities, felt and furs
p.g: Sima Qian opens his chapter on the Xiongnu with their way of life: they move their herds of horses, cattle and sheep in search of water and grass, have no walled cities, fixed homes or farming, though each group has its own pasture land, and they keep no written records. Later in the passage he adds that from the ruler down they eat meat and wear hides, felt and furs. It is the oldest Chinese model of the 'people without cities' that later writers used for the Tartars.
p.q: 逐水草遷徙，毋城郭常處耕田之業，然亦各有分地。毋文書，以言語為約束。
p.s: Sima Qian, Shiji ch. 110 (Kanseki Repository text)
p.pe: Xiongnu (northern steppe nomads of the Han era)
p.t: They move about following water and grass, and have no walled cities, fixed dwellings or work of tilling fields; yet each has its own allotted land. They have no writing, and make agreements by word of mouth.
p.c: The Xiongnu are not 'Tartars'; the passage is included as the earliest Chinese description of steppe nomad life. Archaeology has since found Xiongnu fortified settlements.
p.tg: xiongnu nomads no cities felt han dynasty

p.h: Inside a Tatar merchant's house in Kazan
p.g: Hoping to see a 'genuine national household', Haxthausen is taken to the home of two merchant brothers and finds the rooms furnished in European style, with Chinese porcelain, mirrors, a Persian carpet and a stone bowl inscribed with Koran verses. He glimpsed a six-foot-wide family sleeping bench, but the women's rooms were closed to him.
p.q: I wished to see a genuine national household, but this no longer exists, at least in Kazan, as the people here too are already affected by European cultivation. The furniture of the rooms into which we were conducted was quite European … In one of the glass cases was a stone bowl, inscribed with texts from the Koran.
p.s: August von Haxthausen (translated by Robert Farie, 1856)
p.tg: house interior merchants koran furniture

p.h: Tatar cottages and little mosques among the vineyards
p.g: Sailing along the south coast of Crimea past Alupka, where Vorontsov's palace stood, Spencer saw terraced vineyards on the slopes and, in the small valleys below, clustered Tatar cottages with their little mosques and slender minarets. It is a brief glimpse of Tatar villages surviving beside the new estates of Russian nobles.
p.q: the whole space between the towering cliffs and the sea, forming a splendid panorama, presented one mass of the richest foliage ; terraced vineyards adorned the hills, mingling their lighter green with the dark cold pine of the mountain; while the miniature valleys beneath glowed with the clustering cots of the Tartars, and their pretty little mosques and slender minarets.
p.s: Edmund Spencer
p.c: Seen from the steamer.
p.tg: crimea villages mosques minarets cottages

p.h: Khiva and Kokand: towns of mud
p.g: Drawing on Alexander Burnes and other authors, Wolff describes the capital of Khiva as a town of mud huts with three stone mosques and a mud palace, living largely by the slave trade, and says Kokand was likewise built of mud except for three stone bazaars.
p.q: The capital of Khiva is a town of mud huts, with three stone mosques, and a mud palace. Its chief trade is in slaves, of whom there are about forty thousand in the Khanat ; and it is said there are many captured Russians, who are slaves in Khiva. … It is, like Khiva, built of mud, with the exception of three stone bazaars.
p.s: Joseph Wolff, summarising Alexander Burnes and other writers
p.pe: Uzbek khanates of Khiva and Kokand
p.c: Second-hand; Wolff did not visit Khiva or Kokand on this journey.

p.h: Log houses with curtained windows
p.g: The houses of Kazan's Tatar town were small plain log cabins like Russian village houses, but inside they always had window curtains, behind which the women hid when anyone passed. On the next page Erman notes the many wooden jetties the Tatars built over Lake Kaban for their ritual washing before prayer.
p.q: The houses of the Tatar town are small and unadorned, like those of Russian villages, constructed of rough logs, without exterior planking. But in their internal arrangements they differ from the Russian cabins; they have, for example, always window curtains, behind which the women are careful to conceal themselves when any one passes by.
p.s: Adolph Erman (translated by W. D. Cooley, 1848)
p.tg: log houses timber women kazan

p.h: Lhasa's walls and gates, built by 'Ginges-Khang'
p.g: Desideri says Lhasa had anciently been an open town, and that 'Ginges-Khang' was the first to protect it with gates and fortifications, with a fort guarding each of the four approaches through the mountains. Ginges-Khang is Desideri's name for Lhazang Khan, the ruler killed by the Dzungars in 1717. The editor's footnote on the same page adds that these defences were built late in the 1600s and pulled down again in 1722 by order of the Kangxi emperor, with only some gates and fragments of wall surviving.
p.q: In ancient times, our missionary goes on to tell us, Lhasa was an open place, Ginges-Khang being the first to protect it at various points with gates and fortifications. Situated in a plain the town is enclosed by mountains so as to leave only four approaches each of them defended by a fortification.
p.s: C. Wessels (1924), paraphrasing Ippolito Desideri's manuscript
p.pe: Lhazang Khan ('Ginges-Khang'), the Qoshot Mongol ruler of Lhasa
p.c: Wessels's footnote insists Ginges-Khang is 'not the famous Mogul despot' (Genghis Khan) but a Tibetan king; modern historians identify him as Lhazang Khan of the Qoshot Mongols. Dating of the walls comes from Koeppen via the editor.
