p.g: The chronicle credits King Nyima Namgyal with building a long mani wall near Leh. Karl Marx's note adds that local people generally claimed the wall was built by the Mongols, and calls that belief an error. A small but telling case of a structure popularly credited to the Mongols that the written record gives to someone else.
p.q: It is generally asserted that it was built by the Mongols, which is an error.
p.s: Karl Marx (Moravian missionary), note to Francke's edition

p.h: Felt yurts that no wind can overturn
p.g: Crossing northern Mongolia with the Russian caravan, Lange describes how the Mongols live from their herds: hides for boots and harness, dung for fuel on the treeless steppe, sheepskins for coats, and sheep's wool for the felts that cover their yurts and beds. He finds the felt huts better than European tents: warm in winter, cool in summer with the side walls removed, proof against wind and rain.
p.q: Aus der Schafswolle machen sie die Filze oder Woilokken, womit ihre Jurten oder Hütten überzogen, und ihr Lager gemacht ist. Diese Filzhütten dienen ihnen wider die Kälte, und sind im Sommer, wenn man die Seitenwände abnimmt, viel schattiger und kühler als unsere Gezelte. Der Wind kann sie nie umwerfen, und kein Regen schlägt durch.
p.s: Lorenz Lange (journal of 1727 to 1728, translated and abridged by P. S. Pallas, 1781)
p.pl: Khalkha Mongolia (between Selenginsk and the Tola River)
p.t: From the sheep's wool they make the felts or voiloks with which their yurts or huts are covered and their beds made. These felt huts protect them against the cold, and in summer, when the side walls are taken off, are much shadier and cooler than our tents. The wind can never blow them over, and no rain comes through.
p.tg: yurts felt mongols dung fuel

p.h: Granite houses and beds heated from below
p.g: Gützlaff found Kin-chow small and plain. Its houses were built of the local granite, with few comforts apart from brick sleeping platforms warmed by a fire lit underneath (the kang). It is a precise, humble picture of domestic building on the edge of 'Tartary'.
p.q: Kin-chow itself has very little to attract the attention of visitors ; it is not a large or handsome place. The houses are built of granite ( which abounds here) ; and are without any accommodations, except a peculiar kind of sleeping places, which are formed of brick; and so constructed, that they can be heated, by fires kindled beneath them.
p.s: Karl Gützlaff (1832)
p.pe: Chinese and Manchu townspeople of Liaodong
p.tg: granite kang heated beds houses

p.h: Manchu country: 'none but houses of Earth'
p.g: From a Russian report, Avril describes the homeland of the Bogdoi, the Manchus who had conquered China. He says the houses there were all of earth, and that the people traded sables, black fox skins and ginseng, had few cattle and small unshod horses.
p.q: In all the Province of Bogdoi, you shall meet with none but houses of Earth … which people drive a great Trade in Sables and Black Fox-Skins, as likewise in Ginseng Roots : But they are not rich in Cattel ; their Horses are very small ; nor do their owners ever shooe 'em.
p.s: Philippe Avril (English translation, 1693)
p.c: Second-hand, from a relation Avril says came out of the Moscow treasury (archives).
p.tg: manchus earth houses furs ginseng

p.h: Nogai round huts of bulrushes, each with its hawk
p.g: Bruce says the Nogais around Astrakhan lived mostly in small round huts of bulrushes or canes with a smoke hole at the top, and that even the smallest had a hawk, since they were great falconers. On the next page he says they packed the huts onto carts in summer and moved with their herds.
p.q: The Nagayans live for the most part in round huts made of bull-rushes, or canes, and seldom exceed twelve or thirteen yards in circumference, with a hole at the top to let out the smoak ; yet the least of these huts has a falcon, or hawk, as those Tartars are great masters of this sport
p.s: Peter Henry Bruce (published 1782)
p.c: This description closely follows Adam Olearius's account of the 1630s and may be borrowed rather than observed.

p.h: A governor's cabinet of dug-up antiquities
p.g: At Krasnoyarsk the governor showed Holman his collection of 'Tartar' dresses, weapons and armour, along with objects dug up around the province: metal vases that Holman guessed once held the ashes of great chiefs, copper and stone hatchets, knives and arrowheads. These are the kind of finds that came from the kurgans (burial mounds) of the Yenisei and Minusinsk region.
p.q: The governor, on the Tuesday, most obligingly submitted to my inspection his cabinet of curiosities, comprising a large collection of Tartar dresses, weapons, and armour, as also many curious remains that had been dug up in different parts of his government; amongst the rest, metal vases, which had probably been the depositaries of the ashes of the great and powerful of their day
p.s: James Holman (1825)
p.pe: Unknown ancient peoples of the Yenisei region
p.c: The idea that the vases held ashes is Holman's guess. Compare Erman's report of Minusinsk kurgan bronzes (W011, T0014 n152).

p.h: Great monuments were Ming, not Tartar
p.g: Ellis repeats a remark that China's great national monuments and best works of art all date from the Ming dynasty, and adds his own jibe that the Tartar conquerors brought barbarism without their ancestors' energy. It is an opinion about who built China's monuments, not a survey.
p.q: It has been remarked that all the great national monuments were executed in the reign of the Ming dynasty; the best works of art of all kinds belong to the same period, so that the last Tartar conquerors of China would seem to have communicated the barbarism without the energy of their ancestors.
p.s: Henry Ellis
p.c: A prejudiced generalisation; the Qing built a great deal, including the palaces and temples at Chengde described by Barrow (W058).
p.tg: monuments ming qing builders

p.h: Birch-bark yurts gleaming white on the Sagai steppe
p.g: Staying some days with the Tatars by Lake Ilkul on the Sagai steppe, Sievers praises their fine horses and cattle, sold to merchants as far as Moscow, notes that traders always bring brandy because 'one bargains better with a drunk Tatar than a sober one', and says he saw no sign of religion. Their yurts, he writes, were clean and roomy and all built of birch bark, shining a dazzling white against the green meadows and hills.
p.q: Ihre Jurten sind reinlich, geräumig, und alle von Birkenrinde gebauet, die bey Sonnenschein eine blendende Weisse in … der Ferne von sich geben und aufs Angenehmste mit dem … Grün der Wiesen und Berge contrastiren.
p.s: Johann Sievers, letters from Siberia, in Neueste Nordische Beyträge vol. 7 (1796), edited by P. S. Pallas
p.t: Their yurts are clean, roomy, and all built of birch bark, which in sunshine give off a dazzling whiteness into the distance and contrast most pleasantly with the green of the meadows and hills.

p.h: Summer huts, winter log houses on the Baraba steppe
p.g: The Baraba people between the Irtysh and the Ob lived in villages of low wooden houses 'like those of the Siberian Tartars', heated by an open fire with a smoke-hole that was stopped once the wood burned down. In summer they moved into tall huts. They farmed oats, barley, millet and buckwheat and paid tribute in furs to both the tsar and the Kalmyk khan. Ides calls them insolent and villainous, a judgment coloured by frontier politics.
p.q: they live in low built wooden Houses, like those of the Siberian Tartars; they are not at all acquainted with the use of Stoves or Ovens … Their Houses are ranged into Villages; they set up high Hutts in the Summer, but in Winter retire into their warm wooden dwellings. They are very much addicted to Agriculture, and sow Oats, Barley, Millet, and Buck-wheat.
p.s: Evert Ysbrants Ides (English translation, 1706)
p.pe: Barabinsky (Baraba), whom Ides calls a sort of Kalmyks

p.h: Some Tartars in houses, others in tents

p.q: The Bogdoi, Yousbeck, and Bucharsky Tartars, more towards China, live in Houses, and continue Winter and Summer in the same place; but the Cullmick, and several Hordes of Western Tartars, who border more towards the C'zar's Dominions, live in Tents, and move Northward and Southward, according to the Seasons of the Year,

p.q: Sie kommen aus ihrem Lande, legen ihre Schiffe im Itil, welches ein großer Fluß ist, vor Anker und bauen sich an dessen Ufern große Häuser von Holz. In so einem Hause leben ihrer zehn oder zwanzig, auch mehr oder weniger, zusammen.

p.h: The khan's campaign tent, big enough for sixty
p.g: Before the winter campaign de Tott describes Tartar tents in detail: folding lattice walls, roof rods hooked to a ring, felt covering bound with a girth, and snow banked against the walls instead of posts or ropes. p.q: This covering is bound with a girth, and a few shovels full of snow, thrown up against the walls, prevents the external air from penetrating, and perfectly consolidates these tents, without either posts or cordage… The tent of the Kam was of this kind, but so large, that more than sixty persons might conveniently sit round the wood fire.

p.h: Old wells lined with pine and tile

He adds that Kalmyk and Tatar tradition credited such works to Janibeg Khan, who ruled from the Akhtuba and died in 1357.
p.q: Probably these wells were so called by the Calmucs, because they had been in former times boarded at the sides with pine by the Tartars, and the wood for the purpose might have been brought on the Volga from northern Russia, as it is at this day. Fragments of tiles are still to be found in the sand, and appear also to have been used in forming the wells.
p.s: Heinrich August Zwick (English edition, 1831)

p.h: Stone statues on the burial mounds
p.g: Along the Tashla Pallas saw the rough-hewn stone statues that stand on burial mounds across the steppe from the Kuban to the Dnieper, always facing east. p.q: If we may judge from the costume and form of the face, they uniformly appear to have been made by a people related to the Mongolians, who formerly inhabited those countries. … All these statues are erected on moderately large sepulchral hills, and their faces are exposed towards the East.

p.h: Round felt tents, some carried whole on carts
p.g: Carpini gives his own short description of Mongol dwellings: round, tent-shaped, built of slender rods, with a round window at the top for light and smoke, a central fire, and felt walls, roof and door. Some can be taken apart and loaded on pack animals; others travel whole on carts pulled by one ox or by several.
p.q: Leurs logemens sont ronds, en forme de tentes, & faits auec des verges & bastons fort deliez; & au dessus, droit au milieu, y a vne fenestre ronde, par où la lumiere entre, & la fumée sort; car ils font tousiours leur feu au milieu: les parois & toits de ces logis sont couuerts de feutres … Quelques-vnes sont fort aisées à deffaire & refaire
p.s: John of Plano Carpini (French translation by Pierre Bergeron, 1634)
p.t: Their dwellings are round, shaped like tents, and made with very slender rods and sticks; and on top, right in the middle, there is a round window through which the light comes in and the smoke goes out, for they always make their fire in the middle; the walls and roofs of these dwellings are covered with felts … Some are very easy to take down and put up again

p.h: Towers on the hills credited to Alexander
p.g: Cook describes Derbent's huge walls of natural shell-stone and then notes towers on the hills to the west. The inhabitants told him Alexander the Great built them and ran them all the way to the Black Sea to hold back the Dagestan Tartars. This echoes the old legend of Alexander's wall against Gog and Magog.
p.q: Upon the tops of the hills, west from Derbent, are to be seen some towers, which the inhabitants say were built by Alexander the Great; and that he continued these towers from Derbent west to the Black Sea, in order to curb the Dagestan Tartars.
p.s: John Cook (published 1770)
p.c: Local tradition; the Derbent walls are Sasanian Persian work of the 6th century, not Alexander's.

p.h: Stone statues left by Cumans and other Turks
p.g: Presenting drawings of inscribed stone columns near Abakan on the upper Yenisei, Klaproth notes that they closely resemble the stone statues scattered over the steppe north of the Caucasus. Those, he says, are the only monuments the Cumans and other Turkic peoples left behind there.
p.q: D'ailleurs, ces mêmes statues ressemblent beaucoup à celles qu'on voit assez fréquemment dans les vastes plaines situées au nord du Caucase, entre la mer Noire et la mer Caspienne, et qui sont les seuls monumens que les Comans et autres peuples turcs nous ont laissés de leur séjour dans ces contrées.
p.s: Julius Klaproth (paper read to the Asiatic Society, 2 December 1822)
p.pe: ancient Turkic peoples of South Siberia; Cumans of the steppe
p.t: Moreover, these same statues closely resemble those seen fairly often on the vast plains north of the Caucasus, between the Black Sea and the Caspian, which are the only monuments that the Cumans and other Turkic peoples have left us of their stay in those regions.
p.c: Klaproth worked from drawings made by others (Müller's artist Lursenius, Strahlenberg, Pallas), not from the stones themselves.

p.h: The wall between China and Tartary, 'which I saw and measured'
p.g: Pinto says a Chinese king, after wars with the Tartar, closed the whole border of the two empires with a wall, built in 27 years by 750,000 men over 315 leagues. He claims to have seen and measured it: six fathoms high and forty palms thick, with an earth rampart faced with mortar at its foot, and watchtowers of two storeys on black ironwood posts instead of towers.
p.q: Este muro vy eu algũas vezes, & o medy, que he por todo geralmente de seis braças dalto, & quarenta palmos de largo no mociço da parede, mas das quatro braças para baixo corre hum entulho a modo de terrapleno, alamborado da face de fora de hũ betume como argamassa
p.s: Fernão Mendes Pinto (Peregrinaçam, Lisbon 1614)
p.pe: Chinese builders; Tartars as the enemy
p.t: This wall I saw several times, and measured it, and it is generally throughout six fathoms high and forty palms wide in the thickness of the wall, but from four fathoms down there runs a fill like an earthen rampart, sloped on the outer face with a cement like mortar
p.c: Pinto's Tartar episodes are widely regarded as fictional or built from hearsay; treat as claimed travel. His 'Chinese chronicle' history of the wall is unreliable.

p.h: The word for a dwelling was 'yurt'
p.g: In the merchants' glossary the Latin word 'mansio' (dwelling, lodging) is given in Persian as 'manzel' and in Cuman as 'yurt'. Kuun adds that the word is widespread across the Turkic languages and compares the Mongol 'ger' (house). The steppe word for home and camp-place was the same word English later borrowed for the felt tent.
p.q: mansio manxel yurt … Vox late patens in dominio linguarum turcicae originis. Cf. mongolicum ger «domus», «habitatio»
p.s: Codex Cumanicus, Latin-Persian-Cuman glossary (Italian part, dated 11 July 1303), ed. Geza Kuun 1880, with Kuun's footnote
p.t: dwelling (Latin) / manzel (Persian) / yurt (Cuman) … A word widespread in the domain of the languages of Turkic origin. Compare Mongolian ger, 'house', 'dwelling'.
p.c: A glossary entry, not a description; 'yurt' in Cuman meant a dwelling place or homeland rather than specifically a felt tent.

p.h: Walls rebuilt after the Tartar fire, a Kremlin by Italians
p.g: Possevino classifies Muscovite fortresses: some of stone and brick, some of earth banks woven with wicker and rammed hard, some of squared timbers filled with earth. Moscow's outer wall of the wattle and earth kind was put up after 'the Tartar fire', while the two stone citadels of Moscow were built for Ivan's father Vasily by a Milanese architect with Italian workmen. Here the Tartars burn, and Italians build.
p.q: Aliæ ex saxis, et lateribus, quales duæ sunt, quæ ciuitati Moscuæ hærent … Aliæ aggeribus vimine contextis, & ad duritiem pressis: quale Smolencium est, ipsiusq; Moscuæ mœnium ambitus, post Tartaricum incendium excitatus. … Arces autem Moscuæ duas Principis huius parens Basilius ædificari iussit, Mediolanense architecto, Italis operarijs.
p.s: Antonio Possevino, S.J. (Moscovia, Vilnius 1586)
p.t: Some are of stones and bricks, like the two that adjoin the city of Moscow ... Others are of earth banks woven with wicker and pressed hard: such is Smolensk, and the circuit of the walls of Moscow itself, raised after the Tartar fire. ... The two citadels of Moscow were ordered built by this prince's father Vasily, with a Milanese architect and Italian workmen.
p.c: The attribution of the Kremlin works to Italian masters is broadly right, though Possevino compresses the history (much was done under Ivan III as well as Vasily III).

p.h: Tents woven from yak hair
p.g: On the high plain beyond Phari and the Tongla mountain, Turner saw herds of yaks and 'Tartar tents' made entirely from the animals: the tent cloth woven from yak hair, and the guy ropes spun from it too. These are the black tents of Tibetan herders, quite different from the round felt yurts of the Mongols.
p.q: On its skirts were large herds of the bushy-tailed cattle, grazing; and we saw some Tartar tents, formed from the hair of these cattle, woven into cloth; the ropes also which fastened them to iron pins driven into the ground, were spun from the same materials.
p.s: Samuel Turner (1800)

p.h: The Great Wall measured: earth, brick and blue bricks that were really burned
p.g: Using Captain Parish's survey for Macartney's embassy, Davis gives the wall's make-up: an earthen core faced on both sides with masonry and brick, a platform of square bricks, 20 feet high including the parapet, 25 feet thick at the base. The bricks are bluish, which made people doubt they were fired, until old kilns were found and Dr Abel showed in 1816 that Chinese clay burns blue. The wall, he says, was a useful barrier until Chinggis Khan overran it.
p.q: The body of the wall consists of an earthen mound, retained on each side by walls of masonry and brick, and terraced by a platform of square bricks. The total height, including a parapet of five feet, is twenty feet, on a basis of stone projecting two feet under the brick-work,
p.s: John Francis Davis, summarising Captain Parish's survey (Macartney embassy)
p.pe: Chinese builders (the wall as a barrier against the Tartars)

p.h: Jurten: tents that pack up and move
p.g: Around Nerchinsk the mounted Tungus lived in portable huts they called jurten (yurts): a frame of jointed wooden poles that could be packed and carried whenever they moved, covered with hair and other material, with a smoke-hole at the top and the fire in the middle. Ides says religion was much alike 'throughout all great Tartary' up to the Mongols.
p.q: They all live in Hutts, called in their Language Jurten, the inside of which is composed of wooden Poles jointed together, that whenever they are willing to remove their Dwellings, as they frequently do, they may conveniently pack and carry them altogether. This wooden work when set up is thatched all over with Hair and Rubbish, except only the Smoak-hole left open at the top.
p.s: Evert Ysbrants Ides (English translation, 1706)
p.tg: yurt jurten portable tents

p.h: Village houses built into the hillside
p.g: On the south coast, below the Baidar pass, Alexander found houses unlike any he had seen: roofs carried on low stone walls on three sides, with the fourth side set against the slope like Swiss chalets, among fruit trees and poplars. The villagers wore the same Tatar dress as before, but he thought their features Grecian and both men and women very handsome.
p.q: The houses, as well as their inhabitants, were now totally different from what we had hitherto seen : the roofs were supported on three sides by low stone walls, and the fourth rested against the side of the declivity (after the manner of Swiss chalets) … but their features were Grecian, and both men and women were extremely handsome.
p.s: James Edward Alexander (1830)
p.pe: Crimean Tatars of the south coast

p.h: Hazara villages guarded by loop-holed towers
p.g: Most Hazaras live in villages, not tents, though some use 'Tartar tents' like the Aimaqs. Each village has a defensive tower with a kettle-drum to sound the alarm. On the page before, Elphinstone says their houses are thatched and half sunk into the hillsides.
p.q: The Hazaurehs generally live in villages of from twenty to two hundred houses, though some live in Tartar tents like the Eimauks. Each village is defended by a high tower, capable of containing ten or twelve men, and full of loop-holes.
p.s: Mountstuart Elphinstone (1815)

p.h: Doors to the east, men south, women north
p.g: Inside a Yakut winter hut the door always faced east, the fireplace stood near the middle with room to walk around it, and benches and small sleeping cabins lined the walls. Men sat on the south side and women on the north. A hut where someone had died was abandoned to ruin as a home of demons.
p.q: They always take care that the doors of their huts shall face the east. The fire-place is nearly in the middle; the back of the chimney towards the door, and a free passage quite round it. The sides of the hut are furnished with benches and small cabins, which serve for sleeping places. … The men keep the south side, and the women the north.
p.s: Martin Sauer (1802)

p.h: Grave mounds and brick foundations on the steppe
p.g: Crossing the steppe, Zwick stopped at kurgans, the grave mounds Russians call by that name. He thinks they come from many ages and peoples, but credits most of them to the Tartars of the medieval Volga empire whose ruined cities he names, and on the next page notes two mounds holding the remains of a square brick building.
p.q: Such tumuli are every where to be found on the steppes, and most plentifully on the willowy shores of the Volga … They probably belong to different ages, and different races of men, but the majority are undoubtedly to be ascribed to the Tartars … I saw a great number of these hillocks, near the ruins of their principal cities Serag and Tschigis.
p.s: Heinrich August Zwick (English edition, 1831)
p.pe: Golden Horde Tatars (as Zwick supposes), and older peoples
p.c: The dating and attribution of the mounds are Zwick's guesses; the omitted words name the empire in a garbled form ('Eamschatkan' in the OCR, apparently for Kipchak).

p.h: A brick tower among the Turkmen pastures
p.g: Riding through Goklen Turkmen pastures, Fraser reached the Gonbad-e Kavus, a hollow brick tower on a mound that he guessed at 150 feet high. He admired its fired bricks and lime mortar, and judged it to be of early Islamic ('Arabic') origin, though he could not read its inscription. The nomads grazing around it were not credited with building it.
p.q: It has been built of the finest fire-baked bricks, large, square, and about two inches and a half thick, with which also, placed flat, the roof has been covered ; and so well have they stood, that not above one or two of the whole have been yet displaced. The whole is cemented with lime, and of the most excellent masonry
p.s: James Baillie Fraser
p.pe: Goklen Turkmens (camped around it); builders unknown to Fraser
p.c: Fraser could not read the date. The tower is now known to be the tomb of the Ziyarid ruler Qabus, built around 1006 to 1007.

p.h: Turkmen tents like those of the Georgian Tartars
p.g: On the Caspian coast Muraviev compared Turkmen dwellings to those of the 'Tartars in Georgia' (Turkic-speaking Muslims of the Caucasus): reed mats on long poles covered with felt. He also notes that Turkmen women did not hide from strangers and wore very tall headdresses edged with gold or silver.
p.q: The dwelling-places of the Turcomans are constructed like those of the Tartars in Georgia, that is to say, they consist of rush mats stretched on long poles, the whole being covered with felt. Their women are not kept in privacy
p.s: Nikolai Muraviev (translated by W. S. A. Lockhart, 1871)

p.h: They spared the houses to winter in them
p.g: Roger watched Tartar and Cuman raiders return from a night of slaughter in the villages, loaded with spoil. Yet they burned neither grain, straw nor houses. He guessed, and later confirmed, that they meant to winter there and needed shelter and food for their horses. It is a telling detail: these herders used the settled country's buildings rather than destroying them.
p.q: Verumtamen nec fruges nec stramina nec domos aliquas combusserunt, sed in praeseruationem vitae omnia haec induxerunt. Pro eo conieci firmiter ipsos velle in illis partibus hiemare, vel familias suas dimittere, ut in hieme pro equis domos et victualia inuenirent. Quod totum postmodum didici esse verum.
p.s: Master Roger (Rogerius), Carmen miserabile, in the 1885 Budapest edition (Chronica minora)
p.pe: Tartars and Cumans of Batu's army
p.t: Yet they burned neither the crops, nor the straw, nor any houses, but brought all these in to keep themselves alive. From this I firmly concluded that they meant to winter in those parts, or leave their families there, so that in winter they would find shelter and provisions for their horses. All of which I afterwards learned to be true.

p.t: and they would raise a pavilion from Khitai whose walls were made of latticed wood … and it is called Sir[a] Ordu.

p.h: A king's palace amid Tatar tents at Dam
p.g: Describing the northern province of Chang, della Penna says that at Dam, the summer seat of the Tatar king of Tibet, there was nothing but the king's palace; everyone else, mostly Tatars and some Tibetans, lived in tents of felt and of cloth woven from hair. Beyond that, at Nakchu, there was a last fortress and again only tents.
p.q: in Dam there is nothing else but the palace belonging to the King and his court, the remainder of the inhabitants (which are mostly Tatars and the other Tibetans) dwelling in tents of felt and of cloth woven out of hair. Two days distant from Dam is Nak chu ka, where is the last fortress of Tibet, but no other dwellings except tents
p.s: Francesco Orazio della Penna, Capuchin missionary (English version in Markham's appendix, from Klaproth's edition)

p.h: Kungur's Tatar caves, now ice-cellars
p.g: On his way home Cochrane stopped at Kungur, a town of 1,100 houses. Before it became a provincial capital, he says, it was a favourite place of the Tartars, and the caves where they lived were still shown to visitors, now used as ice-cellars and storehouses.
p.q: Formerly it was the capital of a province, and previous to that period, a favourite place of the Tartars. The caves where they resided, are still shewn in the light of useful curiosities, inasmuch as they are converted into ice-cellars, and storehouses.
p.s: John Dundas Cochrane (1824)
p.c: Local tradition. Kungur is famous for its natural ice cave; the idea that Tatars lived in it is folklore, not evidence of Tatar cave cities.

p.h: Kurgans built by others, dug up by everyone
p.g: Describing the Crimean gold in the Hermitage, Kohl credits the southern burial mounds to the Greeks of Taurida and older peoples of the Caucasus and Siberia. The Tartars appear not as builders but as one of many later peoples, with Goths, Huns and Cossacks, who dug into the kurgans and melted down the treasure.
p.q: the countless graves of the Greeks of Taurus, and of the original inhabitants of the Caucasus and Siberia, have been objects of zealous research … the Tartars and the Cossacks of the present day, have plundered them, and melted down the treasures found therein. The greater part of the kurgans and mohilos of South Russia, have been long since burrowed like rabbit-warrens
p.s: J. G. Kohl (English abridged translation, 1844)
p.pe: Tatars among later plunderers of ancient graves
p.c: The list of plunderers ('Alarics' and a garbled name, probably Huns) is rhetorical.

p.h: Houses of stone below and sun-dried brick above
p.g: Gerard describes the flat-roofed, two-storey houses of Spiti: stone on the ground floor and unburnt (sun-dried) brick on the upper floor, which he hears is the rule across Ladakh too. In a footnote elsewhere he explains that the climate is so dry that such brick houses last as well as stone. Firewood is so scarce it is brought by yak and stacked on the roofs.
p.q: The lower half of the houses here, and I have heard, throughout most part of Ludak, is built of stone, and the upper of unburnt bricks : they are two stories high, and flat roofed.
p.s: Alexander Gerard (ed. George Lloyd, 1841)

p.h: A Lhasa monastery 'reserved for the Tartars'
p.g: In his tour of Lhasa's temples Desideri notes three more Gelugpa temples and monasteries, one of them in the north-eastern quarter 'reserved for the Tartars', that is for Mongol monks who came to study in Tibet. Elsewhere he says the great monastic universities drew students from Ladakh, Tartary and China. The editor could find no later confirmation that this house was specially for Tartars.
p.q: "There are at Lhasa", the narrator continues, "three other idolatrous temples and monasteries of the same sect [the Gelugpa or Yellow-caps]. One is situated in the north-eastern quarter and is reserved for the Tartars. The other two lie towards the east, one near the town-limit, the other just on it, both called by the same name Ramo-cce."
p.s: Ippolito Desideri, in C. Wessels's English translation (1924); bracketed words are Wessels's
p.c: 'Idolatrous' is the missionary's own religious judgement. Wessels identifies the house tentatively with the Muru monastery and notes that later writers do not mention its being for Tartars.

p.h: A Lama's tomb with 'Chinese, or Tartar' decoration
p.g: Turner describes the mausoleum of the previous Panchen Lama at Tashilhunpo. He sorts its style carefully: Indian-looking pillars and arches inside, Chinese or 'Tartar' decoration outside (the tented canopy and imperial dragon), and a plain but solid stone building with cement. p.q: the external decorations are of Chinese, or Tartar origin, similar to those of the watch tower, or temple of the former; the tented canopy and imperial dragon. As far as the mason has been concerned … a plain substantial building of stone, with cement.
p.s: Samuel Turner (1800)

p.h: Kurgans: graves or ash heaps from Tartar tents?
p.g: Crossing the steppe she notes many conical mounds (kurgans) like those on the plain of Troy. She reports a view that they are heaps of ash from Tartar camps and adds her own twist: that the Tartars buried their dead beneath the ash to make cheap monuments. On the next page she suggests this is the origin of mound burial across Europe.
p.q: Some people contend that they are not tombs, but hillocks formed by the ashes thrown out of the Tartar tents while encamped on the spot; which is a fact, and a very wise measure too, as, by making the graves of their companions the bases of these conic hillocks, they prevent putrid exhalations, while they raise a rude monument to departed friends without either trouble or expence
p.s: Maria Guthrie (letter, translated by Matthew Guthrie, 1802)
p.c: A speculation presented as fact; most steppe kurgans are ancient burial mounds far older than the Tatars.
p.tg: kurgans tumuli burial theory

p.h: The khan's palace: 'painted Chinese structure'
p.g: Like Baron de Tott thirty years earlier, Maria Guthrie reaches for 'Chinese' to describe the painted palace of the khans. She says its interior is a maze (a 'Scythian labyrinth') with separate women's quarters, and on the next page describes the court mosque whose slender minaret sways under the climber.
p.q: The palace, which, as said before, rises in the middle of this curious Tauric city, to add greatly to the singularity and romantic appearance of the scene, is a curious species of painted Chinese structure, well suited to such a group of oddities.
p.s: Maria Guthrie (letter, translated by Matthew Guthrie, 1802)
p.c: She admits she lacks the vocabulary of 'oriental architecture'; 'Chinese' is an impression, not a statement about builders.

p.h: 'They have no town': low log houses and summer tents
p.g: An anonymous description of the Kalmyks printed by Weber says the Baraba people, whom it calls a kind of Kalmyk paying tribute both to the tsar and to the Zunghar khan, live like the Siberian Tatars in low wooden houses built close to the ground, with a smoke hole closed once the fire burns down. They have no town or fixed dwelling: in summer light huts and tents, in winter their warm wooden houses. It adds that they grow oats, barley and buckwheat but spit out rye bread.
p.q: Sonsten ist diese Nation ein böses und streitbar Volk, wohnet wie die Siberischen Tartarn in hölzernen Häusern, welche ganz niedrig auf die Erde gezimmert … Sie haben keine Stadt noch andere beständige Wohnung, sondern wohnen des Sommers in leicht aufgeschlagenen Hütten und Gezelten, die sie gar hurtig wissen abzubrechen und aufzuschlagen. Des Winters aber ziehen sie in ihre warme hölzerne Wohnungen.
p.s: Anonymous description of the Kalmyks, printed in Weber
p.pe: Baraba people (described as a kind of Kalmyk) and Siberian Tatars
p.t: Otherwise this nation is a wicked and warlike people, and lives like the Siberian Tartars in wooden houses built quite low on the ground … They have no town or other fixed dwelling, but live in summer in lightly pitched huts and tents, which they know how to strike and set up very quickly. In winter, however, they move into their warm wooden dwellings.

p.h: Black sarcophagi with white turbans
p.g: Two domed mausoleums beside the palace held the remains of a long line of khans. Inside, Alexander was startled to find black sarcophagi on the floor with white turbans at their heads; outside, the graves had carved marble headstones topped with turbans, shaded by cypresses.
p.q: a burial ground attached, contained the remains of a long line of khans : on entering the former it was rather startling to see black sarcophagi on the floor, with white turbans at the head. In the open air the tombs were adorned with carved and turbaned headstones of marble, which, with the accompanying cypress, give such effect to Moslem cemeteries.
p.s: James Edward Alexander (1830)

p.h: No towns outside the peninsula
p.g: Chevalier says Lesser Tartary stretched far beyond the Crimean peninsula across the steppe as far as the Don, but that outside the peninsula there were no towns or villages at all. The Tartars simply moved their camps to wherever the grazing was good; the next page says they used huts and 'travelling sheds' only in winter.
p.q: There are no Towns nor yet Villages, but in the Chersonesus, the rest being only incultivated Plains, yet of themselves very fruitful, and the Tartars encamp up and down in them as they find more or less forrage
p.s: Pierre Chevalier (translated by Edward Brown, 1672)

p.h: Gher, ourto and ordo: words for Mongol dwellings
p.g: In a footnote Timkovsky explains the vocabulary: the felt tent the Russians call a jourta or kibitka is a gher in Mongol; a cluster of tents forming a village or station is an ourto; oulous means empire or people; and ordo (the root of 'horde') means a chateau or imperial palace. It is a neat reminder that the famous Tartar 'horde' was originally the ruler's camp-palace.
p.q: Such a tent (made of felt,) … is in Mongol called gher; several tents together, forming a kind of village or station, are called ourto. Oulous, or olos, signifies in Mongol, empire, people; ordo, a chateau, or imperial palace.
p.s: George Timkowski (English translation, 1827)

p.h: An octagonal stone tomb with a Tatar inscription
p.g: Near the rivulet Jaman-Kul, Klaproth describes the oldest monument of Little Kabarda: an octagon of hewn stone about twelve feet high with an arched door, windows and a collapsed vault, ringed by about a hundred earth mounds. Its Tatar inscription names 'Ckoban-Chan son of Berdi-beg' and the Islamic year 860 (1455).
p.q: It is an edifice of hewn stone, and round it are about a hundred hillocks of earth called Bugri… The building is an octagon, each of its sides measuring six feet… On the stone inserted over the door is engraved a Tartar inscription in three lines, of which only these words ‘Ckoban-Chan son of Berdi-beg, in the year 860’ (A. D. 1455) are legible.
p.s: Julius Klaproth (English translation, 1814)
p.tg: mausoleum hewn stone inscription octagon

p.h: At Merv, only the burnt brick survived
p.g: Fraser doubts the tales of marble palaces at Merv. His informants said the main surviving ruins were a mosque and college credited to Timur, the tomb of the Seljuk sultan Sanjar and an arsenal, which lasted because they were built of fired brick.
p.q: there are no ruins to prove the existence of the marble palaces, and baths, and tombs, which have been vaguely attributed to it ; the chief remains are those of a fine large mosque, with a medressa, built by Timoor Shah ; of the mausoleum of Sooltaun Sanjer, and of a fine arsenal, all of which having been constructed of burnt brick, have partly escaped
p.s: James Baillie Fraser
p.pe: Former Seljuk and Timurid rulers; Merv then under Bukhara
p.c: From informants. On the same page a footnote doubts the huge death tolls given for the Mongol sack of Merv.
p.tg: merv ruins burnt brick sanjar timur

p.h: A Buddhist temple of stuccoed brick on the Volga
p.g: At Prince Tumene's island seat, Adèle attended a service in the Kalmyk 'pagoda'. She describes the din of drums, gongs, conch shells and three-metre trumpets, and the building itself: large windows, slender columns of stuccoed brick, a domed gallery and walls hung with painted tapestries of spirits and monsters. This was a settled Kalmyk prince's temple, not a tent.
p.q: The temple, lighted by a row of large windows, is adorned with slender columns of stuccoed brick work, the lightness of which reminds one of the graceful Moorish architecture. A gallery runs all round the dome, which is also remarkable for the extreme delicacy of its workmanship.
p.s: Adèle Hommaire de Hell (English translation, 1847)

p.h: Balkh: stone and brick houses and a marble castle of the Uzbek khan
p.g: Describing the Uzbek khanate of Balkh, Deguignes calls Balkh the most important town held by the 'Mahometan Tartars': large and populous, mostly built of stone or brick, with earth ramparts faced by a wall, a trading hub between Bukhara and India, and a khan's castle 'in the oriental style' built almost entirely of marble from nearby quarries. He also calls Balkh's Uzbeks the most civilised of the Muslim Tartars.
p.q: La ville de Balkh, à présent la plus considérable de toutes les villes que les Tartares Mahométans possedent, est grande & bien peuplée, la plupart de ses bâtimens sont bâtis de pierre ou de brique … Le château du Khan est un grand bâtiment à l'orientale, presque tout bâti de marbre dont on trouve des carrières fort belles dans les montagnes voisines.
p.s: Joseph de Guignes
p.t: The town of Balkh, at present the most considerable of all the towns the Mahometan Tartars possess, is large and well peopled; most of its buildings are built of stone or brick … The Khan's castle is a large building in the oriental style, almost entirely built of marble, of which there are very fine quarries in the neighbouring mountains.
p.c: Deguignes never saw Balkh; the description is borrowed from earlier compilations and is not dated precisely.
p.tg: balkh uzbeks stone brick marble

p.h: 'Vagabond Tartars' with huts by the rivers
p.g: Bruce reports what an envoy sent by Peter the Great to the 'northern Tartar princes' found on a journey toward the Lena. He said they were all wandering Tartars in tents, rich only in cattle, but that along the rivers there were some houses or huts and a little corn, where their khans usually lived. The prince of the Yakuts turned him back.
p.q: He reported, that they were all vagabond Tartars, living in tents, and shifting their residence from place to place for pasturage, as all their riches consisted in herds of cattle ; but he observed a sort of houses, or huts, on the sides of rivers, and some corn, and in these situations their chams generally resided.
p.s: Peter Henry Bruce, reporting the czar's envoy (published 1782)
p.c: Second-hand; the envoy is not named and the peoples are not identified beyond the Yakuts.
p.tg: siberia tents huts yakuts exploration

p.h: Birch-bark summer yurts and earth-covered winter huts
p.g: East of Tomsk, Pallas describes the dwellings of baptised Tatars: summer yurts of poles or bent birch rods shaped like a Kalmyk tent but covered with boiled and stitched white birch bark, and winter huts of thin birch logs shaped like a box, heaped with earth for warmth, with a clay-and-brushwood fireplace and a square smoke hole.
p.q: Die hiesigen getauften Tataren wohnen im Sommer in elenden Jurten, die theils aus spitz zusammen gestüzten Stangen, theils aus Birkenstäben die von der Erde herauf um einige grosse Reife befestigt und gebrochen, die Gestalt eines Calmückischen Zeltes vorstellen, und mit stark gekochten und zusammen genehten weissen Birkenrinden gedeckt werden, bestehen.
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (Reise, first edition, St Petersburg 1771-1776)
p.pe: Baptised Siberian Tatars of the Krasnoyarsk district
p.t: The baptised Tatars here live in summer in wretched yurts made partly of poles leaned together to a point, partly of birch rods fixed and bent from the ground up around some large hoops, which take the shape of a Kalmyk tent and are covered with strongly boiled, sewn-together white birch bark.

p.h: Bronze star instruments from the Tartar era
p.g: On a hill at Nanjing, Ricci inspected huge bronze astronomical instruments: armillary spheres, a globe, a gnomon on a great marble base. He later saw identical ones at Peking and concluded they came from the same caster, made when the Tartars ruled China. Because they were so well made, he guessed a foreigner trained in European sciences had built them. They were set for the wrong latitude at Nanjing, which he took as a sign they had been moved.
p.q: Spectavit etiam P. Matthaeus post annos aliquot similes Pechini machinas, aut easdem potius, ita nihil aliae ab aliis discrepabant, nihil ut dubium videatur, ab eodem fusas artifice: & quidem eo tempore fusas constat, quo Tartari Sinis imperitabant. unde non temere coniectare possumus, eas ab aliquo externo perito disciplinarum nostrarum fuisse conflatas.
p.s: Matteo Ricci, edited and translated into Latin by Nicolas Trigault (1615)
p.t: Some years later Father Matteo saw similar instruments at Peking, or rather the same, so little did they differ from one another, so that there seems no doubt they were cast by the same craftsman; and it is certain they were cast at the time when the Tartars ruled the Chinese. From this we may reasonably guess that they were made by some foreigner skilled in our sciences.
p.c: Ricci's guess about a foreign maker is doubtful: historians usually credit the designs to the Yuan astronomer Guo Shoujing, and the Peking set he saw was a Ming copy of the Yuan originals.

p.h: Felt tents pitched beside a domed tomb
p.g: Crossing the mountains west of Kashgar in deep winter, Izzet Ullah notes Kirghiz felt tents lining the road (p. 321). At the stage called Mizar Gumbaz he found a domed building with Kirghiz tombs and the living Kirghiz camped in tents beside it: permanent structures for the dead, portable ones for the living.
p.q: Mizar Gumbuz, … west by north, eight hours. A building with a cupola and Kirghiz tombs; their tents were also pitched near the building; supplies plentiful;
p.s: Mir Izzet Ullah (translated by H. H. Wilson)
p.pl: Tian Shan, between Kashgar and Osh

p.h: Vogul log rooms with an ice skylight, retold
p.g: The chapter on the 'Siberian Tartars' called Voguls repeats, almost word for word, Adam Brand's description of their houses, with one change: the compiler says they are square wooden rooms like those of Russian peasants rather than 'Tartar houses'. The smoke hole is still sealed with a lid of ice that lets in daylight.
p.q: Ihre Wohnungen sind viereckigte hölzerne Kammern, wie die Russischen Bauren haben. An statt des Ofens haben sie Camin oder Feuer-Herd, worauf sie Holz brennen und darbei ihre Speise kochen. Das Rauch-Loch, so oben im Tach ist, wird, so bald das … zu Kohlen gebrennet ist, mit einem Deckel von Eiß
p.s: Anonymous compiler (Der allerneueste Staat von Siberien, Nuremberg 1720)
p.t: Their dwellings are square wooden rooms such as the Russian peasants have. Instead of a stove they have a fireplace or hearth, on which they burn wood and cook their food. The smoke hole at the top of the roof, as soon as the [wood] has burned to coals, [is covered] with a lid of ice
p.c: Copied from Adam Brand's journal (1698; see W274), with small changes.
p.tg: houses ice window voguls copying
